questions.question_text: Which one of the following is a powerful electrophile used to attack on the electrons of benzene ring?
questions.explanation_short: Cl+ (a positively charged chlorine electrophile) is the powerful electrophile that attacks benzene's electron-rich ring in electrophilic aromatic substitution.
questions.explanation_long: Benzene's ring has a delocalized pi-electron cloud that attracts electron-deficient (electrophilic) species. In chlorination reactions, a Lewis acid catalyst helps generate Cl+ from Cl2, and this positively charged chlorine species is what actually attacks the ring.
questions.explanation_trick: Electrophilic aromatic substitution needs a positively-charged attacking species — here, Cl+.

explanation_options.a: FeCl2 is not typically the active catalyst form; it lacks the correct oxidation state used in this reaction.
explanation_options.b: FeCl4– is a negatively charged byproduct ion, not the electrophile attacking the ring.
explanation_options.c: Correct — Cl+ is the actual electrophilic species generated to attack benzene's ring.
explanation_options.d: Cl2 itself is not electrophilic enough on its own to directly attack benzene without first being activated to Cl+.

aliases: Which one of the following is a powerful electrophile used to attack on the electrons of benzene ring?
FeCl2

questions.question_text: Order of reactivity of alkenes with hydrogen halide is:
questions.explanation_short: Reactivity of alkenes with hydrogen halides increases as the H-X bond gets weaker, following the order HI > HBr > HCl (HF is least reactive, contrary to intuition based on H-F polarity alone).
questions.explanation_long: Even though HF has the most polar bond, its H-X bond strength is very high, making it least reactive in electrophilic addition. Bond strength decreases down the group (HF > HCl > HBr > HI), so reactivity — which depends on how easily H-X breaks — increases in the opposite order: HI > HBr > HCl > HF.
questions.explanation_trick: Reactivity with alkenes: weaker H-X bond = faster reaction. Order: HI > HBr > HCl > HF.

explanation_options.a: This places HBr ahead of HI, reversing the correct reactivity order.
explanation_options.b: This omits HCl entirely and doesn't represent the full standard reactivity order.
explanation_options.c: HF is actually the least reactive of the four, not more reactive than HI as this option suggests.
explanation_options.d: Correct — HI > HBr > HCl matches the established order of alkene-hydrogen halide reactivity.

questions.question_text: The given three hydrocarbons (benzene, naphthalene and anthracene) are:
questions.explanation_short: Benzene, naphthalene and anthracene are aromatic hydrocarbons — one, two and three fused benzene rings.
questions.explanation_long: All three are made only of carbon and hydrogen and contain delocalised π-electron ring systems obeying Hückel's rule, which makes them aromatic. Naphthalene and anthracene are polycyclic (fused-ring) aromatics.
questions.explanation_trick: Benzene rings → aromatic.

explanation_options.a: Alicyclic compounds have rings without aromatic delocalisation (e.g. cyclohexane).
explanation_options.b: Correct — all three are aromatic hydrocarbons.
explanation_options.c: Acyclic means open-chain, with no rings at all.
explanation_options.d: Heterocyclic rings contain atoms other than carbon, such as N, O or S.

aliases: The given three hydrocarbons are Benzene Naphthalene Anthracene
Alicyclic hydrocarbons

questions.question_text: The compound (CH₃)₂CH–CH₂–Cl is commonly called isobutyl chloride. What is its correct IUPAC name?
questions.explanation_short: The IUPAC name for isobutyl chloride, (CH3)2CH-CH2-Cl, is 1-chloro-2-methylpropane — naming the longest chain from the end nearest the chlorine substituent.
questions.explanation_long: The longest carbon chain is propane (3 carbons), with a methyl branch at carbon 2 and chlorine at carbon 1. Numbering from the end giving the lowest locants, the correct IUPAC name is 1-chloro-2-methylpropane.
questions.explanation_trick: Isobutyl = 2-methylpropyl group. Attach "chloro" at position 1: 1-chloro-2-methylpropane.

explanation_options.a: Correct — 1-chloro-2-methylpropane is the proper IUPAC name for isobutyl chloride.
explanation_options.b: This name incorrectly implies a 4-carbon main chain (butane) rather than the correct 3-carbon propane chain.
explanation_options.c: "Isobutyl chloride" is the common (trivial) name, not the systematic IUPAC name being asked for.
explanation_options.d: This name misplaces the substituent positions relative to the actual structure.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following was used as one of the earliest antiseptic and disinfectant?
questions.explanation_short: Phenol was one of the earliest antiseptics and disinfectants, famously used by Joseph Lister in early antiseptic surgery.
questions.explanation_long: Phenol (carbolic acid) has documented historical use as one of the first chemical antiseptics, pioneered by Joseph Lister in the 1800s to reduce surgical infections by killing bacteria on surfaces and wounds.
questions.explanation_trick: Phenol = carbolic acid = Lister's pioneering antiseptic.

explanation_options.a: Correct — phenol (carbolic acid) is historically recognized as one of the earliest antiseptics/disinfectants.
explanation_options.b: Ether is primarily known historically as an anesthetic, not an antiseptic.
explanation_options.c: Ethanol is also an antiseptic but not the one specifically noted as one of the earliest historically.
explanation_options.d: Methanol is toxic and not used as an antiseptic.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following is NOT able to denature the ethanol?
questions.explanation_short: Ethanol is denatured with poisonous or foul-tasting additives such as methanol, pyridine and acetone — lactic acid is not one of them.
questions.explanation_long: Methylated spirit is made undrinkable by adding methanol, pyridine, acetone and dyes. Lactic acid is a harmless food acid and cannot denature ethanol.
questions.explanation_trick: Denaturants are toxic or foul — lactic acid is neither.

explanation_options.a: Methanol is the classic toxic denaturant.
explanation_options.b: Correct — lactic acid is not used to denature ethanol.
explanation_options.c: Pyridine is added for its foul smell and taste.
explanation_options.d: Acetone is used as a denaturant.

questions.question_text: HO⁻ attacks a carbon bearing Br in a single concerted step (backside attack, SN2 mechanism) as Br⁻ leaves. What is the configuration of the product relative to the reactant?
questions.option_a: 100% same of the configuration of reactant
questions.explanation_short: SN2 backside attack causes complete inversion of configuration (like an umbrella flipping inside out) — 100% opposite from the reactant's original configuration.
questions.explanation_long: In an SN2 mechanism, the nucleophile (HO⁻) attacks from the side directly opposite the leaving group (Br⁻) in a single concerted step. This backside attack forces the molecule's configuration to invert completely, producing a product with 100% inverted (opposite) stereochemistry — known as Walden inversion.
questions.explanation_trick: SN2 = backside attack = complete (100%) inversion, like an umbrella flipping in the wind.

explanation_options.a: 100% same configuration (retention) is the outcome of an SN1 mechanism with front-side attack, not SN2's backside attack.
explanation_options.b: A partial (50%) retention also suggests racemization, inconsistent with a single concerted SN2 step.
explanation_options.c: A partial (50%) inversion suggests some racemization, which happens in SN1, not the clean single-step SN2 mechanism described.
explanation_options.d: Correct — a concerted SN2 backside attack always gives 100% inversion of configuration.

questions.question_text: How will you distinguish between methanol and ethanol?
questions.explanation_short: Methanol and ethanol are distinguished by the iodoform test, since ethanol (having a CH3-CH(OH)- structure) gives a positive iodoform test while methanol does not.
questions.explanation_long: The iodoform test detects compounds with a CH3-CH(OH)- or CH3-CO- group. Ethanol has this structural feature and produces a yellow iodoform precipitate, while methanol lacks it and gives a negative result — making this test a reliable way to distinguish the two.
questions.explanation_trick: Iodoform test positive = has a CH3-CH(OH)- group. Ethanol passes, methanol doesn't.

explanation_options.a: The Lucas test distinguishes classes of alcohols (primary/secondary/tertiary) generally, not specifically methanol from ethanol.
explanation_options.b: The silver mirror (Tollens') test is for aldehydes, not for directly distinguishing these two alcohols.
explanation_options.c: Simple oxidation of both would give different products (formaldehyde/formic acid vs. acetaldehyde/acetic acid) but isn't the standard distinguishing test referenced here.
explanation_options.d: Correct — the iodoform test gives a positive result for ethanol but not methanol, distinguishing the two.

questions.question_text: To produce absolute alcohol (100%) from rectified spirit (95.6% alcohol), the remaining 4.4% water must be removed by a drying agent such as
questions.explanation_short: Calcium oxide (quicklime) is used as a drying agent to remove the remaining water from rectified spirit, producing absolute (100%) alcohol.
questions.explanation_long: Rectified spirit (about 95.6% ethanol) can't be purified further by simple distillation due to the ethanol-water azeotrope. Adding a strong drying/dehydrating agent like calcium oxide (CaO), which reacts with and removes water, allows the remaining pure ethanol to be distilled off as absolute alcohol.
questions.explanation_trick: CaO (quicklime) reacts with water — used to strip the last bit of water out of rectified spirit.

explanation_options.a: Correct — calcium oxide is the classic drying agent used to convert rectified spirit into absolute alcohol.
explanation_options.b: Calcium chloride can form an ethanol complex, making it unsuitable as a drying agent for ethanol specifically.
explanation_options.c: Calcium carbonate is not an effective drying/dehydrating agent for removing water from ethanol.
explanation_options.d: Carbon monoxide is a gas with no water-absorbing/drying properties.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following is also called silver mirror test?
questions.explanation_short: Tollens' reagent (ammoniacal AgNO₃) gives the silver mirror test for aldehydes.
questions.explanation_long: Aldehydes reduce Tollens' reagent, [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺, to metallic silver, which coats the tube as a shiny mirror. Fehling's and Benedict's solutions give a red Cu₂O precipitate instead, and the iodoform test gives yellow CHI₃.
questions.explanation_trick: Silver mirror = Tollens'.

explanation_options.a: Fehling's test gives a brick-red precipitate, not a mirror.
explanation_options.b: The iodoform test gives a yellow precipitate.
explanation_options.c: Correct — Tollens' reagent deposits a silver mirror.
explanation_options.d: Benedict's test gives a red/orange precipitate.

questions.question_text: When acetaldehyde reacts with 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine (2,4-DNPH), which one of the following products is formed? NO2 CH3 CH3 C N NH NO2 C N NH NO2
questions.option_b: CH3 NO2 NO 2 CH3 CH3 C N NH NO 2 C N NH NO2

questions.question_text: Both aldehydes and ketones are planer to the neighborhoods of carbonyl (C=O) group. Which one of the following bonds is distorted towards the oxygen atoms?
questions.option_b: Sigma bond of C and H
questions.option_c: Sigma bond of C and O
questions.option_d: Sigma bond of C and C 4 3 2 1
questions.explanation_short: The pi-bond electrons of the C=O group are pulled (distorted) toward the more electronegative oxygen atom, creating the carbonyl's characteristic polarity.
questions.explanation_long: Oxygen is more electronegative than carbon, so in the C=O double bond, the pi-electron cloud is unevenly distributed, shifted toward oxygen. This creates a partial negative charge on oxygen and partial positive on carbon, making the carbonyl carbon electrophilic.
questions.explanation_trick: C=O polarity comes from the pi-bond electrons being pulled toward the more electronegative oxygen.

explanation_options.a: Correct — the pi-bond of C=O is the one distorted toward oxygen, creating the carbonyl's polarity.
explanation_options.b: The sigma C-H bond isn't part of the carbonyl group's polarity discussion at all.
explanation_options.c: The sigma bond between C and O is much less affected by this electron distortion compared to the more polarizable pi-bond.
explanation_options.d: The sigma C-C bond isn't part of the carbonyl group's polarity discussion at all.

questions.question_text: In CH₃–CH(CH₃)–CH(CH₃)–COOH the carbons are numbered 4, 3, 2, 1 from left to right (C-1 is the COOH carbon). Which one is the α-carbon atom?
questions.explanation_short: The α-carbon is the one directly attached to the –COOH carbon — carbon 2 in this numbering.
questions.explanation_long: Carbons are numbered from the carboxyl carbon (C-1). The carbon next to it, C-2, is the α-carbon; C-3 is β and C-4 is γ. In CH₃–CH(CH₃)–CH(CH₃)–COOH the α-carbon is therefore C-2.
questions.explanation_trick: α = next door to the functional carbon.

explanation_options.a: C-1 is the carboxyl carbon itself.
explanation_options.b: C-3 is the β-carbon.
explanation_options.c: Correct — C-2 is attached to the COOH carbon, so it is the α-carbon.
explanation_options.d: C-4 is the γ-carbon.

aliases: In CH3 CH CH COOH which one is α-carbon atom? CH3 CH3

questions.question_text: The specific substances (metabolite) that fits on the enzyme surface and is converted to products is called
questions.explanation_short: The specific molecule that fits into an enzyme's active site and gets converted into products is called the substrate.
questions.explanation_long: Enzymes are highly specific catalysts, and the molecule they act on — binding to the enzyme's active site via a complementary shape (lock-and-key or induced fit) and being chemically transformed — is termed the substrate.
questions.explanation_trick: Substrate = the molecule that fits the enzyme's active site and gets converted to product.

explanation_options.a: A co-factor is a helper molecule/ion needed for enzyme activity, not the molecule being transformed.
explanation_options.b: A prosthetic group is a tightly/permanently bound cofactor, not the substrate being converted.
explanation_options.c: An isoenzyme is a different structural variant of an enzyme performing the same reaction, not the reactant molecule.
explanation_options.d: Correct — the substrate is the specific molecule that fits the enzyme and is converted into products.

questions.question_text: Polymide is formed due to the condensation od hexane-dioic acid with
questions.explanation_short: Nylon-6,6 (a polyamide) forms from hexanedioic acid and hexane-1,6-diamine.
questions.explanation_long: Condensing hexanedioic (adipic) acid with hexane-1,6-diamine links amide bonds and releases water, giving nylon-6,6. The '6,6' is the six carbons in each monomer, with the amine groups at both ends of the diamine (positions 1 and 6).
questions.explanation_trick: Nylon-6,6 = 6-carbon acid + 6-carbon diamine (1,6).

explanation_options.a: A 1,5-diamine is not the nylon-6,6 monomer.
explanation_options.b: Correct — hexane-1,6-diamine.
explanation_options.c: A 1,4-diamine is not the nylon-6,6 monomer.
explanation_options.d: A 2,5-diamine has non-terminal amines and does not form nylon-6,6.

questions.question_text: Haemoglobin is a
questions.explanation_short: Haemoglobin is a transport protein that carries oxygen in the blood.
questions.explanation_long: Proteins are classified by function. Haemoglobin binds O₂ in the lungs and releases it in the tissues, so it is a transport protein. Structural or building proteins include collagen and keratin.
questions.explanation_trick: Haemoglobin carries → transport.

explanation_options.a: Genetic material is nucleic acid, not a protein like haemoglobin.
explanation_options.b: Building (structural) proteins include collagen and keratin.
explanation_options.c: Correct — haemoglobin transports oxygen.
explanation_options.d: Structural proteins include keratin and collagen, not haemoglobin.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following polymer is polystyrene?
questions.explanation_short: Polystyrene is –[CH₂–CH(C₆H₅)]ₙ–, the polymer of styrene (phenylethene).
questions.explanation_long: Styrene, CH₂=CH–C₆H₅, polymerises by addition to give a chain with a phenyl group on every other carbon. The other options are polyethene, PTFE (Teflon) and polypropene.
questions.explanation_trick: Styrene → phenyl (C₆H₅) side group.

explanation_options.a: Correct — a phenyl side group makes it polystyrene.
explanation_options.b: –[CH₂–CH₂]ₙ– is polyethene.
explanation_options.c: –[CF₂–CF₂]ₙ– is PTFE (Teflon).
explanation_options.d: A CH₃ side group makes polypropene.

aliases: Which one of the following polymer is polystyrene? CH2 CH n CF2 CF2
C 6 H5

questions.question_text: Out of these which nitrogen base is NOT present in DNA?
questions.explanation_short: Uracil is found in RNA; DNA uses thymine instead.
questions.explanation_long: DNA contains adenine, guanine, cytosine and thymine. RNA replaces thymine with uracil, so uracil is the base not present in DNA.
questions.explanation_trick: U only in RNA.

explanation_options.a: Adenine is present in both DNA and RNA.
explanation_options.b: Guanine is present in both DNA and RNA.
explanation_options.c: Correct — uracil is absent from DNA.
explanation_options.d: Thymine is found in DNA.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following is an example of co-polymer?
questions.explanation_short: A copolymer is made from two or more different types of monomers linked together; polyamide (like nylon) is an example, built from two distinct monomer types (a diamine and a diacid).
questions.explanation_long: Unlike homopolymers (polystyrene, PVC, polyvinyl acetate — all made from a single repeating monomer), a copolymer incorporates two or more chemically distinct monomers in its chain. Nylon (polyamide) is formed from a diamine and a diacid monomer, making it a classic copolymer example.
questions.explanation_trick: Homopolymer = one monomer type. Copolymer = two or more different monomer types (like nylon's diamine + diacid).

explanation_options.a: Correct — polyamide (nylon) is built from two different monomer types, making it a copolymer.
explanation_options.b: Polystyrene is a homopolymer made from a single repeating styrene monomer.
explanation_options.c: Polyvinyl acetate is a homopolymer made from a single repeating vinyl acetate monomer.
explanation_options.d: Polyvinyl chloride is a homopolymer made from a single repeating vinyl chloride monomer.

questions.question_text: The biggest source of acid rain is the oxide of
questions.explanation_short: Sulphur oxides (SO₂, SO₃) from burning fossil fuels are the biggest source of acid rain.
questions.explanation_long: Sulphur impurities in coal and oil burn to SO₂, which is oxidised to SO₃ and dissolves in rainwater as sulphuric acid. Nitrogen oxides also contribute, but sulphur oxides are the largest source.
questions.explanation_trick: Acid rain: mostly SOₓ, then NOₓ.

explanation_options.a: Nitrogen oxides contribute, but less than sulphur oxides.
explanation_options.b: Correct — sulphur oxides are the biggest source.
explanation_options.c: O is not something that forms 'its oxide' as a pollutant.
explanation_options.d: CO₂ gives only weak carbonic acid; normal rain is already slightly acidic from it.

questions.question_text: Burning of which one of the following waste is considered as useful industrial fuel or to produce electricity
questions.explanation_short: Burning plastic waste is used as a source of industrial fuel/electricity generation because plastics, being petroleum-derived, have high calorific (energy) value.
questions.explanation_long: Plastics are made from hydrocarbons and burn with a high energy release, similar to fuel oil. This makes waste-to-energy incineration of plastic a recognized (if environmentally debated) industrial fuel source, unlike metals (non-combustible), paper, or grass (lower energy content, often composted instead).
questions.explanation_trick: Plastic = petroleum-based = high energy content when burned = usable as industrial fuel.

explanation_options.a: Metals don't burn/combust and can't serve as a fuel source.
explanation_options.b: Grass/biomass has relatively low calorific value compared to plastic.
explanation_options.c: Paper has some fuel value but far lower calorific content than plastic.
explanation_options.d: Correct — plastic waste's high calorific value from its petroleum origin makes it usable as an industrial fuel.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is the correct dot and cross diagram of bonding between two chlorine atoms?
questions.option_a: Cl atoms combine but the product is drawn as a single Cl with an octet
questions.option_b: One electron is transferred from one Cl to the other, leaving two separate atoms
questions.option_c: Each Cl contributes one electron to a shared pair, giving Cl–Cl with an octet on both
questions.option_d: One electron is transferred and the atoms are left without octets
questions.explanation_short: In Cl₂ each chlorine atom shares one electron to form a single bonding pair, and both end up with an octet.
questions.explanation_long: Chlorine has seven valence electrons. In the correct dot-and-cross diagram (C), each atom contributes one electron to a shared pair between them, leaving both with eight electrons — a covalent Cl–Cl bond. The other diagrams show electron transfer or a single atom instead of a shared pair.
questions.explanation_trick: Same element, non-metal → share, don't transfer.

explanation_options.a: Shows the two atoms merging into one Cl, not a Cl₂ molecule.
explanation_options.b: Transfers an electron and leaves two separate atoms — not a covalent bond.
explanation_options.c: Correct — one shared pair gives Cl–Cl with an octet on both atoms.
explanation_options.d: Transfers an electron and leaves the atoms without octets.

questions.question_text: The equation that represents standard enthalpy of atomization of hydrogen is:
questions.explanation_short: Enthalpy of atomisation forms 1 mole of gaseous atoms: ½H₂(g) → H(g), ΔH = +218 kJ mol⁻¹ (endothermic).
questions.explanation_long: Standard enthalpy of atomisation is the enthalpy change when one mole of gaseous atoms forms from the element in its standard state. For hydrogen that is ½H₂(g) → H(g). Breaking the bond absorbs energy, so ΔH is positive (+218 kJ mol⁻¹).
questions.explanation_trick: Atomisation: one mole of atoms, always endothermic.

explanation_options.a: Starting from H₂O describes decomposing water, not atomising hydrogen.
explanation_options.b: Starts from water and has the wrong sign.
explanation_options.c: Correct — ½H₂(g) → H(g), ΔH = +218 kJ mol⁻¹.
explanation_options.d: Right equation, but bond breaking is endothermic, so the sign must be positive.

aliases: The equation that represents standard enthalpy of atomization of hydrogen is: 1 1 1
H2O(l) H2(g) + O(g) +218 kJ mol-1

questions.question_text: Standard enthalpy of combustion of graphite at 25 °C is –393.51 kJ mol⁻¹ and that of diamond is –395.41 kJ mol⁻¹. The enthalpy change for graphite is:
questions.explanation_long: Using Hess's law, the enthalpy of converting graphite to diamond is the combustion enthalpy of graphite minus that of diamond: (−393.51) − (−395.41) = +1.90 kJ mol⁻¹. It is positive because diamond is the higher-energy form.
questions.explanation_trick: ΔH(transition) = ΔHc(start) − ΔHc(end).

explanation_options.a: Right magnitude, wrong sign — diamond is higher in energy than graphite.
explanation_options.b: The subtraction gives 1.90, not 2.1.
explanation_options.c: Both the sign and the magnitude are wrong.
explanation_options.d: Correct — ≈ +1.91 kJ mol⁻¹ (graphite → diamond).

aliases: Standard enthalpy of combustion of graphite at 25 oC is –393.51 kJ mol-1 and that of diamond is –395.41 kJ mol-1. The enthalpy change for graphite is:

questions.question_text: 10.0 grams of glucose are dissolved in water to make 100 cm³ of its solution, its molarity is:
questions.explanation_short: Molarity = moles of solute ÷ volume in liters; with 10 g glucose (molar mass 180 g/mol) in 0.1 L, molarity = (10/180)/0.1 ≈ 0.55 mol/L.
questions.explanation_long: First find moles of glucose: 10 g ÷ 180 g/mol ≈ 0.0556 mol. Then divide by volume in liters (100 cm³ = 0.1 L): 0.0556/0.1 ≈ 0.55 mol/L.
questions.explanation_trick: Molarity = (mass/molar mass) / volume in liters. Glucose's molar mass is 180 g/mol.

explanation_options.a: Correct — working through mass/molar mass/volume gives approximately 0.55 mol/L.
explanation_options.b: 0.1 mol/L is too low given the actual mass and volume specified.
explanation_options.c: 10 mol/L would require far more glucose than the 10 g given for this small volume.
explanation_options.d: 1 mol/L is roughly double the correctly calculated molarity.

aliases: 10.0 grams of glucose are dissolved in water to make 100 cm3 of its solution, its molarity is:

questions.question_text: Given solution contains 16.0 g of CH₃OH, 92.0 g of C₂H₅OH and 36 g of water. Which statement about mole fraction of the components is true?
questions.option_a: Mole fraction of CH₃OH is highest among all
questions.option_b: Mole fraction of C₂H₅OH and H₂O is the same
questions.option_c: Mole fraction of CH₃OH and C₂H₅OH is same components
questions.option_d: Mole fraction of H₂O is the lowest among all
questions.explanation_short: Moles: CH₃OH 16/32 = 0.5, C₂H₅OH 92/46 = 2.0, H₂O 36/18 = 2.0 — so ethanol and water have equal mole fractions.
questions.explanation_long: Mole fraction depends on moles, not mass. Ethanol and water both give 2.0 mol, so their mole fractions are equal (2/4.5 ≈ 0.44 each), while methanol, at 0.5 mol, has the lowest.
questions.explanation_trick: Convert to moles first: 16/32, 92/46, 36/18.

explanation_options.a: Methanol has the fewest moles (0.5), so its mole fraction is lowest, not highest.
explanation_options.b: Correct — C₂H₅OH and H₂O are both 2.0 mol.
explanation_options.c: Methanol (0.5 mol) and ethanol (2.0 mol) differ.
explanation_options.d: Water ties for the highest mole fraction, not the lowest.

aliases: Given solution contains 16.0 g of CH3OH, 92.0 g of C2H5OH and 36 g of water. Which statement about mole fraction of the components is true?
Mole fraction of CH3OH is highest among all

questions.question_text: Study the following facts: Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻, E° = +0.76 V; Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻, E° = −0.34 V. Which reaction is feasible?
questions.explanation_short: Zn is more easily oxidised (E°ox = +0.76 V) than Cu, so zinc metal reduces Cu²⁺: Cu²⁺ + Zn → Cu + Zn²⁺.
questions.explanation_long: Adding Zn → Zn²⁺ (+0.76 V) to Cu²⁺ → Cu (+0.34 V) gives a cell voltage of +1.10 V, which is positive, so the reaction is spontaneous. This is the Daniell cell reaction.
questions.explanation_trick: The more reactive metal gives up electrons to the less reactive metal's ions.

explanation_options.a: The reverse of the spontaneous reaction (E = −1.10 V).
explanation_options.b: Both species are already oxidised — nothing supplies the electrons.
explanation_options.c: Correct — Zn reduces Cu²⁺ (E°cell = +1.10 V).
explanation_options.d: Zn²⁺ appears on both sides and there is no electron donor.

aliases: Study the following facts Zn Zn+2 + 2e― Eo = +0.76 V Cu Cu+2 + 2e― Eo = – 0.34 V
Cu + Zn+2 Cu+2 + Zn

questions.question_text: Keeping in mind the electrode potential, which one of the following reactions is feasible?
questions.explanation_short: Iron is above copper in the electrochemical series, so Fe displaces Cu: Fe + CuSO₄ → FeSO₄ + Cu.
questions.explanation_long: A metal can reduce the ions of any metal with a higher (more positive) reduction potential. Fe (−0.44 V) is more reactive than Cu (+0.34 V), so the displacement works. Zn and Cd are less reactive than Mg and cannot displace it, and Cu cannot reduce Zn²⁺.
questions.explanation_trick: More reactive metal displaces less reactive metal from its salt.

explanation_options.a: Cu is less reactive than Zn and cannot reduce Zn²⁺.
explanation_options.b: Zn is less reactive than Mg, so it cannot displace Mg.
explanation_options.c: Correct — Fe displaces Cu from CuSO₄.
explanation_options.d: Cd is less reactive than Mg, so it cannot displace Mg.

aliases: Keeping in mind the electrode potential, which one of the following reactions is feasible?
Zn+2 + Cu Cu+2 + Zn

questions.question_text: What is the correct relation between pH and pK?
questions.explanation_short: Henderson–Hasselbalch: pH = pKa + log([Base]/[Acid]), which is the same as pH = pKa − log([Acid]/[Base]).
questions.explanation_long: For a buffer, pH = pKa + log([salt/base]/[acid]). Since log(x) = −log(1/x), this can also be written pH = pKa − log([Acid]/[Base]), which is the form printed in B. Option D is the same relation in its usual form; the paper's key gives B.
questions.explanation_trick: Flip the fraction inside the log → flip the sign.

explanation_options.a: Wrong sign for [Acid]/[Base].
explanation_options.b: Correct — pH = pKa − log([Acid]/[Base]) (the key's answer).
explanation_options.c: Wrong sign for [Base]/[Acid] — this would lower pH as base increases.
explanation_options.d: Mathematically the same as B (the usual textbook form), but the key marks B.

aliases: What is the correct relation between pH and pK? Acid Base
pH = pKa + log[ ]

questions.question_text: Which one of the following is the correct presentation for Ksp? AgCl → Ag⁺ + Cl⁻
questions.explanation_short: Solids are left out of an equilibrium expression, so for AgCl ⇌ Ag⁺ + Cl⁻, Ksp = [Ag⁺][Cl⁻].
questions.explanation_long: The solubility product is the product of the ion concentrations in a saturated solution, each raised to its stoichiometric coefficient. The undissolved solid AgCl has constant activity and does not appear, so Ksp = [Ag⁺][Cl⁻].
questions.explanation_trick: Ksp = ions only, no solid.

explanation_options.a: Inverted, and wrongly includes the solid.
explanation_options.b: Correct — Ksp = [Ag⁺][Cl⁻].
explanation_options.c: Includes the solid AgCl, which is omitted from Ksp.
explanation_options.d: Contains no ion concentrations at all.

aliases: Which one of the following is the correct presentation for Ksp? AgCl → Ag+ + Cl-
Ksp = [AgCl] / ([Ag+1][Cl-1])

questions.question_text: In spite of all the torture, the police has failed to _________ any confession from the thief.
questions.explanation_short: "Elicit" means to draw out — the police failed to elicit a confession.
questions.explanation_long: You elicit (draw out or obtain) information or a confession from someone. "Convince" takes a person as its object, not a confession, and "refuse" and "agree" do not fit the meaning.
questions.explanation_trick: Elicit a response / a confession.

explanation_options.a: You convince a person, not a confession.
explanation_options.b: Correct — to elicit a confession is to draw it out.
explanation_options.c: The police wouldn't 'refuse' a confession they were trying to get.
explanation_options.d: 'Agree any confession' is ungrammatical.

questions.question_text: It is the duty of a teacher to _________ moral values in his students besides teaching.
questions.explanation_short: To "inculcate" is to instil values firmly through repeated teaching.
questions.explanation_long: Teachers inculcate (instil) moral values in students. "Tell", "record" and "suggest" do not collocate with 'moral values in students'.
questions.explanation_trick: Inculcate values in someone.

explanation_options.a: You tell something to someone, not 'in' them.
explanation_options.b: Recording values does not make sense here.
explanation_options.c: Correct — inculcate moral values in students.
explanation_options.d: 'Suggest values in students' is unidiomatic.

questions.question_text: Many of the houses in Murree have basic __________.
questions.explanation_short: "Amenities" means useful or desirable features/facilities — houses in Murree have basic amenities (like water, electricity).
questions.explanation_long: "Amenities" refers to conveniences or facilities that make a place comfortable to live in, fitting naturally with describing what basic features a house provides.
questions.explanation_trick: Amenities = facilities/conveniences of a place (e.g. "basic amenities" = water, electricity, etc.).

explanation_options.a: Correct — "amenities" fits perfectly with describing basic facilities a house has.
explanation_options.b: "Accuracy" means precision/correctness, unrelated to house facilities.
explanation_options.c: "Affinity" means a natural liking or connection, unrelated to house facilities.
explanation_options.d: "Array" means an ordered arrangement or display, not typically used for house facilities.

questions.question_text: Youngsters who indulge in love affairs are usually __________ in worldly manners.
questions.explanation_short: "Addled" means muddled or confused — inexperienced in worldly matters.
questions.explanation_long: The sentence needs an adjective meaning confused or inexperienced. "Addled" fits. "Adjoined" means next to, "adjured" means solemnly urged, and "adhesive" means sticky.
questions.explanation_trick: Addled = muddled.

explanation_options.a: Adjoined means next to or attached.
explanation_options.b: Correct — addled means confused.
explanation_options.c: Adjured means solemnly commanded.
explanation_options.d: Adhesive means sticky.

questions.question_text: He picked up one or two magazines and after a hurried glance on the contents carefully replaced them.
questions.explanation_short: The spot-the-error sentence's mistake is the preposition "on" — it should be "at a hurried glance" not "on the contents," but the grammatically correct preposition after "glance" is typically "at."
questions.explanation_long: "Glance" is conventionally followed by the preposition "at" (a glance at something), not "on." The underlined segment "on" is the grammatical error in this sentence.
questions.explanation_trick: "Glance at" is the fixed idiomatic pairing — watch for wrong prepositions substituted in for it.

explanation_options.a: "Picked up" is grammatically correct as used.
explanation_options.b: "A hurried" is grammatically correct as used.
explanation_options.c: Correct — "on" is the wrong preposition; it should be "at" (glance at the contents).
explanation_options.d: "Replaced" is grammatically correct as used.

questions.question_text: His guests found it fun to watch him to make tea – mixing careful spoonful from different caddies.
questions.explanation_short: The error is in "to make" — after "watch him," the correct form is the bare infinitive "make," not "to make."
questions.explanation_long: Verbs of perception like "watch" typically take a bare infinitive (watch him make) rather than a full infinitive with "to" (watch him to make) — making "to make" the grammatical error here.
questions.explanation_trick: "Watch/see/hear + someone + bare infinitive" (no "to") is the standard grammatical pattern.

explanation_options.a: "It fun" is grammatically fine as used in this context.
explanation_options.b: "To watch" is grammatically correct as the main verb form here.
explanation_options.c: Correct — "to make" should be the bare infinitive "make" after the perception verb "watch."
explanation_options.d: "Careful spoonful" isn't the underlined grammatical error being tested here.

questions.question_text: You have put your life in his hands many a times.
questions.explanation_short: The error is "many a times" — the correct idiom is "many a time" (singular), since "many a" is always followed by a singular noun.
questions.explanation_long: "Many a" is a fixed idiomatic construction that takes a singular noun even though it means "many" — so it should be "many a time," not "many a times."
questions.explanation_trick: "Many a" + singular noun always — never plural, despite the plural meaning.

explanation_options.a: "Put your life" is grammatically correct as used.
explanation_options.b: "In his hands" is grammatically correct as used.
explanation_options.c: Correct — "many a" must be followed by a singular noun, so "times" is the error (should be "time").
explanation_options.d: "Times" itself is the plural form causing the error when following "many a," but the underlined segment tested is "many a" paired with it.

questions.question_text: Chips, thinking it over a good many time, always added to himself that Kathie would have approved
questions.explanation_short: The error is "a good many time" — it should be "a good many times" (plural), since "a good many" (unlike "many a") takes a plural noun.
questions.explanation_long: Unlike "many a" (which takes singular), the phrase "a good many" functions like an ordinary quantifier and requires a plural noun — so "a good many time" is wrong; it should be "a good many times."
questions.explanation_trick: "A good many" + plural noun (opposite rule from "many a" + singular).

explanation_options.a: Correct — "a good many time" should be "a good many times" (plural), since "a good many" needs a plural noun.
explanation_options.b: "Added to himself" is grammatically correct as used.
explanation_options.c: "Would have approved" is grammatically correct as used.
explanation_options.d: "Have been amused" isn't the underlined segment being tested for this error.

questions.question_text: But the men ate their supper in good appetites.
questions.explanation_short: The error is the preposition "in" — the correct idiom is "with good appetites," not "in good appetites."
questions.explanation_long: The standard idiomatic preposition pairing is "eat with a good appetite," using "with," not "in." The underlined "in" is therefore the grammatical error.
questions.explanation_trick: "Eat with an appetite" — fixed idiomatic preposition pairing to memorize.

explanation_options.a: "Men" is grammatically correct as used.
explanation_options.b: "Ate" is grammatically correct as used.
explanation_options.c: "Their" is grammatically correct as used.
explanation_options.d: Correct — "in" should be "with," matching the idiom "eat with a good appetite."

questions.question_text: A common sense of failure is a mistaken ambition of the boys on the part of his parents.
questions.explanation_short: Of the underlined words (of / of / on / of), the error marked is the last one, in "on the part of his parents".
questions.explanation_long: The sentence is awkward, and the paper's key marks the fourth underlined segment — the final 'of' in 'on the part of his parents' — as the error. Note the pronoun 'his' also clashes with 'the boys' (it should be 'their'), so this final phrase is where the sentence breaks down.
questions.explanation_trick: Check that pronouns agree with their nouns: boys → their.

explanation_options.a: The 'of' in 'sense of failure' is used correctly.
explanation_options.b: The 'of' in 'ambition of the boys' is not the marked error.
explanation_options.c: 'on the part' is a correct idiom.
explanation_options.d: Correct — the key marks the final segment, 'of his parents' (his ≠ the boys).

aliases: A common sense of failure is a mistaken ambition of the boys on the part of his parents.
of

questions.question_text: Choose the CORRECT sentence.
questions.option_a: Tourism is burgeoned over the last fifteen years.
questions.option_b: Tourism will burgeoned over the last fifteen years.
questions.option_c: Tourism have burgeoned over the last fifteen years.
questions.option_d: Tourism has burgeoned over the last fifteen years.
questions.explanation_short: The correct sentence is "Tourism has burgeoned over the last fifteen years" — using "has" for present perfect tense with a singular subject.
questions.explanation_long: "Tourism" is a singular, uncountable noun, so it needs the singular present-perfect auxiliary "has," not "have." "Burgeoned" (past participle) with "has" correctly forms present perfect tense: "has burgeoned."
questions.explanation_trick: Singular subject + present perfect = "has" + past participle.

explanation_options.a: "Is burgeoned" incorrectly uses passive-style construction where an active present-perfect form is needed.
explanation_options.b: "Will burgeoned" incorrectly pairs future tense "will" with a past participle form.
explanation_options.c: "Have burgeoned" incorrectly uses the plural auxiliary for the singular subject "Tourism."
explanation_options.d: Correct — "has burgeoned" properly matches the singular subject with present perfect tense.

aliases: Tourism is burgeoned over the last fifteen years.

questions.question_text: Choose the CORRECT sentence.
questions.option_a: His remains were interred in the new cemetery.
questions.option_b: His remains were entered in the new cemetery.
questions.option_c: His remains was interred in the new cemetery.
questions.option_d: His remains was entered in the new cemetery.
questions.explanation_short: The correct sentence is "His remains were interred in the new cemetery" — "remains" is treated as plural, taking "were," and "interred" (buried) is the correct verb, not "entered."
questions.explanation_long: "Remains" (referring to a body) is grammatically plural, requiring "were." The correct verb for burial is "interred," not "entered" (which means something else entirely — to go into).
questions.explanation_trick: "Remains" = plural noun, takes "were." "Interred" = buried (don't confuse with "entered").

explanation_options.a: Correct — "were interred" properly uses plural agreement and the correct burial verb.
explanation_options.b: "Were entered" uses the wrong verb — "entered" doesn't mean buried.
explanation_options.c: "Was interred" incorrectly uses singular "was" with the plural noun "remains."
explanation_options.d: "Was entered" has both the wrong verb and incorrect singular agreement.

aliases: His remains were interred in the new cemetery.

questions.question_text: Choose the CORRECT sentence.
questions.option_a: They had died in the same day.
questions.option_b: They had died over the same day.
questions.option_c: They had died on the same day.
questions.option_d: They had died of the same day.
questions.explanation_short: Specific days take "on": they died on the same day.
questions.explanation_long: English uses 'on' for days and dates (on Monday, on the same day), 'in' for longer periods and 'at' for times.
questions.explanation_trick: at a time, on a day, in a month or year.

explanation_options.a: 'in' is used for months, years and longer periods.
explanation_options.b: 'over' implies a span of time.
explanation_options.c: Correct — on the same day.
explanation_options.d: 'died of' names a cause, not a time.

questions.question_text: Choose the CORRECT sentence.
questions.option_a: She had turned on the supper steaks when the telephone rang.
questions.option_b: She had turned over the supper steaks when the telephone rang.
questions.option_c: She had turned into the supper steaks when the telephone rang.
questions.option_d: She had turned in the supper steaks when the telephone rang.
questions.explanation_short: The correct sentence is "She had turned over the supper steaks when the telephone rang" — "turned over" (flipped) is the correct phrasal verb for cooking.
questions.explanation_long: "Turn over" is the standard phrasal verb meaning to flip food while cooking, matching the context of cooking steaks. Other prepositions ("on," "into," "in") don't form a correct cooking-related phrasal verb here.
questions.explanation_trick: "Turn over" the steaks = flip them while cooking — the correct phrasal verb.

explanation_options.a: "Turned on" doesn't fit the cooking context of flipping steaks.
explanation_options.b: Correct — "turned over" is the proper phrasal verb for flipping food while cooking.
explanation_options.c: "Turned into" implies transformation into something else, not flipping while cooking.
explanation_options.d: "Turned in" typically means to submit or go to bed, not flipping food.

questions.question_text: Choose the CORRECT sentence.
questions.option_a: Empty of concord is the soul of wit.
questions.option_b: Empty of concord is the role of wit.
questions.option_c: Empty of concord is the sole of wit.
questions.option_d: Empty of concord is the howl of wit.
questions.explanation_short: "Empty of concord is the soul of wit" — 'soul' in the sense of the essence of something, as in 'brevity is the soul of wit'.
questions.explanation_long: The sentence tests the homophones soul/sole and near-rhymes. 'Soul' means essence, the sense used in Shakespeare's 'brevity is the soul of wit'. 'Sole' (a fish, or the bottom of a foot), 'role' and 'howl' do not fit.
questions.explanation_trick: Essence → soul, not sole.

explanation_options.a: Correct — soul (essence) of wit.
explanation_options.b: 'role of wit' does not carry the idiom's meaning.
explanation_options.c: 'sole' is a homophone trap (fish / foot).
explanation_options.d: 'howl of wit' is meaningless.

questions.question_text: Choose the CORRECT sentence.
questions.option_a: The cheery trees stand over the woodland ride.
questions.option_b: The cheery trees stand about the woodland ride.
questions.option_c: The cheery trees stand beside the woodland ride.
questions.option_d: The cheery trees stand on the woodland ride.
questions.explanation_short: "The cherry trees stand about the woodland ride" echoes Housman's line "And stands about the woodland ride" — 'about' means all around.
questions.explanation_long: In A. E. Housman's poem 'Loveliest of Trees', the cherry 'stands about the woodland ride / Wearing white for Eastertide'. 'About' here means around or along the path, which is the answer the key marks. ('Cheery' in the options is a misprint of 'cherry'.)
questions.explanation_trick: Housman: 'stands about the woodland ride'.

explanation_options.a: Trees cannot stand 'over' a path.
explanation_options.b: Correct — 'about' (around) matches the original line.
explanation_options.c: 'beside' is plausible modern English but is not the phrasing the key marks.
explanation_options.d: Trees do not stand 'on' a riding path.

aliases: The cheery trees stand over the woodland ride.

questions.question_text: Choose the CORRECT sentence.
questions.option_a: He made me to write the sum on the slip and to sign my name in a book.
questions.option_b: He made me write the sum on/at the slip and to sign my name in a book.
questions.option_c: He made me to write the sum on the slip and sign my name in a book.
questions.option_d: He made me to write the sum in a slip and to sign my name in a book.
questions.explanation_short: The correct sentence is "He made me write the sum on the slip and sign my name in a book" — "made" (causative verb) takes a bare infinitive, not "to write"/"to sign."
questions.explanation_long: "Made" as a causative verb (meaning "forced/caused") is followed by a bare infinitive without "to": "made me write... and sign." Using "to write" or "to sign" after "made" is grammatically incorrect.
questions.explanation_trick: "Made someone do something" — bare infinitive, no "to," throughout the sentence.

explanation_options.a: "To write" is the incorrect infinitive form after the causative verb "made."
explanation_options.b: "On/at the slip" introduces an unnecessary preposition ambiguity not present in the correctly worded sentence.
explanation_options.c: Correct — this version properly uses the bare infinitives "write" and "sign" after the causative "made."
explanation_options.d: "To write... in a slip" both uses the wrong infinitive form and an incorrect preposition.

aliases: He made me to write the sum on the slip and to sign my name in a book.

questions.question_text: Choose the CORRECT sentence.
questions.option_a: I am looking forward to secure excellent marks in MCAT.
questions.option_b: I am looking forward to securing excellent marks in MCAT.
questions.option_c: I am looking forward securing excellent marks in MCAT.
questions.option_d: I am looking forward secure excellent marks in MCAT.
questions.explanation_short: The correct sentence is "I am looking forward to securing excellent marks in MCAT" — "look forward to" is followed by a gerund (-ing form), not a bare infinitive.
questions.explanation_long: The phrase "look forward to" ends in the preposition "to," which must be followed by a gerund (verb+ing), not a bare infinitive: "looking forward to securing," not "to secure."
questions.explanation_trick: "Look forward to" + gerund (-ing) — "to" here is a preposition, not part of an infinitive.

explanation_options.a: "To secure" incorrectly uses the bare infinitive after the preposition "to" in this idiom.
explanation_options.b: Correct — "to securing" properly uses the gerund form required after the idiom "look forward to."
explanation_options.c: Omitting "to" entirely breaks the required idiomatic phrase "look forward to."
explanation_options.d: Both omitting "to" and using the bare infinitive "secure" are incorrect here.

aliases: I am looking forward to secure excellent marks in MCAT.

questions.question_text: Choose the CORRECT sentence.
questions.option_a: The study of population growth indicates one of the greatest paradox of our time.
questions.option_b: The study of population growth indicate one of the greatest paradox of our time.
questions.option_c: The study of population growth indicates one of the greatest paradoxes of our time.
questions.option_d: The study of population growth indicates one of the greatest paradox in our time.
questions.explanation_short: The correct sentence is "The study of population growth indicates one of the greatest paradoxes of our time" — "paradoxes" (plural) is needed since "one of the greatest [plural noun]" is the standard construction.
questions.explanation_long: "One of the greatest ___" requires a plural noun (one of the greatest paradoxes), and the singular subject "the study" correctly takes the singular verb "indicates."
questions.explanation_trick: "One of the greatest/best [plural noun]" — always plural after "one of the."

explanation_options.a: "Paradox" (singular) doesn't fit the required "one of the greatest [plural]" construction.
explanation_options.b: "Indicate" incorrectly uses a plural verb form with the singular subject "the study."
explanation_options.c: Correct — "indicates" agrees with the singular subject and "paradoxes" is correctly pluralized.
explanation_options.d: "Paradox in our time" both keeps the noun singular incorrectly and changes the correct preposition "of."

aliases: The study of population growth indicates one of the greatest paradox of our time.

questions.question_text: Choose the CORRECT sentence.
questions.option_a: In North Africa, he barely escaped assassination at the hand of the governor of the province.
questions.option_b: In North Africa, he barely escaped from assassination at the hands of the governor of the province.
questions.option_c: In North Africa, he barely escaped from assassination at the hand of the governor of the province.
questions.option_d: In North Africa, he barely escaped assassination at the hands of the governor of the province.
questions.explanation_short: "Escape" takes a direct object (escaped assassination), and the idiom is "at the hands of".
questions.explanation_long: When 'escape' means to avoid something, it takes the object directly: escaped assassination, not escaped from assassination ('escape from' is for places, e.g. escape from prison). The fixed phrase is 'at the hands of' (plural). Only D gets both right. Note: this paper's printed key marks B, but 'escaped from assassination' is unidiomatic.
questions.explanation_trick: Escape a fate; escape from a place; at the hands of.

explanation_options.a: 'at the hand of' should be 'at the hands of'.
explanation_options.b: 'escaped from assassination' is unidiomatic.
explanation_options.c: Has both errors: 'from' and 'hand'.
explanation_options.d: Correct — escaped assassination at the hands of.

aliases: In North Africa, he barely escaped assassination at the hand of the governor of the province.

questions.question_text: EMPATHY
questions.explanation_short: EMPATHY means the ability to understand and share another's feelings, closest in meaning to "Sympathy" among the given choices.
questions.explanation_long: Empathy involves emotionally understanding and relating to someone else's feelings, which overlaps closely with the concept of sympathy (compassionate concern for others), making it the nearest match among these options.
questions.explanation_trick: Empathy ≈ Sympathy — both involve feeling/understanding what another person feels.

explanation_options.a: "Understanding" is related but too general — it doesn't capture the emotional/feeling component central to empathy.
explanation_options.b: "Animosity" (hostility) is essentially the opposite of empathy.
explanation_options.c: "Friendship" is a relationship type, not a direct synonym for the emotional concept of empathy.
explanation_options.d: Correct — "sympathy" is the closest match to empathy among the given options.

questions.question_text: FELICITY
questions.explanation_short: FELICITY means great happiness.
questions.explanation_long: Felicity is intense happiness or bliss; it can also mean a pleasing aptness of expression.
questions.explanation_trick: Felicity ≈ 'feliz' (happy).

explanation_options.a: Boredom is roughly the opposite.
explanation_options.b: Business is unrelated.
explanation_options.c: Correct — felicity = happiness.
explanation_options.d: Relaxation is not the same as happiness.

questions.question_text: UNCANNY
questions.explanation_short: UNCANNY means strange or mysterious in an unsettling way, closest in meaning to "Strange" among the choices.
questions.explanation_long: "Uncanny" describes something eerily strange or beyond normal explanation, making "strange" the clear nearest synonym among the given options.
questions.explanation_trick: Uncanny = eerily strange/mysterious (uncanny resemblance, uncanny accuracy).

explanation_options.a: "Exact" doesn't capture the strangeness/eeriness central to "uncanny."
explanation_options.b: "Opposite" is unrelated in meaning to "uncanny."
explanation_options.c: "Good" has no meaningful connection to "uncanny."
explanation_options.d: Correct — "strange" is the closest synonym to "uncanny."

questions.question_text: VIRULENT
questions.explanation_short: VIRULENT means extremely harmful, poisonous or bitterly hostile.
questions.explanation_long: A virulent disease is severe and harmful; virulent criticism is bitterly hostile. The closest meaning is 'harmful'.
questions.explanation_trick: Virulent ~ virus → harmful.

explanation_options.a: Progressive means advancing.
explanation_options.b: Correct — virulent = harmful.
explanation_options.c: Healthy is the opposite.
explanation_options.d: Positive does not match.

questions.question_text: RAPT
questions.explanation_short: RAPT means completely absorbed or enchanted — nearest to 'bewitched'.
questions.explanation_long: Rapt attention is total absorption. The word also means transported with delight, so 'bewitched' is the closest match. 'Rapid' is a sound-alike trap.
questions.explanation_trick: Rapt = enraptured, not rapid.

explanation_options.a: A trumpet is unrelated.
explanation_options.b: Correct — rapt = bewitched or enthralled.
explanation_options.c: Rapid is a sound-alike trap meaning fast.
explanation_options.d: Rash means reckless.

questions.question_text: PEDAGOGY
questions.explanation_short: PEDAGOGY is the method and practice of teaching.
questions.explanation_long: Pedagogy (from the Greek for 'leading a child') is the art, science and methods of teaching.
questions.explanation_trick: Pedagogue = teacher.

explanation_options.a: The study of children's medicine is paediatrics.
explanation_options.b: Correct — pedagogy = the study of teaching methods.
explanation_options.c: Cultural heritage is unrelated.
explanation_options.d: Pectoral muscles are unrelated.

questions.question_text: INDICTMENT
questions.explanation_short: An INDICTMENT is a formal accusation or charge.
questions.explanation_long: To indict is to formally charge someone with a crime, and an indictment is that accusation.
questions.explanation_trick: Indict (pronounced 'indite') = accuse.

explanation_options.a: Humiliation is not the meaning.
explanation_options.b: 'Offended' is an adjective and a different idea.
explanation_options.c: Correct — indictment = accusation.
explanation_options.d: Invisible is unrelated.

questions.question_text: MITIGATION
questions.explanation_short: MITIGATION means the act of lessening severity or intensity of something, closest in meaning to "Alleviation."
questions.explanation_long: "Mitigation" refers to reducing the severity, seriousness, or painfulness of something (like mitigating circumstances that lessen blame), directly matching "alleviation" (relief/lessening).
questions.explanation_trick: Mitigation = lessening/easing severity — "mitigating circumstances" reduce the blame/punishment.

explanation_options.a: Correct — "alleviation" (lessening/easing) closely matches the meaning of "mitigation."
explanation_options.b: "Classification" (categorizing) is unrelated in meaning to mitigation.
explanation_options.c: "Formidable" (intimidating/impressive) is unrelated in meaning to mitigation.
explanation_options.d: "Poisonous" is unrelated in meaning to mitigation.

questions.question_text: CONCERTED
questions.explanation_short: CONCERTED means done through combined, coordinated effort — closest in meaning to "Strenuous" (requiring great effort) among the choices.
questions.explanation_long: "Concerted" describes an effort made through planned, joint coordination (a "concerted effort"), which connotes significant combined exertion, aligning it with "strenuous" among the given choices.
questions.explanation_trick: Concerted effort = coordinated, combined, significant effort.

explanation_options.a: Correct — "strenuous" (requiring notable effort) is the closest match among the choices to "concerted."
explanation_options.b: "Furious" (very angry) is unrelated in meaning to "concerted."
explanation_options.c: "Curious" (inquisitive) is unrelated in meaning to "concerted."
explanation_options.d: "Precious" (valuable) is unrelated in meaning to "concerted."

questions.question_text: ARCANE
questions.explanation_short: ARCANE means mysterious, obscure, or understood by only a few — closest in meaning to "Mysterious."
questions.explanation_long: "Arcane" describes knowledge or things that are secret, obscure, or known only to specialists — directly matching "mysterious" as the nearest synonym among these options.
questions.explanation_trick: Arcane = obscure/secret/mysterious knowledge ("arcane rituals," "arcane rules").

explanation_options.a: Correct — "mysterious" is the closest synonym to "arcane."
explanation_options.b: "Furious" (very angry) is unrelated in meaning to "arcane."
explanation_options.c: "Arid" (dry) is unrelated in meaning to "arcane."
explanation_options.d: "Clear" is essentially opposite in meaning to "arcane" (which means obscure, not clear).

questions.question_text: In _____________ response, β-cells produce plasma cells that synthesize antibodies and release in blood plasma and tissue fluid.
questions.explanation_short: In humoral immunity, B-cells (which mature into plasma cells) produce antibodies that are released into blood plasma and tissue fluid to fight pathogens.
questions.explanation_long: Humoral response is the branch of adaptive immunity mediated by B-lymphocytes, which differentiate into plasma cells producing large quantities of soluble antibodies that circulate in body fluids (blood and lymph), as opposed to cell-mediated immunity, which relies on direct cell-to-cell action by T-cells.
questions.explanation_trick: Humoral = fluid-based (antibodies in blood plasma), driven by B-cells.

explanation_options.a: Cell-mediated immunity involves T-cells acting directly, not antibody-producing plasma cells.
explanation_options.b: "Hormonal" is not an immunity classification term at all.
explanation_options.c: Correct — humoral response is exactly this B-cell/plasma-cell/antibody pathway.
explanation_options.d: "Phototactic" relates to movement toward/away from light, unrelated to immunity.

questions.question_text: Passive immunity is used against:
questions.explanation_short: Passive immunity (ready-made antibodies given directly, e.g. as antitoxin) is used against tetanus, since the fast-acting toxin requires immediate antibody protection rather than waiting for the body to build its own.
questions.explanation_long: Tetanus toxin acts quickly and dangerously, so instead of waiting weeks for active immunity to develop, patients are often given passive immunity — pre-formed antibodies (anti-tetanus serum) that act immediately, especially after injury with unknown vaccination status.
questions.explanation_trick: Passive immunity = ready-made antibodies given directly — used for fast-acting threats like tetanus.

explanation_options.a: Malaria is caused by a parasite, generally not addressed with passive antibody immunity in this classic sense.
explanation_options.b: Typhoid is typically addressed with vaccines or antibiotics, not classic passive immunity.
explanation_options.c: Dengue doesn't have a standard passive-antibody treatment approach like tetanus antitoxin.
explanation_options.d: Correct — passive immunity via anti-tetanus serum is a classic real-world application against tetanus.

questions.question_text: B-lymphocytes are named due to their relationship with:
questions.explanation_short: B-lymphocytes are named after the bursa of Fabricius in birds, where they were first shown to mature.
questions.explanation_long: The 'B' comes from the bursa of Fabricius, a lymphoid organ in birds where these cells were discovered. In humans they mature in bone marrow, which also conveniently starts with B, but the name comes from the bursa.
questions.explanation_trick: B for bursa; T for thymus.

explanation_options.a: The 'B' does not stand for blood.
explanation_options.b: Correct — named after the bursa of Fabricius.
explanation_options.c: Human B cells mature in bone marrow, but the name comes from the bursa.
explanation_options.d: The bile duct is unrelated.

questions.question_text: In light independent stage of photosynthesis, the CO₂ combines with _______ to form an unstable 6-carbon intermediate.
questions.explanation_short: In the Calvin cycle (light-independent reactions), CO2 combines with ribulose bisphosphate (RuBP) to form an unstable 6-carbon intermediate that quickly splits into two 3-carbon molecules.
questions.explanation_long: Carbon fixation is the first step of the Calvin cycle: CO2 is added to the 5-carbon RuBP by the enzyme RuBisCO, briefly forming an unstable 6-carbon compound that immediately splits into two molecules of glycerate-3-phosphate (GP/3-PGA).
questions.explanation_trick: CO2 + RuBP (via RuBisCO) → unstable 6-carbon intermediate → splits into two GP molecules.

explanation_options.a: Correct — ribulose bisphosphate is the CO2 acceptor molecule in the Calvin cycle's carbon fixation step.
explanation_options.b: Hexose sugar is a later product of the Calvin cycle, not the initial CO2 acceptor.
explanation_options.c: Glycerate-3-phosphate is actually the product formed after the unstable intermediate splits, not the CO2 acceptor itself.
explanation_options.d: Glyceraldehyde phosphate is a later intermediate in the cycle, not the initial CO2 acceptor.

aliases: In light independent stage of photosynthesis, the CO 2 combines with _______ to form an unstable 6-carbon intermediate.
Ribulose bisphosphate

questions.question_text: In glycolysis, glycerate-1,3-bisphosphate is converted into glycerate-3-phosphate by losing _____________ phosphate molecules.
questions.explanation_short: Glycerate-1,3-bisphosphate gives one phosphate to ADP (making ATP) and becomes glycerate-3-phosphate.
questions.explanation_long: In this glycolysis step, phosphoglycerate kinase transfers the phosphate at C-1 of 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate to ADP. One phosphate is lost, and 3-phosphoglycerate remains.
questions.explanation_trick: Bis (2) → mono (1): one phosphate lost.

explanation_options.a: It has only two phosphates to begin with.
explanation_options.b: Losing two would leave no phosphate, but 3-phosphate still has one.
explanation_options.c: Correct — one phosphate is transferred to ADP.
explanation_options.d: It has only two phosphates to begin with.

questions.question_text: Malate is oxidized by _______ to oxaloacetate in Krebs’s Cycle.
questions.explanation_short: Malate dehydrogenase oxidises malate to oxaloacetate using NAD⁺, which is reduced to NADH.
questions.explanation_long: In the final step of the Krebs cycle, malate is oxidised to oxaloacetate and NAD⁺ accepts the electrons. FAD is used earlier, at the succinate → fumarate step.
questions.explanation_trick: Krebs: FAD only at succinate; NAD everywhere else.

explanation_options.a: ATP is not an electron acceptor.
explanation_options.b: NADP is used mainly in photosynthesis and biosynthesis, not the Krebs cycle.
explanation_options.c: Correct — NAD⁺ oxidises malate.
explanation_options.d: FAD works at the succinate step, not malate.

questions.question_text: In electron transport chain, the electrons from NADH and FADH₂ are passed to;
questions.explanation_short: In the electron transport chain, electrons from both NADH and FADH2 ultimately converge and are passed to coenzyme Q (ubiquinone).
questions.explanation_long: NADH donates electrons at Complex I, while FADH2 donates at Complex II — both pathways converge and pass their electrons to coenzyme Q (ubiquinone), the shared electron carrier that then feeds Complex III.
questions.explanation_trick: NADH and FADH2 both funnel their electrons into coenzyme Q — the common convergence point.

explanation_options.a: Cytochrome a is involved later in the chain (Complex IV), not the initial convergence point.
explanation_options.b: Cytochrome a3 is part of Complex IV, much later in the chain.
explanation_options.c: "Co-enzyme c" isn't a standard electron transport chain component name.
explanation_options.d: Correct — coenzyme Q is where electrons from both NADH and FADH2 pathways converge.

aliases: In electron transport chain, the electrons from NADH and FADH2 are passed to;
Cytochrome a

questions.question_text: Carriers of the respiratory chain are located on:
questions.explanation_short: The respiratory (electron transport) chain carriers sit in the inner mitochondrial membrane.
questions.explanation_long: Cytochromes, coenzyme Q and the protein complexes of the electron transport chain are embedded in the folded inner membrane (the cristae), where ATP synthase also sits.
questions.explanation_trick: ETC → inner membrane (cristae).

explanation_options.a: The matrix holds the Krebs cycle enzymes.
explanation_options.b: The outer membrane is permeable and has no respiratory chain.
explanation_options.c: Correct — the inner membrane of mitochondria.
explanation_options.d: Glycolysis happens in the cytoplasm, not the respiratory chain.

questions.question_text: In cystic fibrosis, liposomes-microscopic vesicles are sued which are coated with:
questions.explanation_short: In cystic fibrosis gene therapy, liposomes (microscopic lipid vesicles) are coated with the healthy copy of the gene to deliver it into affected lung cells.
questions.explanation_long: Gene therapy for cystic fibrosis uses liposomes as a delivery vehicle — the healthy CFTR gene is packaged into these lipid vesicles, which then fuse with cell membranes to deliver the functional gene into the patient's cells.
questions.explanation_trick: Cystic fibrosis gene therapy: healthy gene wrapped in a liposome, delivered to lung cells.

explanation_options.a: Correct — liposomes used in CF gene therapy are coated with the healthy version of the defective gene.
explanation_options.b: A whole chromosome would be far too large and impractical to package into a liposome for this purpose.
explanation_options.c: A generic protein coating doesn't describe the specific gene-delivery mechanism used in this therapy.
explanation_options.d: Carbohydrate coating doesn't describe the gene-delivery mechanism used here.

questions.question_text: The DNA formed by the reverse transcription is called:
questions.explanation_short: DNA copied from an RNA template by reverse transcriptase is called complementary DNA (cDNA).
questions.explanation_long: Reverse transcriptase uses mRNA as a template to make a complementary DNA strand. cDNA is widely used in cloning because it lacks introns.
questions.explanation_trick: Reverse transcription → cDNA.

explanation_options.a: rDNA means recombinant (or ribosomal) DNA.
explanation_options.b: 'dDNA' is not a standard term.
explanation_options.c: Correct — cDNA (complementary DNA).
explanation_options.d: Too general a term.

questions.question_text: Bacterial cells take up recombinant plasmids when they are treated with:
questions.explanation_short: Bacterial cells are made competent to take up recombinant plasmids by treating them with calcium chloride (CaCl2), which helps destabilize the cell membrane for DNA uptake.
questions.explanation_long: CaCl2 treatment is a standard laboratory technique in molecular biology (heat-shock transformation) that makes bacterial cell membranes more permeable, allowing plasmid DNA to enter the cell during genetic engineering procedures.
questions.explanation_trick: CaCl2 treatment = the classic method to make bacteria "competent" for plasmid uptake.

explanation_options.a: Correct — CaCl2 treatment is the standard method used to make bacterial cells competent for plasmid uptake.
explanation_options.b: NaCl is not the standard reagent used for bacterial transformation competency.
explanation_options.c: KCl is not the standard reagent used for bacterial transformation competency.
explanation_options.d: NaOH is too caustic/destructive and not used for this gentle membrane-permeabilization purpose.

aliases: Bacterial cells take up recombinant plasmids when they are treated with:
CaCl2

questions.question_text: Which one of the following is made up of radioactively labelled nucleotides?
questions.explanation_short: A gene probe is a short, radioactively (or otherwise) labelled nucleotide sequence used to detect complementary DNA sequences in a sample.
questions.explanation_long: Gene probes are single-stranded DNA fragments labelled with a radioactive isotope, designed to hybridize (bind) specifically to a complementary target sequence — commonly used to locate specific genes within genomic DNA or libraries.
questions.explanation_trick: Gene probe = short labelled DNA sequence used to "fish out" a matching gene.

explanation_options.a: Phage DNA is the genetic material of a bacteriophage, not specifically a labelled detection tool.
explanation_options.b: A genomic library is a collection of DNA fragments, not itself a labelled detection tool.
explanation_options.c: Recombinant DNA is DNA that's been artificially combined from different sources, not specifically a labelled probe.
explanation_options.d: Correct — a gene probe is specifically made of radioactively labelled nucleotides for detecting complementary sequences.

questions.question_text: A technique in transgenic animals in which desired gene is inserted into the eggs of animal is called:
questions.explanation_short: Microinjection inserts the desired gene directly into a fertilised egg with a fine glass needle.
questions.explanation_long: In microinjection, cloned DNA is injected into a pronucleus of a fertilised egg, which is then implanted in a foster mother. Embryonic stem cell and retrovirus methods deliver the gene by other routes.
questions.explanation_trick: Gene into the egg by needle = microinjection.

explanation_options.a: The embryonic stem cell method modifies cultured stem cells, not eggs.
explanation_options.b: Correct — microinjection into the egg.
explanation_options.c: Retroviruses carry genes into cells by infection.
explanation_options.d: Virus vectors are a delivery vehicle, not direct insertion into eggs.

questions.question_text: Ozone is a layer of atmosphere extending from ___________ km above earth and absorbs ultraviolent radiations.
questions.explanation_short: The ozone layer extends roughly from 10 to 50 km above Earth's surface (spanning the stratosphere), where it absorbs harmful ultraviolet radiation.
questions.explanation_long: The ozone layer is concentrated in the stratosphere, generally described as occupying the altitude range of about 10-50 km, where ozone molecules absorb most of the sun's damaging UV-B and UV-C radiation before it reaches the surface.
questions.explanation_trick: Ozone layer = stratosphere = roughly 10-50 km altitude.

explanation_options.a: Correct — 10-50 km is the standard textbook range given for the ozone layer's location.
explanation_options.b: 50-60 km is too high — this range is above where the ozone layer is concentrated.
explanation_options.c: 5-30 km underestimates the ozone layer's actual altitude range.
explanation_options.d: 10-80 km overextends far beyond where the ozone layer's protective concentration actually exists.

questions.question_text: Light rays from the sun are absorbed by CO₂ and re-radiate as ________ radiations.
questions.explanation_short: CO₂ absorbs and re-emits infra-red radiation — the greenhouse effect.
questions.explanation_long: The Earth's surface, warmed by sunlight, emits infra-red radiation. Greenhouse gases such as CO₂ absorb it and re-radiate it as infra-red, trapping heat in the atmosphere.
questions.explanation_trick: Greenhouse = infra-red.

explanation_options.a: Ultraviolet is absorbed mainly by ozone, not CO₂.
explanation_options.b: Indigo is visible light.
explanation_options.c: Correct — infra-red.
explanation_options.d: Green is visible light.

aliases: Light rays from the sun are absorbed by CO2 and re-radiate as ________ radiations.
Ultraviolent

questions.question_text: The gases which are produced by burning of fossils fuels and are responsible for acid rain are:
questions.explanation_short: Sulfur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen, produced by burning fossil fuels, are the main gases responsible for acid rain.
questions.explanation_long: When fossil fuels burn, they release SO2 and various nitrogen oxides (NOx), which react with water vapor in the atmosphere to form sulfuric and nitric acids — the primary chemical cause of acid rain.
questions.explanation_trick: Acid rain culprits: SO2 (sulfur dioxide) and NOx (nitrogen oxides) from burning fossil fuels.

explanation_options.a: CFCs are associated with ozone layer depletion, not primarily with acid rain.
explanation_options.b: CO2 and CO are greenhouse/toxic gases but are not the primary acid-rain-forming gases (they don't readily form strong acids like SO2/NOx do).
explanation_options.c: HCl isn't a standard major combustion product responsible for acid rain in this context.
explanation_options.d: Correct — SO2 and nitrogen oxides from fossil fuel combustion are the primary acid rain contributors.

questions.question_text: During successions, the first organisms that develop on bare rock are:
questions.explanation_short: Lichens are the pioneer organisms that first colonize bare rock during ecological succession, breaking it down to eventually form soil.
questions.explanation_long: Lichens (a symbiosis of fungi and algae/cyanobacteria) can survive on bare rock with minimal nutrients, slowly breaking down the rock surface and contributing organic matter — making them the classic pioneer species in primary succession on rock.
questions.explanation_trick: Bare rock succession always starts with lichens — the classic pioneer species.

explanation_options.a: Correct — lichens are the textbook pioneer organisms in primary succession on bare rock.
explanation_options.b: Shrubs come much later in succession, once sufficient soil has developed.
explanation_options.c: Moss typically colonizes after lichens have begun breaking down the rock and creating some soil.
explanation_options.d: Herbs establish after mosses, once more soil and organic matter are present — not as the first colonizers.

questions.question_text: Trophic level of a herbivore in given food-web is: Fox Owl Dog Bettle Rat Rabbit Grass
During maternal mitosis, non-disjunction of autosomal chromosome pair results in the formation of an egg having 24 chromosomes in:
questions.explanation_short: Non-disjunction of an autosome (chromosome 21) gives an egg with 24 chromosomes → trisomy 21, Down's syndrome.
questions.explanation_long: If chromosome 21 fails to separate, the egg carries 24 chromosomes. Fertilisation then gives 47 chromosomes with three copies of 21 — Down's syndrome. Klinefelter's, Turner's and Jacob's syndromes involve sex chromosomes, not autosomes.
questions.explanation_trick: Autosomal trisomy → Down's; sex-chromosome errors → Turner's, Klinefelter's, Jacob's.

explanation_options.a: Klinefelter's (XXY) is a sex-chromosome condition.
explanation_options.b: Correct — autosomal non-disjunction gives Down's syndrome.
explanation_options.c: Turner's (XO) is a sex-chromosome condition with a missing chromosome.
explanation_options.d: Jacob's (XYY) is a sex-chromosome condition.

questions.question_text: Typical symptoms like enlarged breasts and small testis in male are attributed to:
questions.explanation_short: Enlarged breasts (gynaecomastia) and small testes in males are signs of Klinefelter's syndrome (XXY).
questions.explanation_long: The extra X chromosome in Klinefelter's syndrome (47, XXY) causes low testosterone, small testes, infertility and breast enlargement in males.
questions.explanation_trick: Klinefelter = XXY male.

explanation_options.a: Down's syndrome is trisomy 21 with different features.
explanation_options.b: Turner's syndrome (XO) affects females.
explanation_options.c: Correct — Klinefelter's syndrome.
explanation_options.d: Phenylketonuria is a metabolic enzyme disorder.

questions.question_text: Fluid mosaic model of plasma membrane states that protein molecules float in a fluid _____ layer.
questions.explanation_short: The fluid mosaic model: proteins float in a fluid phospholipid bilayer.
questions.explanation_long: Singer and Nicolson described the membrane as a fluid bilayer of phospholipids with proteins embedded in or floating on it, forming a shifting mosaic.
questions.explanation_trick: Fluid = phospholipid bilayer; mosaic = proteins.

explanation_options.a: Galactose is a sugar, not the membrane's fluid layer.
explanation_options.b: Correct — phospholipids.
explanation_options.c: Glucose is a sugar.
explanation_options.d: Carbohydrates are attached to the surface but do not form the bilayer.

questions.question_text: How many triplets of microtubules are present in centriole?
questions.explanation_short: A centriole has nine triplets of microtubules (the 9 + 0 arrangement).
questions.explanation_long: Centrioles, and the basal bodies of cilia, are cylinders of nine microtubule triplets with no central pair. Cilia and flagella themselves have a 9 + 2 arrangement of doublets.
questions.explanation_trick: Centriole 9 × 3; cilium 9 × 2 + 2.

explanation_options.a: Ten is not the count.
