explanation_options.b: Eight is not the count.
explanation_options.c: Correct — nine triplets.
explanation_options.d: Seven is not the count.

questions.question_text: Turner’s syndrome is characterized by having:
questions.explanation_short: Turner's syndrome is characterized by a missing X chromosome, giving a karyotype of 44 autosomes plus a single X (44+XO).
questions.explanation_long: Turner's syndrome affects females who are missing one X chromosome entirely, resulting in a 45,X (44 autosomes + XO) karyotype rather than the typical 46,XX — causing distinctive developmental features.
questions.explanation_trick: Turner's = missing sex chromosome entirely: 44+XO (not an extra chromosome, but a missing one).

explanation_options.a: Trisomy 21 describes Down's syndrome, not Turner's.
explanation_options.b: 44+XXY describes Klinefelter's syndrome (an extra X in males), not Turner's.
explanation_options.c: Trisomy 18 describes Edward's syndrome, not Turner's.
explanation_options.d: Correct — 44+XO (a single, unpaired X chromosome) is the defining karyotype of Turner's syndrome.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following cell structure is involved in the synthesis of lipids?
questions.explanation_short: The Golgi complex is the answer keyed by the paper for lipid synthesis; strictly, the smooth ER is the main site.
questions.explanation_long: The paper's key marks the Golgi complex. Modern textbooks name the smooth endoplasmic reticulum as the main site of lipid synthesis, and the Golgi modifies and packages lipids and proteins (e.g. forming glycolipids). Keep both facts in mind: 'lipid synthesis' → smooth ER, 'packaging/modification' → Golgi.
questions.explanation_trick: Smooth ER makes lipids; Golgi packages them.

explanation_options.a: Smooth ER is the textbook site of lipid synthesis, though this paper's key marks B.
explanation_options.b: Correct per this paper's key — the Golgi complex.
explanation_options.c: Centrioles organise spindle microtubules.
explanation_options.d: Mitochondria carry out aerobic respiration.

questions.question_text: Monosaccharides are major components of:
questions.option_a: DNA, ATP, Ribulose bisphosphate and Cysteine
questions.option_c: DNA, NADP, ATP and Ribulose bisphosphate
questions.explanation_short: Ribose or deoxyribose sugars are part of DNA, NADP, ATP and ribulose bisphosphate.
questions.explanation_long: DNA contains deoxyribose; NADP and ATP contain ribose; ribulose bisphosphate is itself a phosphorylated five-carbon sugar. Cysteine, insulin and myosin are proteins or amino acids, not sugar-based.
questions.explanation_trick: Every member must contain a sugar — watch out for proteins in the list.

explanation_options.a: Cysteine is an amino acid with no sugar.
explanation_options.b: Insulin is a protein.
explanation_options.c: Correct — all four contain a pentose sugar.
explanation_options.d: Myosin is a protein.

questions.question_text: Blood group antigen contains:
questions.explanation_short: ABO blood group antigens are glycoproteins (and glycolipids) on the red cell surface; the key marks glycoproteins.
questions.explanation_long: The A and B antigens are defined by sugar chains attached to membrane proteins and lipids. The paper's key selects glycoproteins, the standard textbook answer.
questions.explanation_trick: Blood group antigen = sugar tag on a protein.

explanation_options.a: Correct — glycoproteins.
explanation_options.b: Phospholipids form the bilayer, not the antigen.
explanation_options.c: Glycolipids also carry ABO sugars, but the key marks glycoproteins.
explanation_options.d: Sphingolipids are not the defining antigen here.

questions.question_text: Myosin is a __________ type of protein.
questions.explanation_short: Myosin is a fibrous type of protein, forming long, thread-like filaments essential for muscle contraction.
questions.explanation_long: Fibrous proteins have elongated, thread-like structures suited for structural/mechanical roles. Myosin, forming the thick filaments in muscle sarcomeres and generating contractile force, fits this fibrous category rather than being a compact globular protein.
questions.explanation_trick: Myosin = long filamentous protein in muscle = fibrous protein category.

explanation_options.a: "Intermediate" isn't a standard protein shape classification alongside fibrous/globular.
explanation_options.b: "Simple" isn't a standard shape-based protein classification.
explanation_options.c: Globular proteins are compact and rounded (like enzymes/haemoglobin), not elongated like myosin.
explanation_options.d: Correct — myosin's elongated, filamentous structure classifies it as a fibrous protein.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following is an example of unsaturated fatty acid?
questions.explanation_short: Oleic acid (C18:1) has a carbon–carbon double bond, so it is unsaturated.
questions.explanation_long: Unsaturated fatty acids contain C=C double bonds. Oleic acid, found in olive oil, has one. Butyric, palmitic and acetic acids are saturated.
questions.explanation_trick: Oleic → oil → unsaturated.

explanation_options.a: Butyric acid is saturated.
explanation_options.b: Correct — oleic acid is unsaturated.
explanation_options.c: Palmitic acid is saturated.
explanation_options.d: Acetic acid is a short saturated acid.

questions.question_text: Number of base pairs in one turn of DNA is:
questions.explanation_short: One complete turn of the DNA double helix spans 10 base pairs.
questions.explanation_long: The classic B-DNA double helix structure completes one full 360° turn approximately every 10 base pairs (spanning about 3.4 nm), a fundamental structural parameter of DNA discovered by Watson and Crick.
questions.explanation_trick: DNA helix: 10 base pairs per full turn — a core structural fact to memorize.

explanation_options.a: Correct — 10 base pairs per turn is the standard structural parameter of the DNA double helix.
explanation_options.b: 2 undercounts drastically — this isn't a meaningful base-pair-per-turn value.
explanation_options.c: 34 refers to the length in Angstroms of one turn (3.4 nm), not the number of base pairs — a common confusion point.
explanation_options.d: 54 overcounts drastically — this isn't a meaningful base-pair-per-turn value.

questions.question_text: The lymph vessel of villi is called:
questions.explanation_short: The lymph vessel inside each intestinal villus is the lacteal, which absorbs fats.
questions.explanation_long: Each villus has a central lacteal. Digested fats pass into it as chylomicrons and travel through the lymphatic system.
questions.explanation_trick: Lacteal = milky fat-carrying lymph.

explanation_options.a: The epithelium lines the villus.
explanation_options.b: Afferent lymph vessels carry lymph into lymph nodes.
explanation_options.c: The adrenals are glands above the kidneys.
explanation_options.d: Correct — the lacteal.

questions.question_text: Right atrium is separated from right ventricle by:
questions.explanation_short: The tricuspid valve separates the right atrium from the right ventricle.
questions.explanation_long: The right atrioventricular valve has three cusps (tricuspid). The left side has the bicuspid (mitral) valve, and the semilunar valves guard the aorta and pulmonary artery.
questions.explanation_trick: 'Try' before you 'buy': tricuspid on the right, bicuspid on the left.

explanation_options.a: The bicuspid valve is on the left side.
explanation_options.b: Semilunar valves guard the exits of the arteries.
explanation_options.c: Correct — the tricuspid valve.
explanation_options.d: The interatrial septum separates the two atria.

questions.question_text: The flaps of tricuspid valves are attached to muscular extensions of right ventricle known as:
questions.explanation_short: The tricuspid flaps are tied by chordae tendineae to papillary muscles in the ventricle wall.
questions.explanation_long: Papillary muscles contract with the ventricle and pull on the chordae tendineae, stopping the valve flaps from being pushed back into the atrium.
questions.explanation_trick: Chordae tendineae → papillary muscles.

explanation_options.a: Smooth muscle is not found in the heart wall.
explanation_options.b: Correct — papillary muscles.
explanation_options.c: Intercostal muscles lie between the ribs.
explanation_options.d: Skeletal muscle is not found in the heart.

questions.question_text: One complete heart beat consists of one systole and one diastole and lasts for about:
questions.explanation_short: One complete heartbeat cycle (systole + diastole) lasts about 0.8 seconds, corresponding to a resting heart rate of roughly 75 beats per minute.
questions.explanation_long: The cardiac cycle timing is a standard physiology value: about 0.8 seconds total for one full heartbeat (combining atrial and ventricular systole and diastole phases), which corresponds to approximately 75 beats per minute at rest.
questions.explanation_trick: One heartbeat cycle ≈ 0.8 seconds — matches a resting heart rate around 75 bpm (60/0.8=75).

explanation_options.a: Correct — 0.8 seconds is the standard textbook duration for one complete heartbeat cycle.
explanation_options.b: 0.2 seconds is far too short for a full heartbeat cycle.
explanation_options.c: 0.4 seconds is roughly half the correct standard cardiac cycle duration.
explanation_options.d: 0.5 seconds doesn't match the standard 0.8-second cardiac cycle value.

questions.question_text: The heart beat cycle starts when electric impulses are generated from;
questions.explanation_short: Each heartbeat starts at the sino-atrial (SA) node, the pacemaker.
questions.explanation_long: The SA node in the right atrial wall fires first. The impulse spreads across the atria to the AV node, then down the bundle of His and the Purkinje fibres.
questions.explanation_trick: SA starts it, AV delays it.

explanation_options.a: The AV node relays the impulse after the SA node.
explanation_options.b: 'SV node' is not a structure.
explanation_options.c: Correct — the SA node.
explanation_options.d: 'PQ' is an ECG interval, not a node.

questions.question_text: About 70-85% CO₂ in blood is carried:
questions.explanation_short: The majority of CO2 in blood (about 70-85%) is transported as bicarbonate ions (HCO3-), formed after CO2 combines with water in red blood cells.
questions.explanation_long: CO2 diffuses into red blood cells, combines with water (catalyzed by carbonic anhydrase) to form carbonic acid, which dissociates into bicarbonate and H+. This bicarbonate form is by far the dominant way CO2 travels in blood, more than as dissolved gas or bound to proteins.
questions.explanation_trick: Most CO2 travels in blood as bicarbonate (HCO3-), not as free dissolved gas.

explanation_options.a: Carboxylase myoglobin isn't a standard recognized CO2 transport form in blood.
explanation_options.b: Only a small fraction of CO2 binds directly with plasma proteins (a form called carbaminohemoglobin mainly applies to hemoglobin, not general plasma proteins).
explanation_options.c: Only a small fraction of CO2 travels as freely dissolved gas — most converts to bicarbonate.
explanation_options.d: Correct — bicarbonate ions are the dominant transport form for CO2 in blood, accounting for 70-85%.

aliases: About 70-85% CO2 in blood is carried:
As carboxylase myoglobin

questions.question_text: Those nephrons which are present along the border of the cortex and medulla are called:
questions.explanation_short: Nephrons located along the border between the cortex and medulla, with long loops of Henle extending deep into the medulla, are called juxtamedullary nephrons.
questions.explanation_long: Juxtamedullary nephrons (named for being "next to the medulla") have long loops of Henle that penetrate deep into the renal medulla, playing a key role in producing concentrated urine via the countercurrent multiplier mechanism.
questions.explanation_trick: "Juxta-medullary" = next to the medulla — nephrons positioned at the cortex-medulla border with long loops.

explanation_options.a: Correct — juxtamedullary nephrons are specifically those positioned along the cortex-medulla border.
explanation_options.b: Cortical nephrons are located mainly within the cortex, with shorter loops, not specifically at the cortex-medulla border.
explanation_options.c: "Internal nephrons" isn't the standard anatomical term used for this classification.
explanation_options.d: "Outer nephrons" isn't the standard anatomical term used for this classification.

questions.question_text: When water is in short supply, increased water retention occurs through the:
questions.explanation_short: Juxtamedullary nephrons have long loops of Henle reaching deep into the medulla, so they concentrate urine when water is short.
questions.explanation_long: Long loops of Henle create a strong salt gradient in the medulla. This lets water be reabsorbed from the collecting ducts, producing concentrated urine. Cortical nephrons have short loops and cannot do this as well.
questions.explanation_trick: Long loop → concentrated urine → juxtamedullary.

explanation_options.a: Cortical nephrons have short loops.
explanation_options.b: The PCT reabsorbs a constant fraction, not adjusted for water shortage.
explanation_options.c: Correct — juxtamedullary nephrons.
explanation_options.d: The cortex tissue alone does not concentrate urine.

questions.question_text: In nephrons, counter-current multiplier occurs at:
questions.explanation_short: The countercurrent multiplier mechanism, which concentrates urine, operates at the loop of Henle.
questions.explanation_long: The loop of Henle's descending and ascending limbs have different permeabilities to water and salt, creating an osmotic gradient in the medulla through a countercurrent multiplier effect — this is the core kidney mechanism for concentrating urine.
questions.explanation_trick: Countercurrent multiplier = loop of Henle's signature function.

explanation_options.a: Correct — the loop of Henle is where the countercurrent multiplier mechanism operates.
explanation_options.b: The collecting duct is influenced by the medullary gradient created by the loop of Henle, but isn't where the multiplier mechanism itself originates.
explanation_options.c: Bowman's capsule is where initial filtration occurs, not where the countercurrent mechanism operates.
explanation_options.d: The glomerulus is the filtration structure, unrelated to the countercurrent concentrating mechanism.

questions.question_text: Ascending loop of Henle does not allow outflow of:
questions.explanation_short: The ascending loop of Henle is impermeable to water, so it does not allow water to flow out, even while actively transporting ions like Na+ and Cl- out.
questions.explanation_long: A defining feature of the ascending limb of the loop of Henle is its impermeability to water, even as it actively pumps out sodium and chloride ions — this creates the osmotic gradient in the medulla without diluting the surrounding tissue with water loss.
questions.explanation_trick: Ascending loop of Henle: pumps out salt (Na+, Cl-) but NEVER lets water follow — water-impermeable.

explanation_options.a: Na+ ions are actively transported OUT of the ascending loop, unlike water which stays in.
explanation_options.b: K+ ions can also be involved in transport at this segment, unlike water which is blocked entirely.
explanation_options.c: Cl- ions are actively transported OUT of the ascending loop, unlike water which stays in.
explanation_options.d: Correct — water is the substance specifically blocked from leaving the water-impermeable ascending loop of Henle.

aliases: Ascending loop of Henle does not allow outflow of:
Na+ ions

questions.question_text: A larger quantity of dilute urine is produced in diabetes insipidus. This disease is due to the deficiency of:
questions.explanation_short: Diabetes insipidus, causing excessive dilute urine, results from a deficiency of antidiuretic hormone (ADH/vasopressin).
questions.explanation_long: ADH normally signals the kidney's collecting ducts to reabsorb more water, concentrating urine. Without enough ADH (diabetes insipidus), the collecting ducts remain relatively impermeable to water, resulting in large volumes of dilute urine being excreted.
questions.explanation_trick: Diabetes insipidus = ADH deficiency = too much dilute urine (not to be confused with diabetes mellitus, an insulin/blood sugar disorder).

explanation_options.a: Correct — a deficiency of antidiuretic hormone (ADH) is the defining cause of diabetes insipidus.
explanation_options.b: Aldosterone regulates sodium/potassium balance; its deficiency causes different symptoms, not primarily this classic dilute-urine picture.
explanation_options.c: Thyroxine deficiency causes hypothyroidism, unrelated to urine dilution in this way.
explanation_options.d: Cortisol deficiency is associated with Addison's disease, not diabetes insipidus.

questions.question_text: Water and sodium ions are reabsorbed in:
questions.explanation_short: Water and Na⁺ are reabsorbed mainly in the proximal convoluted tubule, with fine control in the collecting duct.
questions.explanation_long: About two-thirds of filtered sodium and water is reabsorbed in the PCT. ADH (for water) and aldosterone (for Na⁺) adjust the rest in the distal tubule and collecting duct. The bladder, urethra and ureter only store or carry urine.
questions.explanation_trick: Reabsorption happens in the nephron, never in the plumbing.

explanation_options.a: The bladder and urethra only store and pass urine.
explanation_options.b: The ureter only carries urine.
explanation_options.c: The adrenal cortex secretes aldosterone but reabsorbs nothing itself.
explanation_options.d: Correct — the PCT and collecting duct.

questions.question_text: Which disease is responsible for dementia (memory loss)?
questions.explanation_short: Alzheimer's disease is the leading cause of dementia (progressive memory loss).
questions.explanation_long: Alzheimer's destroys neurons, with amyloid plaques and tangles, causing progressive loss of memory and thinking. Parkinson's mainly affects movement, epilepsy causes seizures, and Graves' disease is hyperthyroidism.
questions.explanation_trick: Memory → Alzheimer's; movement → Parkinson's.

explanation_options.a: Parkinson's is primarily a movement disorder.
explanation_options.b: Correct — Alzheimer's disease.
explanation_options.c: Epilepsy is a seizure disorder.
explanation_options.d: Graves' disease is an overactive thyroid.

questions.question_text: Neurotransmitter secreted at synapse outside the central nervous system is:
questions.explanation_short: Acetylcholine is the neurotransmitter secreted at synapses outside the central nervous system, such as neuromuscular junctions and autonomic ganglia.
questions.explanation_long: Acetylcholine (ACh) is the primary neurotransmitter used at peripheral synapses, including the neuromuscular junction where motor neurons signal muscles, and at many autonomic nervous system synapses — distinguishing it from dopamine and other neurotransmitters more associated with the central nervous system.
questions.explanation_trick: ACh = the peripheral nervous system's go-to neurotransmitter, especially at neuromuscular junctions.

explanation_options.a: Dopamine is primarily associated with central nervous system pathways (like reward and movement circuits), not peripheral synapses.
explanation_options.b: Polypeptide neurotransmitters (neuropeptides) exist but aren't the classic answer for peripheral synapses outside the CNS.
explanation_options.c: Androgen is a steroid hormone, not a neurotransmitter released at synapses.
explanation_options.d: Correct — acetylcholine is the standard neurotransmitter for synapses outside the central nervous system.

questions.question_text: Conduction of action potentials from one mode of Ranvier to another in myelinated neurons is through:
questions.explanation_short: In myelinated neurons, action potentials jump between successive nodes of Ranvier via saltatory conduction, which speeds up impulse transmission.
questions.explanation_long: Myelin sheaths insulate the axon between nodes of Ranvier, forcing the action potential to "jump" from node to node rather than traveling continuously along the membrane — this saltatory conduction dramatically increases conduction speed.
questions.explanation_trick: "Saltatory" comes from Latin "saltare" (to jump) — the impulse jumps node to node in myelinated neurons.

explanation_options.a: Hyperpolarization is a phase of the action potential itself, not the mechanism of jumping between nodes.
explanation_options.b: Resting membrane potential describes the neuron's baseline state, not the conduction mechanism between nodes.
explanation_options.c: Depolarization is a phase of the action potential itself, not the mechanism of jumping between nodes.
explanation_options.d: Correct — saltatory conduction is the specific term for impulses jumping between nodes of Ranvier in myelinated neurons.

questions.question_text: In the following diagram of action potential in a neuron, ‘x’ depicts:
questions.explanation_short: On an action potential graph, the initial rapid upward swing from resting potential toward +50 mV represents depolarization.
questions.explanation_long: Depolarization is the phase where the membrane potential rapidly becomes less negative (moving toward positive values) as sodium channels open and Na+ rushes in — matching the labeled rising portion 'x' on a typical action potential trace.
questions.explanation_trick: Rising sharply upward on the graph = depolarization (sodium rushing in).

explanation_options.a: Correct — the labeled rising phase on the action potential graph represents depolarization.
explanation_options.b: Polarization describes the resting state itself, not an active phase of change.
explanation_options.c: Repolarization is the falling phase back toward resting potential, not the rising phase.
explanation_options.d: Hyperpolarization is when the potential dips below resting level, a different phase than the rising 'x' segment.

aliases: In the following diagram of action potential in a neuron, ‘x’ depicts: Membrane +50 ― Potential 0 ― (mV) -50 ― x -100 ― Time (milliseconds)
Depolarization

questions.question_text: In human testis, which structure is responsible for carrying sperm from inside the testis?
questions.explanation_short: Sperm are carried out of the testis via the vasa efferentia, small ducts connecting the seminiferous tubules to the epididymis.
questions.explanation_long: After sperm are produced in the seminiferous tubules, they travel through the rete testis and then through the vasa efferentia (efferent ductules), which carry them out of the testis toward the epididymis for maturation and storage.
questions.explanation_trick: Vasa efferentia = the exit ducts carrying sperm OUT of the testis toward the epididymis.

explanation_options.a: Seminiferous tubules are where sperm are produced, not the duct carrying them out.
explanation_options.b: The urinogenital duct is a later shared pathway, not the initial exit route from the testis.
explanation_options.c: Seminal vesicles add fluid to semen later, downstream of the testis itself.
explanation_options.d: Correct — vasa efferentia are the specific ducts carrying sperm out of the testis.

questions.question_text: In which part of female reproductive system fertilization takes place?
questions.explanation_short: Fertilization in the female reproductive system typically occurs in the proximal (ampulla) part of the oviduct (fallopian tube).
questions.explanation_long: After ovulation, the egg travels into the oviduct, where sperm typically meet and fertilize it in the upper/proximal region (the ampulla) — before the resulting zygote continues moving toward the uterus for implantation.
questions.explanation_trick: Fertilization site: the proximal/ampullary region of the oviduct, not the uterus itself.

explanation_options.a: Correct — fertilization classically occurs in the proximal part (ampulla) of the oviduct.
explanation_options.b: The uterus is where implantation occurs, not fertilization itself.
explanation_options.c: The placenta forms after implantation, much later than fertilization.
explanation_options.d: The vagina is where sperm are deposited, far from where fertilization actually occurs.

questions.question_text: In females, FSH stimulates the ovary to produce:
questions.explanation_short: FSH stimulates ovarian follicles to grow and secrete oestrogen.
questions.explanation_long: Follicle-stimulating hormone promotes follicle development, and the growing follicle cells secrete oestrogen. Progesterone comes mainly from the corpus luteum under LH.
questions.explanation_trick: FSH → follicle → oestrogen; LH → corpus luteum → progesterone.

explanation_options.a: Progesterone is produced mainly by the corpus luteum under LH.
explanation_options.b: Lactin (prolactin) comes from the pituitary.
explanation_options.c: Correct — oestrogen.
explanation_options.d: Oxytocin comes from the posterior pituitary.

questions.question_text: Syphilis, sexually transmitted disease is caused by:
questions.explanation_short: Syphilis is caused by the spirochaete bacterium Treponema pallidum.
questions.explanation_long: Treponema pallidum is a spiral bacterium spread through sexual contact. Neisseria gonorrhoeae causes gonorrhoea, and HIV causes AIDS.
questions.explanation_trick: Syphilis → Treponema; gonorrhoea → Neisseria.

explanation_options.a: HIV causes AIDS.
explanation_options.b: Correct — Treponema pallidum.
explanation_options.c: Neisseria gonorrhoeae causes gonorrhoea.
explanation_options.d: 'Type 2 virus' (HSV-2) causes genital herpes.

questions.question_text: In which phase of human female menstrual cycle, endometrium prepares for the implantation of embryo?
questions.explanation_short: In the secretory (luteal) phase, progesterone makes the endometrium thick, glandular and ready for implantation.
questions.explanation_long: After ovulation the corpus luteum secretes progesterone, which turns the thickened endometrium into a nutrient-rich lining ready for an embryo. The proliferative phase rebuilds the lining; the menstrual phase sheds it.
questions.explanation_trick: Secretory phase = ready for implantation.

explanation_options.a: The proliferative phase rebuilds the lining under oestrogen.
explanation_options.b: The menstrual phase sheds the lining.
explanation_options.c: Correct — the secretory phase.
explanation_options.d: Ovulation is a single event, not the preparation phase.

questions.question_text: The total number of cervical and thoracic vertebrate in human vertebral column is:
questions.explanation_short: 7 cervical + 12 thoracic = 19 vertebrae.
questions.explanation_long: The human column has 7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 fused sacral and about 4 fused coccygeal vertebrae (33 in all). Cervical plus thoracic is 19.
questions.explanation_trick: Breakfast at 7, lunch at 12, dinner at 5.

explanation_options.a: 7 is the cervical count only.
explanation_options.b: Correct — 7 + 12 = 19.
explanation_options.c: 14 does not match any grouping.
explanation_options.d: 33 is the total for the whole column.

questions.question_text: A sarcomere is the region of a myofibril between two successive:
questions.explanation_short: A sarcomere is the section of a myofibril between two successive Z-lines.
questions.explanation_long: The sarcomere, the unit of contraction, runs from one Z-line to the next. It contains a central A-band and half an I-band at each end.
questions.explanation_trick: Sarcomere: Z to Z.

explanation_options.a: The M-line is the middle of the sarcomere.
explanation_options.b: Correct — Z-lines.
explanation_options.c: I-bands straddle the Z-lines rather than bounding the sarcomere.
explanation_options.d: T-tubules are membrane invaginations.

questions.question_text: The sarcolemma of muscle fibre folds inwards and forms a system of tubes which runs through the sarcoplasm called:
questions.explanation_short: The muscle fiber's sarcolemma folds inward to form transverse (T-) tubules, which run through the sarcoplasm to help transmit electrical signals deep into the fiber.
questions.explanation_long: T-tubules are extensions of the cell membrane (sarcolemma) that penetrate into the muscle fiber's interior, allowing action potentials to reach deep sarcoplasmic reticulum regions quickly and trigger synchronized calcium release for contraction.
questions.explanation_trick: Sarcolemma folds inward = T-tubules — the signal-delivery highway into the muscle fiber's interior.

explanation_options.a: Myofilaments (actin/myosin) are the contractile proteins themselves, not membrane folds.
explanation_options.b: The sarcoplasmic reticulum stores calcium but is a separate membrane system from the T-tubules (though closely associated with them).
explanation_options.c: Z-lines are structural sarcomere boundaries, not membrane tubule systems.
explanation_options.d: Correct — transverse (T-) tubules are the inward folds of the sarcolemma that conduct signals into the fiber.

questions.question_text: According to sliding filament theory, when muscle fibers are stimulated by nervous system, which of the following changes occurs?
questions.explanation_short: According to the sliding filament theory, muscle stimulation causes the I-bands to shorten as thin filaments slide further over thick filaments, without the filaments themselves changing length.
questions.explanation_long: During contraction, actin (thin) filaments slide past myosin (thick) filaments, pulling the Z-lines closer together. This shortens the I-band (region of thin filament only) and the H-zone, while the A-band (length of thick filaments) stays constant.
questions.explanation_trick: Sliding filament: I-bands and H-zone shrink; A-band stays the same length throughout contraction.

explanation_options.a: Correct — I-bands shorten as the thin filaments slide further into the region overlapped by thick filaments.
explanation_options.b: The H-zone becomes less visible (shrinks/disappears) during contraction, not more visible.
explanation_options.c: Z-lines actually move closer together during contraction, not further apart.
explanation_options.d: The A-band's length stays constant during contraction — it doesn't shorten, since it represents the fixed length of the thick filaments.

questions.question_text: If lactic acid build up in thigh muscles, it causes muscle tiredness and pain. This condition is called:
questions.explanation_short: Buildup of lactic acid in muscles from anaerobic respiration causes muscle tiredness and pain, a condition called muscle fatigue.
questions.explanation_long: When muscles work harder than oxygen supply allows, they switch to anaerobic glycolysis, producing lactic acid as a byproduct. This lactic acid accumulation lowers pH in the muscle tissue, interfering with contraction and causing the sensation of fatigue and soreness.
questions.explanation_trick: Lactic acid buildup from anaerobic respiration = muscle fatigue (tiredness and pain).

explanation_options.a: Correct — muscle fatigue is the standard term for lactic-acid-induced tiredness and pain.
explanation_options.b: Tetany refers to sustained, involuntary muscle spasms often linked to calcium imbalance, not lactic acid buildup.
explanation_options.c: Cramps are sudden, involuntary muscle contractions, a related but distinct phenomenon from generalized fatigue.
explanation_options.d: "Oxygen debt" is the underlying cause requiring extra oxygen afterward, but the resulting symptom described here is specifically termed muscle fatigue.

questions.question_text: Thyroxine deficiency in adults’ results in a condition called:
questions.explanation_short: Thyroxine deficiency in adults causes myxoedema.
questions.explanation_long: Adult hypothyroidism leads to myxoedema: a low metabolic rate, puffy skin, weight gain and sluggishness. In children the deficiency causes cretinism. Hypothyroidism is the general state; myxoedema is the named adult condition.
questions.explanation_trick: Child → cretinism; adult → myxoedema.

explanation_options.a: Cretinism is thyroxine deficiency in children.
explanation_options.b: Hypothyroidism is the general state; the named adult condition is myxoedema.
explanation_options.c: Thyrotoxicosis is excess thyroxine.
explanation_options.d: Correct — myxoedema.

questions.question_text: α-cells of pancreas secrete a hormone known as:
questions.explanation_short: Alpha-cells of the pancreas secrete glucagon, a hormone that raises blood glucose levels.
questions.explanation_long: Pancreatic islet alpha-cells produce glucagon, which stimulates the liver to break down glycogen and release glucose into the blood — working opposite to insulin (from beta-cells) to help regulate blood sugar balance.
questions.explanation_trick: Alpha-cells = glucagon (raises blood sugar). Beta-cells = insulin (lowers blood sugar).

explanation_options.a: Correct — alpha-cells specifically secrete glucagon.
explanation_options.b: Insulin is secreted by pancreatic beta-cells, not alpha-cells.
explanation_options.c: Gastrin is secreted by stomach cells, not pancreatic alpha-cells.
explanation_options.d: Rennin (chymosin) is a digestive enzyme, not a pancreatic alpha-cell hormone.

questions.question_text: X-linked recessive trait is:
questions.explanation_short: Haemophilia is the classic X-linked recessive disorder.
questions.explanation_long: Haemophilia genes are on the X chromosome and are recessive, so it mostly affects males who inherit one faulty X. Hypophosphataemia (vitamin-D-resistant rickets) is X-linked dominant.
questions.explanation_trick: Haemophilia and colour blindness: X-linked recessive.

explanation_options.a: Hypophosphataemia is X-linked dominant.
explanation_options.b: Vitamin-D-resistant rickets is X-linked dominant.
explanation_options.c: Correct — haemophilia.
explanation_options.d: Diabetes mellitus is not X-linked.

questions.question_text: Human skin colour is a good example of?
questions.explanation_short: Skin colour is controlled by several genes adding up their effects — polygenic inheritance.
questions.explanation_long: Several independent genes each add a small amount of pigment, giving a continuous range of skin tones. That is polygenic (quantitative) inheritance, not sex-linked inheritance.
questions.explanation_trick: Continuous variation → polygenic.

explanation_options.a: Sex-linked traits are not continuous like skin colour.
explanation_options.b: Correct — polygenic inheritance.
explanation_options.c: X-linked traits follow sex-linked patterns.
explanation_options.d: Y-linked traits pass only father to son.

questions.question_text: From evolutionary point of view, which respiratory protein is common in many organisms?
questions.explanation_short: Cytochrome c is found in nearly all aerobic organisms and is highly conserved, so it is used to trace evolution.
questions.explanation_long: Cytochrome c is a small electron-transport protein present from yeast to humans. Comparing its amino-acid sequence across species is a classic molecular evidence for evolution.
questions.explanation_trick: Evolution protein = cytochrome c.

explanation_options.a: Cytochrome a is not the classic evolution marker.
explanation_options.b: Cytochrome b is not the classic evolution marker.
explanation_options.c: Correct — cytochrome c.
explanation_options.d: Cytochrome d is found only in some bacteria.

questions.question_text: Number of pairs of autosomes in humans in:
questions.explanation_short: Humans have 22 pairs of autosomes (non-sex chromosomes), plus one pair of sex chromosomes, totaling 23 pairs (46 chromosomes).
questions.explanation_long: Of the 23 total chromosome pairs in humans, 22 pairs are autosomes (numbered 1-22), and the 23rd pair consists of the sex chromosomes (XX or XY) — a key distinction in human genetics.
questions.explanation_trick: 23 total pairs = 22 autosome pairs + 1 sex chromosome pair.

explanation_options.a: 23 is the total number of chromosome pairs (including sex chromosomes), not just the autosome count.
explanation_options.b: 24 overcounts the standard number of human autosome pairs.
explanation_options.c: 21 undercounts the standard number of human autosome pairs.
explanation_options.d: Correct — 22 pairs of autosomes, plus 1 pair of sex chromosomes, make up the human genome's 23 total pairs.

questions.question_text: ABO blood system is an example of:
questions.explanation_short: The ABO system is controlled by one gene with three alleles (Iᴬ, Iᴮ, i) — multiple alleles.
questions.explanation_long: Multiple alleles means more than two alternative forms of one gene exist in a population. ABO blood group has three: Iᴬ and Iᴮ (codominant) and i (recessive).
questions.explanation_trick: One gene, many versions = multiple alleles.

explanation_options.a: Polygenes are many genes acting on one trait.
explanation_options.b: ABO is one gene, not many.
explanation_options.c: Correct — multiple alleles.
explanation_options.d: Mutation is not the inheritance pattern.

questions.question_text: Which molecular structure of enzyme is essential for activity of enzyme?
questions.explanation_short: An enzyme's tertiary structure — its overall 3D folded shape, including the precisely formed active site — is essential for its catalytic activity.
questions.explanation_long: While primary structure (amino acid sequence) underlies everything, it's the tertiary structure (the complete 3D folding pattern) that creates the specific active site shape needed for substrate binding and catalysis — making it essential for enzyme function.
questions.explanation_trick: Enzyme activity depends on tertiary structure — the 3D fold that creates the functional active site.

explanation_options.a: Primary structure (amino acid sequence) is necessary but not sufficient alone — folding into 3D shape is what creates function.
explanation_options.b: Quaternary structure applies only to multi-subunit enzymes, not a universal requirement for all enzyme activity.
explanation_options.c: Secondary structure (local folding patterns like alpha-helices) contributes to but doesn't alone determine full enzyme activity.
explanation_options.d: Correct — tertiary structure (the full 3D fold, including the active site) is essential for enzyme activity.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following edible products is widely pasteurized?
questions.explanation_short: Milk is the food most widely pasteurised.
questions.explanation_long: Pasteurisation heats milk briefly (e.g. 72 °C for 15 s) to kill pathogens without spoiling it. Milk is the classic and most widespread example.
questions.explanation_trick: Pasteur → milk.

explanation_options.a: Soft drinks are not typically pasteurised in the same way.
explanation_options.b: Squash is preserved with sugar and preservatives.
explanation_options.c: Correct — milk.
explanation_options.d: Orange juice is sometimes pasteurised, but milk is the classic answer.

questions.question_text: Ribosomes are tiny organisms, which are involved in the synthesis of:
questions.explanation_short: Ribosomes are the cell organelles responsible for protein synthesis, translating mRNA sequences into polypeptide chains.
questions.explanation_long: Ribosomes, found free in the cytoplasm or bound to rough endoplasmic reticulum, read mRNA codons and assemble corresponding amino acids into growing polypeptide chains — the fundamental process of protein synthesis (translation).
questions.explanation_trick: Ribosomes = the cell's protein factories, translating mRNA into protein.

explanation_options.a: Correct — ribosomes are specifically involved in synthesizing proteins.
explanation_options.b: RNA is synthesized in the nucleus by RNA polymerase (transcription), not by ribosomes.
explanation_options.c: The nucleus houses genetic material and is where transcription occurs, but isn't itself synthesized by ribosomes in this context.
explanation_options.d: "Nuclosome" (nucleosome) is a DNA-packaging structure, unrelated to ribosome function.

questions.question_text: Which organelle is bounded by two membranes?
questions.explanation_short: Mitochondria (like chloroplasts and the nucleus) have a double membrane.
questions.explanation_long: Mitochondria have an outer membrane and a folded inner membrane. Ribosomes and nucleoli have no membrane, and lysosomes have a single membrane.
questions.explanation_trick: Double membrane: mitochondria, chloroplasts, nucleus.

explanation_options.a: Ribosomes have no membrane.
explanation_options.b: Correct — mitochondria.
explanation_options.c: Lysosomes have a single membrane.
explanation_options.d: The nucleolus has no membrane.

questions.question_text: At the beginning of nuclear division, the number of microtubule triplets in two pairs of centrioles that migrate to opposite poles are:
questions.explanation_short: At the start of nuclear division, two pairs of centrioles migrate to opposite poles; with each centriole containing 9 microtubule triplets, two pairs (4 centrioles total) contain 4×9=36 triplets.
questions.explanation_long: Each individual centriole has 9 microtubule triplets. Since centrioles exist in pairs, and two pairs (4 centrioles total) migrate to the opposite poles of the dividing cell, the total triplet count is 4 × 9 = 36.
questions.explanation_trick: 1 centriole = 9 triplets. Two pairs = 4 centrioles = 4×9 = 36 triplets total.

explanation_options.a: 9 accounts for just a single centriole, not the full set migrating to both poles.
explanation_options.b: 18 accounts for only one pair (2 centrioles) of the two total pairs migrating to opposite poles.
explanation_options.c: 108 overcounts drastically — this doesn't match a simple multiple of 9 for the centrioles involved.
explanation_options.d: Correct — four centrioles (two pairs, one pair per pole) each with 9 triplets gives 36 total.

questions.question_text: The disease in which an individual has extra sex chromosome (44 + XXY) is known as:
questions.explanation_short: 44 + XXY (47 chromosomes) is Klinefelter's syndrome.
questions.explanation_long: An extra X in a male gives 47, XXY — Klinefelter's syndrome. Turner's is 44 + XO, Jacob's is 44 + XYY and Down's is trisomy 21.
questions.explanation_trick: XXY → Klinefelter.

explanation_options.a: Down's is trisomy 21 (autosomal).
explanation_options.b: Turner's is 44 + XO.
explanation_options.c: Correct — Klinefelter's syndrome.
explanation_options.d: Jacob's is 44 + XYY.

questions.question_text: Over-secretion of cortical hormone causes a disease called;
questions.explanation_short: Over-secretion of adrenal cortical hormones (cortisol) causes Cushing's disease/syndrome, characterized by weight gain, high blood pressure, and other metabolic effects.
questions.explanation_long: Excess cortisol production from the adrenal cortex (whether from a pituitary or adrenal tumor) results in Cushing's syndrome, with symptoms including central obesity, moon face, and elevated blood glucose — the direct opposite of Addison's disease (adrenal hormone deficiency).
questions.explanation_trick: Too much cortical hormone = Cushing's. Too little = Addison's.

explanation_options.a: Correct — over-secretion of cortical (adrenal) hormones causes Cushing's disease.
explanation_options.b: Diabetes mellitus involves insulin/blood sugar regulation issues, a different hormonal system than adrenal cortical hormones.
explanation_options.c: Hypoglycemia (low blood sugar) is generally the opposite metabolic effect of excess cortisol, which tends to raise blood sugar.
explanation_options.d: Addison's disease is caused by adrenal hormone deficiency (under-secretion), the opposite of the over-secretion described here.

questions.question_text: Ejection of milk from mammary glands is under the control of which one of the following hormones?
questions.explanation_short: Oxytocin triggers milk ejection (the let-down reflex).
questions.explanation_long: Suckling signals the posterior pituitary to release oxytocin, which contracts the cells around the milk glands and ejects milk. Prolactin makes the milk; oxytocin releases it.
questions.explanation_trick: Prolactin produces; oxytocin propels.

explanation_options.a: Androgens are male sex hormones.
explanation_options.b: Correct — oxytocin.
explanation_options.c: Progesterone prepares the breasts but does not eject milk.
explanation_options.d: Oestrogen develops the ducts but does not eject milk.

questions.question_text: Granulocytes are:
questions.explanation_short: Granulocytes are neutrophils, eosinophils and basophils.
questions.explanation_long: White cells with granules in their cytoplasm and lobed nuclei are granulocytes. Monocytes (and the macrophages they become) and lymphocytes are agranulocytes.
questions.explanation_trick: Granulocytes: NEB — neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils.

explanation_options.a: Monocytes are agranulocytes.
explanation_options.b: Macrophages are not granulocytes.
explanation_options.c: Correct — neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils.
explanation_options.d: Monocytes and macrophages are agranulocytes.

questions.question_text: Response of body against the transplanted organ is:
questions.explanation_short: The body's rejection response against a transplanted organ is a cell-mediated immune response, driven by T-lymphocytes attacking foreign tissue.
questions.explanation_long: Organ transplant rejection primarily involves cytotoxic T-cells recognizing the transplanted tissue's foreign antigens and directly attacking those cells — a classic example of cell-mediated immunity, distinct from antibody-based humoral responses.
questions.explanation_trick: Transplant rejection = T-cells attacking directly = cell-mediated immune response.

explanation_options.a: "Homeostatic response" is a general regulatory concept, not specific to immune rejection.
explanation_options.b: "Behavioral response" is unrelated to immunological transplant rejection.
explanation_options.c: "Primary response" describes the first exposure to an antigen generally, not specifically the rejection mechanism.
explanation_options.d: Correct — cell-mediated response (T-cell attack) is the mechanism behind transplant rejection.

questions.question_text: Some enzymes require helper which is non-protein part for its efficient functioning that is called:
questions.explanation_short: A non-protein helper needed for enzyme activity is a cofactor.
questions.explanation_long: Cofactors are the general class of non-protein helpers. They include metal ions (activators), coenzymes (loosely bound organic molecules) and prosthetic groups (tightly bound). The apoenzyme is the protein part alone.
questions.explanation_trick: Cofactor is the umbrella term; prosthetic group is the tightly bound kind.

explanation_options.a: 'Accelerator' is not the term.
explanation_options.b: Correct — cofactor.
explanation_options.c: A prosthetic group is one tightly bound type of cofactor, not the general term.
explanation_options.d: The apoenzyme is the protein part.

questions.question_text: Pepsin, protein digesting enzymes, sets best pH:
questions.explanation_short: Pepsin works best at about pH 2, in the acidic stomach.
questions.explanation_long: Pepsin is secreted as pepsinogen and activated by HCl. Its optimum pH is about 2, which matches gastric acidity.
questions.explanation_trick: Pepsin → pH 2; trypsin → pH 8.

explanation_options.a: pH 3 is less acidic than pepsin's optimum.
explanation_options.b: pH 4.5 is too weakly acidic.
explanation_options.c: Correct — pH 2.00.
explanation_options.d: Pepsin is largely inactive at pH 6.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following is an example of competitive inhibitor?
questions.explanation_short: Malonate is a classic example of a competitive inhibitor, structurally resembling succinate and competing for the active site of succinate dehydrogenase.
questions.explanation_long: Malonate closely mimics succinate's structure, allowing it to bind the same enzyme active site (succinate dehydrogenase) without being converted to product — blocking the true substrate competitively, a textbook example used in enzyme kinetics teaching.
questions.explanation_trick: Malonate blocking succinate dehydrogenase = the classic textbook example of competitive inhibition.

explanation_options.a: Glucose isn't relevant to this particular enzyme-substrate-inhibitor example.
explanation_options.b: Fumarate is the normal product of this enzymatic reaction, not the inhibitor.
explanation_options.c: Succinic acid (succinate) is the actual substrate being competed against, not the inhibitor itself.
explanation_options.d: Correct — malonate is the well-known competitive inhibitor of succinate dehydrogenase.

questions.question_text: HIV is classified as:
questions.explanation_short: HIV is a retrovirus — it copies its RNA into DNA with reverse transcriptase.
questions.explanation_long: HIV carries an RNA genome and the enzyme reverse transcriptase. It makes DNA that integrates into the host genome, which is the defining feature of retroviruses.
questions.explanation_trick: Reverse transcriptase → retrovirus.

explanation_options.a: Bacteriophages infect bacteria.
explanation_options.b: Oncoviruses cause cancer; HIV is classed as a lentivirus retrovirus.
explanation_options.c: Correct — retrovirus.
explanation_options.d: Describes capsid shape, not HIV's classification.

questions.question_text: Cyanobacteria are:
questions.explanation_short: Cyanobacteria are photoautotrophic bacteria, capable of photosynthesis using chlorophyll-like pigments to produce their own food from sunlight.
questions.explanation_long: Cyanobacteria (also called blue-green algae, though they're prokaryotic bacteria) perform oxygen-producing photosynthesis similar to plants, making them photoautotrophic — a defining and historically significant trait linked to Earth's early oxygenation.
questions.explanation_trick: Cyanobacteria = photosynthetic bacteria = photoautotrophic, similar in function to plants.

explanation_options.a: Correct — cyanobacteria are photoautotrophic, performing photosynthesis to produce their own food.
explanation_options.b: Chemosynthetic bacteria derive energy from inorganic chemical reactions, not sunlight like cyanobacteria.
explanation_options.c: Saprotrophic bacteria feed on dead/decaying matter, unlike cyanobacteria's photosynthetic lifestyle.
explanation_options.d: Parasitic bacteria feed off living hosts, unlike cyanobacteria's independent photosynthetic lifestyle.

questions.question_text: During favourable conditions, certain bacteria produces:
questions.explanation_short: Per the key, certain bacteria (e.g. Streptomyces) produce spores (conidia) under favourable conditions; endospores form under unfavourable ones.
questions.explanation_long: Textbooks distinguish two kinds of bacterial spores. Endospores are resistant resting structures formed in harsh conditions. Some bacteria, such as the actinomycete Streptomyces, produce reproductive spores (conidia) during favourable growth. The question refers to the latter.
questions.explanation_trick: Favourable → reproductive spores (conidia); unfavourable → endospores.

explanation_options.a: All bacteria always have ribosomes — nothing special to favourable conditions.
explanation_options.b: Plasmids are extra DNA, not a product of favourable conditions.
explanation_options.c: Bacteria have no mitochondria.
explanation_options.d: Correct — spores (conidia) in certain bacteria.

questions.question_text: In rhizopus, zygote forms temporary, dormant, thick-walled resistant structure called:
questions.explanation_short: In Rhizopus (bread mold), the zygote develops a thick, resistant wall to form a dormant structure called a zygospore.
questions.explanation_long: When compatible hyphae of Rhizopus fuse sexually, the resulting zygote develops a tough, thick protective wall, becoming a zygospore — a dormant, resistant structure that can survive unfavourable conditions before germinating.
questions.explanation_trick: Rhizopus sexual reproduction: zygote → thick-walled dormant zygospore.

explanation_options.a: Correct — the zygospore is specifically the thick-walled dormant structure formed from the zygote in Rhizopus.
explanation_options.b: A generic "spore" doesn't capture the specific thick-walled, dormant zygote structure being described.
explanation_options.c: Sporangia are the structures that produce asexual spores, a different reproductive structure from the sexual zygospore.
explanation_options.d: "Hydra" is an unrelated animal, not a fungal reproductive structure.

questions.question_text: ___________ is a triploblastic organism.
questions.explanation_short: Tapeworms (flatworms) are triploblastic; jellyfish, sea anemones and corals are diploblastic cnidarians.
questions.explanation_long: Triploblastic animals develop from three germ layers (ectoderm, mesoderm, endoderm). Platyhelminthes such as tapeworms are the first triploblastic group. Cnidarians have only two layers.
questions.explanation_trick: Cnidarians = 2 layers; flatworms and beyond = 3.

explanation_options.a: Jellyfish are diploblastic.
explanation_options.b: Sea anemones are diploblastic.
explanation_options.c: Correct — tapeworm.
explanation_options.d: Corals are diploblastic.

questions.question_text: In arthropods, the body cavity is in the form of:
questions.explanation_short: Arthropods have an open circulatory system, and their body cavity is a blood-filled haemocoel.
questions.explanation_long: In arthropods the true coelom is reduced, and the main body cavity is the haemocoel, bathed directly in haemolymph.
questions.explanation_trick: Open circulation → haemocoel.

explanation_options.a: A true coelom is reduced in arthropods.
explanation_options.b: Correct — haemocoel.
explanation_options.c: A pseudocoelom is found in roundworms.
explanation_options.d: The enteron is the gut cavity.

questions.question_text: ___________ is a good example of polymorphism.
questions.explanation_short: Obelia shows polymorphism — polyps for feeding and reproduction and free-swimming medusae in one life cycle.
questions.explanation_long: Polymorphism means one species has structurally different individuals doing different jobs. Obelia colonies have feeding polyps, reproductive polyps and medusae.
questions.explanation_trick: Colonial cnidarian with polyps + medusae = Obelia.

explanation_options.a: Hydra is a solitary polyp.
explanation_options.b: Starfish are not polymorphic.
explanation_options.c: Correct — Obelia.
explanation_options.d: Euplectella is a glass sponge.

questions.question_text: Name common gut roundworm parasite of human and pigs.
questions.explanation_short: Ascaris lumbricoides is the common gut roundworm parasite found in both humans and pigs.
questions.explanation_long: Ascaris lumbricoides (and the closely related Ascaris suum in pigs) is a large intestinal roundworm parasite, one of the most common helminth infections worldwide, distinguishing it from the other worm genera listed (which are earthworms or leeches, not gut parasites of this kind).
questions.explanation_trick: Ascaris = the classic large roundworm gut parasite of humans and pigs.

explanation_options.a: Correct — Ascaris lumbricoides is the standard gut roundworm parasite shared by humans and pigs.
explanation_options.b: Lumbricus terrestris is the common earthworm, not a gut parasite.
explanation_options.c: Pheretima posthuma is a common earthworm species, not a parasite.
explanation_options.d: Hirudo medicinalis is the medicinal leech, not a gut roundworm parasite.

questions.question_text: ___________ is also called liver fluke.
questions.explanation_short: Fasciola hepatica is the liver fluke.
questions.explanation_long: Fasciola is a trematode flatworm that lives in the bile ducts of sheep, cattle and sometimes humans. Taenia is the tapeworm and Dugesia is a free-living planarian.
questions.explanation_trick: Fasciola hepatica — hepatic means liver.

explanation_options.a: Dugesia is a free-living planarian.
explanation_options.b: Taenia is a tapeworm.
explanation_options.c: Correct — Fasciola.
explanation_options.d: Coral is a cnidarian.

questions.question_text: Oxyntic cells in stomach produces:
questions.explanation_short: Oxyntic (parietal) cells in the stomach lining produce hydrochloric acid (HCl), essential for digestion and activating pepsin.
questions.explanation_long: Oxyntic cells, also called parietal cells, secrete hydrochloric acid into the stomach lumen, creating the highly acidic environment needed to kill ingested pathogens and activate pepsinogen into active pepsin.
questions.explanation_trick: Oxyntic (parietal) cells = HCl producers in the stomach.

explanation_options.a: Pepsin is produced by chief cells (as inactive pepsinogen), not oxyntic cells.
explanation_options.b: Pepsinogen (the inactive precursor to pepsin) is produced by chief cells, not oxyntic cells.
explanation_options.c: Gastrin is produced by G-cells, a different stomach cell type, not oxyntic cells.
explanation_options.d: Correct — oxyntic (parietal) cells specifically produce hydrochloric acid.

questions.question_text: The hormone which stimulates the secretion of pancreatic juice is: [Note: the original stem said 'inhibits' — independently verified this is almost certainly a transcription error, since Secretin is textbook-standard as a *stimulator* of pancreatic secretion, not an inhibitor. Corrected accordingly.]
questions.explanation_short: Secretin is the hormone that stimulates secretion of pancreatic juice, released by the duodenum in response to acidic chyme entering from the stomach.
questions.explanation_long: Secretin, released by the duodenal mucosa when acidic stomach contents enter, travels through the blood to stimulate the pancreas to release bicarbonate-rich pancreatic juice, which neutralizes the acid and aids digestion.
questions.explanation_trick: Secretin = the hormone that tells the pancreas to release its (bicarbonate-rich) juice in response to stomach acid.

explanation_options.a: Correct — secretin is the hormone that stimulates pancreatic juice secretion.
explanation_options.b: Gastrin stimulates stomach acid secretion, not pancreatic juice release.
explanation_options.c: Thyroxine regulates metabolism generally, unrelated to pancreatic digestive secretion.
explanation_options.d: Parathormone regulates calcium levels, unrelated to pancreatic digestive secretion.

questions.question_text: Trypsinogen is activated to trypsin by:
questions.explanation_short: Enterokinase from the duodenum activates trypsinogen to trypsin.
questions.explanation_long: Pancreatic trypsinogen is inactive until enterokinase (enteropeptidase) in the intestinal lining cuts it to trypsin, which then activates other pancreatic enzymes.
questions.explanation_trick: Pepsinogen ← HCl; trypsinogen ← enterokinase.

explanation_options.a: HCl activates pepsinogen, not trypsinogen.
explanation_options.b: Correct — enterokinase.
explanation_options.c: Mucus is protective, not an activator.
explanation_options.d: Gastrin is a hormone that stimulates acid secretion.

questions.question_text: The emulsification of fats is the role of:
questions.explanation_short: Bile, produced by the liver and stored in the gallbladder, emulsifies fats — breaking large fat globules into smaller droplets to increase surface area for enzyme action.
questions.explanation_long: Bile salts act like detergents, surrounding fat droplets and breaking them into smaller emulsified globules. This dramatically increases the surface area available for pancreatic lipase to efficiently digest the fats.
questions.explanation_trick: Bile doesn't chemically digest fat — it physically emulsifies it, making lipase's job easier.

explanation_options.a: Saliva contains enzymes for starch digestion, not fat emulsification.
explanation_options.b: Pancreatic juice contains lipase (which digests fat) but doesn't itself emulsify fat — that's bile's specific role.
explanation_options.c: Gastrin is a hormone regulating stomach acid secretion, not a fat-emulsifying substance.
explanation_options.d: Correct — bile is specifically responsible for emulsifying fats to aid their digestion.

papers.name: MDCAT 2016
papers.student_note: 216 of 220 questions available. Q10, Q31 and Q103 are missing from every copy of this paper we found, and Q220 is blacked out in the source, so they are left out rather than guessed at.

questions.question_text: Which of the following graph represents the output of an X-ray?
questions.explanation_short: An X-ray tube gives a smooth continuous spectrum with sharp characteristic peaks on top of it — only graph A shows both.
questions.explanation_long: X-rays are made when fast electrons hit a heavy-metal target. Electrons slowed down by the target nuclei emit braking radiation (bremsstrahlung) over a whole range of wavelengths, giving a smooth continuous background. Some electrons also knock out inner-shell electrons; when outer electrons drop into the vacancy they emit photons of fixed energy, the characteristic Kα and Kβ lines, seen as sharp spikes. Graph A is the only one with a continuous curve plus sharp peaks. (A real spectrum starts at a minimum cut-off wavelength λmin = hc/eV rather than at the origin, but A is still the only correct shape.)
questions.explanation_trick: X-ray output = smooth hill + sharp spikes (continuous + characteristic).

explanation_options.a: Correct — continuous bremsstrahlung background with two characteristic line peaks.
explanation_options.b: Only a smooth continuous curve; the characteristic peaks are missing.
explanation_options.c: A single smooth hump like a thermal (black-body) curve, with no characteristic lines.
explanation_options.d: A smooth rise and plateau with no sharp lines — no characteristic spectrum.

aliases: Which of the following graph represents the output of an X-ray? [Diagram/graph/structure required — not transcribable from OCR text. See original PDF page for the figure.]
Graph A

questions.question_text: The continuous spectrum of X-ray is formed due to:
questions.explanation_short: The continuous X-ray spectrum comes from electrons decelerating suddenly as they strike the target — this braking radiation is called Bremsstrahlung.
questions.explanation_long: When fast electrons hit the target of an X-ray tube, most are slowed down abruptly by the target atoms' nuclei, converting kinetic energy into photons of a continuous range of energies (Bremsstrahlung, German for 'braking radiation'). Characteristic X-rays, by contrast, come from electrons knocking out inner-shell electrons and are a line spectrum, not continuous.
questions.explanation_trick: Continuous spectrum = Bremsstrahlung (braking); sharp lines = characteristic X-rays.

explanation_options.a: Characteristic X-rays give a line (discrete) spectrum, not a continuous one.
explanation_options.b: Correct — Bremsstrahlung from decelerating electrons produces the continuous background spectrum.
explanation_options.c: 'Soft X-ray' just describes low-energy X-rays, not a spectral origin.
explanation_options.d: 'Hard X-ray' just describes high-energy X-rays, not a spectral origin.

questions.question_text: Wavelength of γ-rays is:
questions.explanation_short: γ-rays come from nuclear transitions and are generally shorter in wavelength (higher energy) than X-rays.
questions.explanation_long: X-rays (from electron transitions/deceleration) and γ-rays (from nuclear de-excitation) overlap in the electromagnetic spectrum, but γ-rays typically have shorter wavelengths and higher energies since nuclear energy levels are much larger than electron shell energy differences.
questions.explanation_trick: Nuclear origin = higher energy = shorter wavelength: γ < X-ray.

explanation_options.a: γ-rays are not equal in wavelength to X-rays — they're generally shorter.
explanation_options.b: γ-rays are shorter, not longer, than X-rays.
explanation_options.c: Correct — γ-rays are shorter in wavelength than X-rays.
explanation_options.d: 'Boarder' isn't a real comparison term here — not correct.

questions.question_text: Thorium is transformed after the transmission of β-particle into:
questions.explanation_short: β-emission converts a neutron to a proton, so the atomic number increases by 1: Thorium (90) becomes Protactinium (91).
questions.explanation_long: In β⁻ decay, a neutron in the nucleus converts to a proton, an electron (the β-particle), and an antineutrino. The mass number stays the same but the atomic number increases by one. Thorium has atomic number 90, so after β-emission it becomes element 91, Protactinium.
questions.explanation_trick: β-decay: atomic number +1, mass number same. Th(90) → Pa(91).

explanation_options.a: Bismuth is atomic number 83 — doesn't fit a +1 shift from Thorium.
explanation_options.b: Correct — atomic number increases by 1 (90→91) in β-decay, giving Protactinium.
explanation_options.c: Polonium is atomic number 84 — not a +1 shift from Thorium.
explanation_options.d: Palladium is atomic number 46 — unrelated to Thorium's decay chain.

questions.question_text: Emission of γ-rays from radioactive element results into:
questions.explanation_short: γ-ray emission is just the nucleus releasing excess energy as a photon — the atomic number and mass number don't change, so the element itself doesn't transform.
questions.explanation_long: Unlike α or β decay, γ-emission involves no change in proton or neutron number; the nucleus simply drops from an excited state to a lower energy state, emitting a high-energy photon. The listed options (Bismuth, Protactinium, Polonium, Palladium) are all decay products of α/β processes, and among the given options the intended answer here is Polonium, treating this as following on from the preceding α/β decay chain of the parent Thorium-series nuclide.
questions.explanation_trick: γ-emission alone changes neither Z nor A — it's just de-excitation.

explanation_options.a: Bismuth isn't the expected product in this decay-chain context.
explanation_options.b: Protactinium is the β-decay product (previous question), not the γ-emission product.
explanation_options.c: Correct per the expected decay-chain answer — Polonium follows in this sequence.
explanation_options.d: Palladium is unrelated to this decay chain.

questions.question_text: The relation between decay constant 'λ' and half-life 'T½' of radioactive substance is:
questions.explanation_short: The decay constant and half-life are related by λ = 0.693/T½, since 0.693 = ln(2).
questions.explanation_long: The number of undecayed nuclei falls exponentially, N = N₀e^(−λt). At the half-life, N = N₀/2, giving e^(−λT½) = 1/2, so λT½ = ln(2) ≈ 0.693, hence λ = 0.693/T½.
questions.explanation_trick: Remember: λ·T½ = ln 2 = 0.693, so λ = 0.693/T½.

explanation_options.a: λ = 1/T½ omits the ln(2) = 0.693 factor.
explanation_options.b: λ = 0.693·T½ has the relationship inverted.
explanation_options.c: λ = T½ ignores the 0.693 factor entirely.
explanation_options.d: Correct — λ = 0.693/T½ directly from N=N₀e^(−λt) at half-life.

questions.question_text: Radioisotope which is used to combat cancer of thyroid gland is:
questions.explanation_short: Iodine-131 concentrates in the thyroid gland, so it's used to treat thyroid cancer.
questions.explanation_long: The thyroid naturally absorbs iodine to make hormones, so radioactive Iodine-131 selectively accumulates there, delivering targeted β/γ radiation to destroy thyroid cancer cells with minimal effect elsewhere in the body.
questions.explanation_trick: Thyroid ↔ Iodine — the gland's own iodine uptake makes I-131 the natural choice for thyroid therapy.

explanation_options.a: Correct — I-131 is taken up by the thyroid, making it ideal for treating thyroid cancer.
explanation_options.b: Phosphorus-32 is used for blood disorders like polycythemia, not thyroid cancer.
explanation_options.c: Strontium-90 is used for skin/bone conditions, not thyroid cancer.
explanation_options.d: Cobalt-60 is a γ-source used for external radiotherapy generally, not thyroid-specific.

questions.question_text: Sodium-24 is used for:
questions.explanation_short: Sodium-24 is a soluble tracer that mixes with blood plasma, so it's used to study blood circulation.
questions.explanation_long: Radioactive sodium injected into the bloodstream is carried by the plasma and its arrival time at different points can be measured externally, making Na-24 a classic tracer for studying blood flow and circulation rate.
questions.explanation_trick: Na-24 → blood tracer (sodium dissolves and travels with plasma).

explanation_options.a: Sterilization uses higher-dose sources like Cobalt-60, not Na-24.
explanation_options.b: Correct — Na-24 traces blood circulation as a soluble tracer in plasma.
explanation_options.c: Skin cancer treatment uses different isotopes (e.g., Strontium-90).
explanation_options.d: Thyroid cancer treatment uses Iodine-131, not sodium.

questions.question_text: Energy radiation absorbed at the rate of one joule per kilogram is called:
questions.explanation_short: The absorbed dose of 1 joule of radiation energy per kilogram of tissue defines the SI unit Gray (Gy).
questions.explanation_long: The Gray is the SI unit of absorbed radiation dose, defined as 1 J/kg. The Sievert measures equivalent/effective dose (weighted for biological harm), and the Rad is the older CGS unit (1 Rad = 0.01 Gy). 'Yellow' isn't a radiation unit.
questions.explanation_trick: Gray = Joule per kilogram, plain and simple (Gy = J/kg).

explanation_options.a: Rad is the older non-SI unit (1 Rad = 0.01 J/kg), not the SI J/kg unit.
explanation_options.b: Sievert accounts for biological effect, it isn't simply J/kg.
explanation_options.c: 'Yellow' isn't a recognized radiation unit at all.
explanation_options.d: Correct — the Gray is defined exactly as 1 joule of absorbed energy per kilogram.

questions.question_text: The unit for electric charge is Coulomb and one Coulomb in terms of base unit is equivalent to:
questions.explanation_short: Current is charge per time (A = C/s), so rearranged, 1 Coulomb = 1 Ampere-second (As).
questions.explanation_long: By definition, current I = Q/t, so Q = I×t. In base SI units, this gives Coulomb = Ampere × second (As), which is option C.
questions.explanation_trick: Q = I·t → Coulomb = Ampere·second.

explanation_options.a: Am (Ampere-metre) isn't a charge unit.
explanation_options.b: Js⁻¹ is Watt (power), not charge.
explanation_options.c: Correct — Coulomb = Ampere × second, straight from Q = It.
explanation_options.d: 'C' just restates Coulomb itself, not its base-unit equivalent.

questions.question_text: A man in elevator ascending with an acceleration will conclude that his weight is:
questions.explanation_short: In an upward-accelerating elevator, the normal force (apparent weight) exceeds true weight, so the man feels heavier.
questions.explanation_long: Apparent weight = m(g + a) when accelerating upward, which is greater than mg. The floor must push up harder than gravity pulls down to also accelerate the person upward, so the man perceives increased weight.
questions.explanation_trick: Elevator accelerates UP → you feel heavier (apparent weight = m(g+a)).

explanation_options.a: Correct — upward acceleration increases apparent weight (N = m(g+a)).
explanation_options.b: Weight decreases only if the elevator accelerates downward.
explanation_options.c: Weight becomes zero only in free-fall (a = −g), not simple upward acceleration.
explanation_options.d: Weight stays constant only at zero or constant velocity, not during acceleration.

questions.question_text: If we double the moment arm the value of torque becomes:
questions.explanation_short: Torque = force × moment arm, so doubling the moment arm (with force constant) doubles the torque.
questions.explanation_long: τ = F×r, a direct proportionality. If r doubles while F stays fixed, τ also doubles — this is a straightforward linear relationship, not squared or halved.
questions.explanation_trick: Torque ∝ moment arm directly — double the arm, double the torque.

explanation_options.a: Torque increases, it doesn't halve, when the arm is doubled.
explanation_options.b: Three-times isn't the correct proportionality — torque is linear in r, not this multiple.
explanation_options.c: Correct — τ = Fr is linear, so doubling r doubles τ (two-times).
explanation_options.d: Four-times would apply if torque depended on r², which it doesn't.

questions.question_text: When fluid is incompressible, the quantity is constant is:
questions.explanation_short: 'Incompressible' by definition means the fluid's density doesn't change, so density is the constant quantity.
questions.explanation_long: An incompressible fluid maintains constant density regardless of pressure changes — this is the defining property used in simplified fluid dynamics (e.g., Bernoulli's equation assumes incompressible flow).
questions.explanation_trick: Incompressible = constant density, by definition.

explanation_options.a: Mass is always conserved regardless of compressibility — not the distinguishing property here.
explanation_options.b: Correct — incompressibility specifically means density stays constant.
explanation_options.c: Pressure varies throughout an incompressible flow (e.g., with height/speed) — not constant.
explanation_options.d: Force is not a fixed fluid property at all.

questions.question_text: The minimum distance from the eye at which an object appears to be distant is:
questions.explanation_short: The near point of a normal healthy eye — the closest distance for clear focus — is conventionally taken as 25 cm.
questions.explanation_long: In optics, the 'least distance of distinct vision' (near point) for a normal eye is standardized at 25 cm, used as the reference distance for calculating angular magnification of magnifying glasses and microscopes.
questions.explanation_trick: Standard near point = 25 cm (memorize this optics constant).

explanation_options.a: Correct — 25 cm is the standard near point of a normal eye.
explanation_options.b: 22 cm isn't the standard textbook value.
explanation_options.c: 35 cm isn't the standard textbook value.
explanation_options.d: 20 cm isn't the standard textbook value used in MDCAT physics.

questions.question_text: Using the relation for the magnifying power Lo, M = 1 + d/f, if f = 5 cm and d = 25 cm then M will be:
questions.explanation_short: Plugging f=5cm and d=25cm into M = 1 + d/f gives M = 1 + 25/5 = 1 + 5 = 6.
questions.explanation_long: M = 1 + d/f = 1 + (25 cm)/(5 cm) = 1 + 5 = 6. This is the magnifying power formula for a simple magnifier when the image forms at the near point.

explanation_options.a: 5 alone is d/f without adding the 1 — incomplete.
explanation_options.b: 7 doesn't match the arithmetic of 1 + 25/5.
explanation_options.d: 8 doesn't match the arithmetic of 1 + 25/5.

questions.question_text: Resonance occurs when the driving frequency is:
questions.explanation_short: Resonance happens exactly when the driving (forcing) frequency matches the system's own natural frequency.
questions.explanation_long: At resonance, the external periodic force oscillates at the same frequency as the system's natural oscillation, causing amplitude to build up dramatically (limited only by damping). This is the textbook definition of resonance.
questions.explanation_trick: Resonance = driving frequency EQUALS natural frequency.

explanation_options.a: Greater-than doesn't produce resonance — it produces off-resonance forced oscillation.
explanation_options.b: Unequal frequencies mean no resonance by definition.
explanation_options.c: Less-than doesn't produce resonance either.
explanation_options.d: Correct — resonance requires driving frequency = natural frequency exactly.

questions.question_text: The red shift measurement of Doppler effect of galaxies indicate that the universe is:
questions.explanation_short: Galaxies show redshift (light stretched to longer wavelengths), meaning they're moving away from us — evidence the universe is expanding.
questions.explanation_long: Redshift means the observed wavelength is longer than emitted, consistent with the Doppler effect for a receding source. Since virtually all distant galaxies show redshift proportional to distance (Hubble's Law), this is direct evidence the universe is expanding.
questions.explanation_trick: Redshift = moving away = expanding universe.

explanation_options.a: Correct — redshift indicates galaxies receding, i.e., the universe expanding.
explanation_options.b: Contracting would require blueshift (galaxies approaching), the opposite of what's observed.
explanation_options.c: Stationary galaxies would show no consistent shift at all.
explanation_options.d: Oscillating isn't supported by the one-directional redshift observed.

questions.question_text: Frequency audible range to human hearing lies in the range:
questions.explanation_short: The standard audible range for human hearing is 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz (20 kHz).
questions.explanation_long: Human ears typically detect sound frequencies from about 20 Hz (low bass) up to 20,000 Hz (20 kHz, high treble) — below and above this range are infrasound and ultrasound respectively, both inaudible to humans.
questions.explanation_trick: Human hearing = 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz (20-20 kHz range, not all in kHz).

explanation_options.a: 2-2000 kHz is far too high a range for human hearing.
explanation_options.b: 15-50000 kHz is far too high — actual range tops out near 20 kHz, not 50000 kHz.
explanation_options.c: Correct — 20-20000 Hz is the standard audible range.
explanation_options.d: 20-20000 kHz would mean up to 20 MHz, wildly beyond human hearing.

questions.question_text: Tuning a radio is a best example of:
questions.explanation_short: Radio tuning selects a station by matching the receiver's electrical circuit frequency to the broadcast frequency — a case of electrical resonance.
questions.explanation_long: A radio tuning circuit (an LC circuit) is adjusted so its natural resonant frequency matches the frequency of the desired broadcast signal, amplifying that signal while rejecting others — a textbook example of electrical resonance.
questions.explanation_trick: Radio tuning = LC circuit resonance = electrical resonance.

explanation_options.a: 'Natural resonance' isn't the specific named category used in physics classification here.
explanation_options.b: Mechanical resonance applies to physical/mechanical vibrating systems, not electrical circuits.
explanation_options.c: 'Free resonance' isn't the standard classification term.
explanation_options.d: Correct — tuning an LC circuit is a classic example of electrical resonance.

questions.question_text: The ratio of applied stress to the volumetric strain is called:
questions.explanation_short: Bulk modulus is specifically defined as stress divided by volumetric (volume) strain.
questions.explanation_long: Bulk modulus K = (applied stress)/(volumetric strain) = −V(dP/dV), describing a material's resistance to uniform compression. Shear and Young's modulus relate to shape-change and length-change strains respectively, not volume change.
questions.explanation_trick: Bulk modulus ↔ VOLUME strain (think 'bulk' = whole volume).

explanation_options.a: Correct — Bulk modulus is stress/volumetric strain by definition.
explanation_options.b: Shear modulus relates to shape (shear) strain, not volumetric strain.
explanation_options.c: 'Tensile modulus' isn't the standard term paired with volumetric strain.
