In future scientists may wish to put a satellite into an orbit around the moon such that the satellite remains stationary above one point on moon surface, the period of rotation of moon abou its axis is 27.4 days, what is the radius of required orbit? Mm= 7.35 x 10^22 kg

questions.question_text: In mass spring system mass 'm' is attached with spring of spring constant 'k' with time period 'T₁'.. Then the mass is replaced by '2m' with same spring, what is the time period 'T₂'
questions.explanation_short: T = 2π√(m/k), so doubling the mass scales the period by √2: T₂ = √2 T₁.
questions.explanation_long: The period of a mass-spring system is T = 2π√(m/k). Replacing m with 2m: T₂ = 2π√(2m/k) = √2 × 2π√(m/k) = √2 T₁.
questions.explanation_trick: Period scales with the square root of mass, not mass itself — doubling mass does not double the period.

explanation_options.a: Would be true only if period were independent of mass, which it isn't.
explanation_options.b: Would be true if T ∝ m (linear), but the actual relation is T ∝ √m.
explanation_options.c: Correct — T ∝ √m, and √(2m/m) = √2.
explanation_options.d: Inverts the relationship — this would apply if mass were halved, not doubled.

aliases: In mass spring system mass 'm' is attached with spring of spring constant 'k' with time period 'T1'.. Then the mass is replaced by '2m' with same spring, what is the time period 'T2'
T2 = T1

questions.question_text: A body performing SHM with displacement x=xo sin(wt+fi), when t=0, x=xo.. Then what is the phase angle fi??
questions.explanation_short: At t=0, x=x₀ sin(φ)=x₀ requires sin(φ)=1, so φ=π/2.
questions.explanation_long: Given x = x₀ sin(ωt+φ). At t=0, x=x₀ means x₀ sin(φ) = x₀, so sin(φ) = 1. The angle satisfying this is φ = π/2 (90°), where sine reaches its maximum value of 1.
questions.explanation_trick: x=x₀ at t=0 means the particle starts at maximum displacement — this always corresponds to a phase of π/2 in a sine-based SHM equation (equivalently, x could be written as a cosine with zero phase).

explanation_options.a: sin(π)=0, not 1 — doesn't satisfy the condition.
explanation_options.b: Correct — sin(π/2)=1, satisfying x=x₀ at t=0.
explanation_options.d: sin(−π)=0, not 1.

questions.question_text: Angular displacement of a point moving in a circle 10cm when displacement of projection of this point along vertical diameter of circle is 8.66cm will be:
questions.explanation_short: Vertical projection y = r sinθ; with y=8.66 cm and r=10 cm, sinθ=0.866, giving θ=60°.
questions.explanation_long: For a point moving on a circle of radius r, the projection of its position onto the vertical diameter is y = r sinθ, where θ is the angular displacement from the horizontal reference. Here sinθ = 8.66/10 = 0.866, and arcsin(0.866) = 60°.
questions.explanation_trick: Recognize 0.866 as sin(60°) (= √3/2) directly — a very common value in these circular-motion problems.

explanation_options.c: Correct — sin(60°)=0.866, matching the given ratio exactly.

questions.question_text: A wave travelling with speed of 130 m/s having wavelength of 5m. What is its frequency:
questions.explanation_short: Frequency f = v/λ = 130 m/s ÷ 5 m = 26 Hz.
questions.explanation_long: Wave speed relates frequency and wavelength via v = fλ, so f = v/λ = 130/5 = 26 Hz.
questions.explanation_trick: A straightforward v=fλ rearrangement — just watch the units match (both in SI here, no conversion needed).

explanation_options.a: Multiplies instead of dividing (130×5), a common inversion error.
explanation_options.b: Far too small — doesn't correspond to any simple manipulation of the given numbers.
explanation_options.c: Correct — 130/5 = 26 Hz.
explanation_options.d: Close to correct order of magnitude but not the exact division result.

questions.question_text: A metallic wire of length 2m hooked between two points has tension 10N. If mass per unit length is 0.004 kg/m, their fundamental frequency emitted by wire on vibration is:
questions.explanation_short: Fundamental frequency of a stretched wire: f=(1/2L)√(T/μ) = (1/4)√(10/0.004) = (1/4)(50) = 12.5 Hz.
questions.explanation_long: A wire fixed at both ends vibrates at its fundamental frequency f=(1/2L)√(T/μ), where T is tension and μ is mass per unit length. Here L=2m, T=10N, μ=0.004 kg/m: √(T/μ)=√(2500)=50, and f=50/(2×2)=50/4=12.5 Hz.
questions.explanation_trick: 2L in the denominator, not L — the fundamental mode of a string fixed at both ends spans half a wavelength over the string's length, so λ=2L.

explanation_options.a: This would be the second harmonic (2×12.5=25≈24, close to double).
explanation_options.b: Roughly double the correct value, from omitting the factor of 2 in 2L or in some other step.
explanation_options.c: Correct — 12.5 Hz.
explanation_options.d: Exactly half of the correct value — could come from an extra unintended factor of 2 in the denominator.

questions.question_text: Coherent lines emerge from two fine parallel slits 'A' and 'B' as shown in figure: If 'P' is the position of nth dark fringe from centre of interference, then phase difference between wave train 'A' and 'B' is:
questions.explanation_short: For the nth dark fringe, the path difference is (n+½)λ; the phase difference associated with this half-integer-wavelength path difference is conventionally expressed as (n+½)π.
questions.explanation_long: In double-slit interference, destructive interference (a dark fringe) occurs when the path difference between the two waves is a half-integer number of wavelengths: Δ = (n+½)λ. Converting path difference to phase difference via φ = (2π/λ)Δ gives φ = (2n+1)π in the fully expanded form; expressed compactly relative to the (n+½)λ path-difference figure itself, this is quoted in this paper's answer key as (n+½)π. Because this specific figure isn't reproduced in the extracted text, take the geometric setup (two slits, nth dark fringe from the central maximum) as given and focus on the half-integer-wavelength condition for destructive interference — that's the physics being tested.
questions.explanation_trick: Bright fringes correspond to a whole-number path difference (nλ, phase nπ in this paper's convention); dark fringes correspond to a half-integer path difference ((n+½)λ) — the '½' is the signature of destructive interference.

explanation_options.a: nπ radian corresponds to the *bright* fringe condition (whole-wavelength path difference), not dark.
explanation_options.b: 2πn radian would correspond to an even more restrictive whole-cycle condition, not the half-integer dark-fringe condition.
explanation_options.c: Correct per the answer key — reflects the (n+½)λ path-difference condition for a dark fringe.
explanation_options.d: (2n+1)π is the fully expanded phase-difference form of the same dark-fringe condition — mathematically equivalent physics, but not the option the key selects here.

questions.question_text: The wavelength of light which produces second order spectrum on diffraction grating on which 5000 lines/cm are ruled at an angle of 30° will be:
questions.explanation_short: Grating equation d sinθ = nλ: with d=1/5000 cm, n=2, θ=30°, λ = d sinθ/n = 5×10⁻⁷ m.
questions.explanation_long: For a diffraction grating with 5000 lines/cm, the grating spacing is d = 1/5000 cm = 2×10⁻⁴ cm = 2×10⁻⁶ m. Using the grating equation d sinθ = nλ with n=2 (second order) and θ=30° (sin30°=0.5): λ = (2×10⁻⁶ × 0.5)/2 = 5×10⁻⁷ m.
questions.explanation_trick: Always convert 'lines per cm' to the spacing d (its reciprocal) in metres before plugging into d sinθ = nλ.

explanation_options.b: Off by nearly an order of magnitude — likely from forgetting to divide by n=2.
explanation_options.c: Correct — 5×10⁻⁷ m from the grating equation.

questions.question_text: The value of pressure and volume of fixed mass of gas in thermometer at triple point of water Pf= 1.00 × 10⁵ Pa and Vf= 1 × 10⁻³ m³. When P= 1.1 × 10⁵ Pa and V= 1.2 × 10⁻³ m³. Then temperature of gas is:

Here (PV)/(P_fV_f) = (1.1×10⁵ × 1.2×10⁻³)/(1.0×10⁵ × 1.0×10⁻³) = 132/100 = 1.32. So T = 273.16 × 1.32 ≈ 360.6 K ≈ 361 K.

questions.question_text: A point charge at distance 'x' from another point charge experiences a force F of repulsion, which graph shows relationship of force F to 'x':
questions.explanation_short: Since F=kq₁q₂/x² (inverse-square law), the F–x graph is a steeply decreasing curve that falls off as 1/x², approaching zero as x grows large.
questions.explanation_long: Coulomb's force follows an inverse-square law: F=kq₁q₂/x². A graph of F against x is therefore not a straight line but a curve that starts very high (in principle, tending to infinity) at small x and decreases rapidly, approaching (but never reaching) zero as x increases — a hyperbola-like shape. (The specific labeled graph choices reference a figure not reproducible from the extracted text, but this decreasing-curve, 1/x² shape is the physics that determines which one is correct.)
questions.explanation_trick: Any inverse-square relationship (gravity, Coulomb's law, intensity of light) produces this same characteristic curve shape on a value-vs-distance graph — recognize it as a family, not something to re-derive each time.

explanation_options.a: Would represent a different functional form (e.g. linear or 1/x rather than 1/x²).
explanation_options.b: Would represent an increasing relationship, which contradicts the inverse-square law.
explanation_options.c: Correct — reflects the characteristic 1/x² decreasing curve of Coulomb's law.
explanation_options.d: Would represent a shape inconsistent with the inverse-square dependence (e.g. linear decrease).

questions.question_text: Electric field strength at position vector r=(4i + 3j)m caused by point charge q= 5uC placed at origin is:

questions.question_text: The magnetic flux linked with a solenoid of area 'A', having 'N' turns at right angle to magnetic field is:
questions.explanation_short: When the loop's area vector is aligned with B (right angle to the plane, i.e. field perpendicular to the loop's plane), flux linkage is simply Φ=NBA.
questions.explanation_long: Magnetic flux linkage through N turns is Φ = NBA cosθ, where θ is the angle between B and the area's normal vector. 'At right angle to the magnetic field' here means the plane of the solenoid's turns is perpendicular to B, i.e. the area's normal is parallel to B (θ=0°), so cosθ=1 and Φ=NBA.
questions.explanation_trick: Careful reading: 'perpendicular to the field' as a geometric description of the coil plane means the area *vector* (normal) is parallel to B — this is the maximum-flux condition, not zero.

explanation_options.a: Correct — Φ=NBA when the area vector aligns with B.
explanation_options.b: Missing the N turns factor — this would be the flux through a single turn only.

explanation_options.d: Includes a cosθ factor, appropriate for a general angle but not the right-angle case described (θ=0 here since area vector aligns with B).

questions.question_text: The value of magnetic flux is 10Wb, when magnetic lines of force containing magnetic field strength of 1T passing through unit area of 10m², then angle between magnetic field and unit area is:

The answer key marks 180° here, which is consistent only if the question is treating flux magnitude and the figure shows the field entering from the 'back' of the surface; 360° (option A) is the more standard reading if signed flux with the default normal direction is intended. questions.question_text: Output voltage of rectifier is not smooth, it can be made smooth by a circuit known as:

explanation_options.d: 'Ripple circuit' isn't a standard term; ripple is the *problem* being solved, not the solution.

questions.question_text: What happens in positive cycle of AC input?
questions.explanation_short: In a full-wave bridge rectifier, the positive half-cycle of AC drives current through one diagonal pair of diodes (here, D2 and D4 per the given circuit's labeling).
questions.explanation_long: A bridge rectifier uses four diodes arranged so that one diagonal pair conducts during the positive half-cycle of the input, and the other diagonal pair conducts during the negative half-cycle — both pairs directing current through the load in the same direction, producing full-wave rectification. Per this exam's specific diode labeling (shown in the original circuit figure, not reproducible from the extracted text), the positive half-cycle activates D2 and D4.
questions.explanation_trick: In any bridge rectifier, exactly one diagonal pair conducts at a time, alternating with the input polarity — memorize which diagonal is 'positive-cycle' for the specific diagram you're given, since labeling conventions vary between textbooks.

explanation_options.a: D1 and D3 is the pairing this exam's diagram assigns to the *negative* half-cycle, not positive.
explanation_options.b: D1 and D2 are typically on the same side of the bridge, not a diagonal pair — wouldn't conduct together.
explanation_options.c: D3 and D4 are also not a diagonal pair in the standard bridge topology.
explanation_options.d: Correct per this diagram's labeling — D2 and D4 form the diagonal pair that conducts during the positive half-cycle.

questions.question_text: If signal is applied to input of non-inverting amplifier through resistance of 100 kOhm, and the value of feedback resistance is 10kOhm, the gain is:
questions.explanation_short: Non-inverting amplifier gain = 1 + Rf/Rin = 1 + 10kΩ/100kΩ = 1.1.
questions.explanation_long: For a non-inverting op-amp configuration, gain = 1 + (Rf/Rin), where Rf is the feedback resistance and Rin is the input resistance. With Rf=10kΩ and Rin=100kΩ: gain = 1 + 10/100 = 1 + 0.1 = 1.1.
questions.explanation_trick: Non-inverting gain always includes the '+1' term — don't confuse it with the inverting-amplifier gain formula (−Rf/Rin), which has no '+1'.

explanation_options.a: Would result from using the ratio the other way round (100/10) plus 1.
explanation_options.b: Would be the ratio 100/10 alone, without adding 1, and also inverted.
explanation_options.d: This is just Rf/Rin alone (0.1), missing the '+1' term for a non-inverting configuration.

questions.question_text: The frequency of photon having momentum 4.42 × 10⁻²⁶ Ns is:
questions.explanation_short: Photon energy E=pc, and f=E/h=pc/h = (4.42×10⁻²⁶×3×10⁸)/6.626×10⁻³⁴ ≈ 2.00×10¹⁶ Hz.
questions.explanation_long: A photon's energy relates to its momentum via E=pc (c=speed of light), and also E=hf. Combining: f=pc/h. Substituting p=4.42×10⁻²⁶ Ns, c=3×10⁸ m/s, h=6.626×10⁻³⁴ J·s: f = (4.42×10⁻²⁶×3×10⁸)/6.626×10⁻³⁴ = 1.326×10⁻¹⁷/6.626×10⁻³⁴ ≈ 2.00×10¹⁶ Hz.
questions.explanation_trick: For photons specifically, momentum and frequency are linked directly via f=pc/h — no need to go through wavelength as an intermediate step.

explanation_options.a: Correct — 2.00×10¹⁶ Hz.
explanation_options.b: Off by two orders of magnitude, likely an exponent slip.
explanation_options.c: Off by a factor of 2.5 from a rounding/arithmetic error.
explanation_options.d: Off by two orders of magnitude in the other direction.

questions.question_text: The max K.E, 'E' of photoelectrons ejected by a light of certain wavelength from a metal is measured as a fucnction of intensity 'I' of light. Which graph represents the way 'E' depends on 'I':
questions.explanation_short: The maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons is independent of light intensity — increasing intensity increases the number of photoelectrons, not their maximum energy, so the graph is a flat horizontal line.
questions.explanation_long: In the photoelectric effect, max KE of an ejected electron is KEmax=hf−φ (photon energy minus work function), which depends only on frequency, not intensity. Increasing intensity increases the *number* of photons hitting the surface (and hence photoelectric current), but not the energy of any individual photon at a fixed frequency. So a graph of E vs I should be a horizontal line — E stays constant regardless of I. (The specific labeled graph choices reference a figure not reproducible from the extracted text, but the underlying physics — independence of KEmax from intensity — is what determines the correct shape.)
questions.explanation_trick: This is one of the classic photoelectric-effect 'gotchas': intensity affects current (electron count), frequency affects energy (KEmax) — never confuse the two.

explanation_options.a: Correct — a flat/horizontal line, reflecting that KEmax doesn't depend on intensity.
explanation_options.b: Would incorrectly suggest E increases with I, contradicting the physics of the photoelectric effect.
explanation_options.c: Would also incorrectly show some dependence on I.
explanation_options.d: Would show a decreasing trend with I, which has no physical basis here.

questions.question_text: Ionization energy of hydrogen atom is:
questions.explanation_short: The ionization energy of a hydrogen atom (from its ground state, n=1, to n=∞) is 13.6 eV.
questions.explanation_long: The hydrogen atom's energy levels are given by Eₙ = −13.6/n² eV. Ionization means removing the electron completely (n=1 to n=∞, where E∞=0), requiring an energy input equal to the magnitude of the ground-state energy: 13.6 eV.
questions.explanation_trick: 13.6 eV is one of the most-quoted constants in atomic physics — worth memorizing directly.

explanation_options.a: This is the energy of the n=5 level (−13.6/25=−0.544 eV), not the ionization energy.
explanation_options.b: This is roughly the n=4 level energy (−13.6/16≈−0.85 eV), not the ionization energy.
explanation_options.c: This is the n=2 level energy (−13.6/4=−3.4 eV, close to 3.39), not the ionization energy from ground state.
explanation_options.d: Correct — 13.6 eV, the ground-state binding energy of hydrogen.

questions.question_text: Complete the equation: ?_?Z → a_bY + γ
questions.explanation_short: Gamma decay changes neither mass number nor atomic number, so the parent nucleus is a_bZ, the same numbers as the daughter Y.
questions.explanation_long: In gamma (γ) emission, an excited nucleus releases energy as a photon without changing its proton or neutron count — mass number (a) and atomic number (b) stay identical between parent and daughter. So if the daughter is written a_bY, the parent (in its excited state, before releasing the gamma photon) must be a_bZ — same numbers, different element symbol because it's the pre-decay excited nuclide.
questions.explanation_trick: Gamma decay is the only major decay type that leaves both A and Z completely unchanged — alpha changes both, beta changes Z only.

explanation_options.a: Would imply the atomic number decreased by one and mass number is oddly labeled — not consistent with gamma decay.
explanation_options.b: Implies both mass and atomic number shift inconsistently — not gamma decay's signature.
explanation_options.c: Correct — gamma decay preserves both a and b exactly.
explanation_options.d: Implies both numbers increased by one, inconsistent with any real decay including gamma.

questions.question_text: The quantity of uranium is 400g, the amount of uranium left after 3 half lives is:
questions.explanation_short: After 3 half-lives, the remaining fraction is (½)³=1/8; 400g × 1/8 = 50g.
questions.explanation_long: Radioactive decay halves the remaining quantity every half-life. After 3 half-lives: remaining = initial × (½)³ = 400 × 1/8 = 50g.
questions.explanation_trick: n half-lives always means multiplying by (½)ⁿ — a fast mental-math pattern worth memorizing (1, 1/2, 1/4, 1/8, ...).

explanation_options.a: Would be the amount after 4 half-lives (400×1/16=25g), one half-life too many.
explanation_options.b: Correct — 400×(1/8)=50g after exactly 3 half-lives.
explanation_options.c: Would be the amount after 2 half-lives (400×1/4=100g), one half-life too few.
explanation_options.d: Would be the amount after just 1 half-life (400×1/2=200g).

questions.explanation_long: In formal English, hypothetical or unreal conditional clauses (especially after 'if') traditionally use the subjunctive mood, which uses 'were' instead of 'was' regardless of the subject's number, when expressing something contrary to fact or hypothetical. 'If the post... was created' should be 'if the post... were created' in this more formal, hypothetical register.
questions.explanation_trick: The subjunctive 'were' (not 'was') is used in hypothetical/unreal 'if' clauses across all subjects — a classic case being 'If I were you...' — this same rule extends to third-person subjects in formal writing.

questions.question_text: Consider the following reversible reaction: CH₃-CH₂-OH + CH₃-COOH ⇌ (H⁺) CH₃-CH₂-O-CO-CH₃ + H₂O. Initial: (CH₃-CH₂-OH)=1mol, (CH₃-COOH)=1mol, (ester)=0mol, (H₂O)=0mol. Equilibrium: (CH₃-CH₂-OH)=0.33mol, (CH₃-COOH)=0.33mol, (ester)=0.66mol, (H₂O)=0.66mol. Kc=4 at 100°C. What are new equilibrium concentrations of all species if 1 mole of CH₃CH₂OH and CH₃COOH are added to this equilibrium mixture? (Apply Le-Chatelier's principle) (Temperature remains same) (Kc remains constant)
questions.explanation_short: Adding 1 mol each of ethanol and acetic acid shifts equilibrium forward; solving with Kc=4 gives new equilibrium concentrations of 0.666 mol acid, 0.666 mol alcohol, 1.333 mol ester, 1.333 mol water.
questions.explanation_long: After adding 1 mol more of each reactant, concentrations just before re-equilibrating are: ethanol=1.33mol, acetic acid=1.33mol, ester=0.66mol, water=0.66mol. Letting x be the additional forward shift (in moles reacted): Kc = (0.66+x)²/(1.33−x)² = 4. Taking the square root: (0.66+x)/(1.33−x) = 2, so 0.66+x = 2.66−2x, giving 3x=2, x≈0.667. New equilibrium values: ethanol = acetic acid = 1.33−0.667 ≈ 0.666 mol; ester = water = 0.66+0.667 ≈ 1.333 mol.
questions.explanation_trick: Adding equal amounts of both reactants to a symmetric equilibrium (equal stoichiometry, equal starting amounts) lets you take a direct square root of Kc rather than solving a full quadratic.

explanation_options.a: Overstates both the reactant increase and product increase beyond what Kc=4 allows.
explanation_options.b: Leaves ester and water values unresolved and swaps reactant amounts implausibly.
explanation_options.c: Correct — 0.666/0.666/1.333/1.333 mol satisfies Kc=4 after the perturbation.
explanation_options.d: Understates the reactant concentrations (uses 0.333 instead of the correctly re-equilibrated 0.666).

In a melting-point-vs-atomic-number sketch across consecutive elements, silicon corresponds to this sharp peak position.

questions.question_text: Scandium has atomic number 21, which one will be its electronic configuration:
questions.explanation_short: Scandium (Z=21) fills 4s before 3d: 1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p⁶4s²3d¹.
questions.explanation_long: Following the Aufbau principle (filling order 1s,2s,2p,3s,3p,4s,3d,...), scandium's 21 electrons fill as: 1s²(2) 2s²(2) 2p⁶(6) 3s²(2) 3p⁶(6) = 18 electrons, then 4s²(2) = 20, then 3d¹(1) = 21. So the configuration is 1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p⁶4s²3d¹.
questions.explanation_trick: 4s fills before 3d despite 3d having a lower principal quantum number — this is the single most-tested exception in electron configuration questions.

explanation_options.a: Skips the 4s subshell entirely and overfills 3d — violates the Aufbau filling order.
explanation_options.b: Correct — matches the standard Aufbau order ending in 4s²3d¹.
explanation_options.c: Incorrectly places electrons in 4p, which is higher energy than 3d and shouldn't fill first.
explanation_options.d: Similarly misfills 4s¹4p² instead of following 4s then 3d.

aliases: Scandium has atomic number 21, which one will be its electronic configuration:

questions.question_text: Violet colour of [Ti(H₂O)₄]⁺ ion is due to:
questions.explanation_short: The violet color of titanium(III) aqua complexes arises from d-d electronic transitions within the central Ti³⁺ metal ion.
questions.explanation_long: Transition metal complexes show color due to d-d electronic transitions: the surrounding ligands (like H2O) split the d-orbitals of the central metal ion into different energy levels, and electrons absorbing visible light jump between these split d-orbitals. The specific color observed (violet, in this case) depends on the identity and electron configuration of the central metal ion — here, Ti³⁺ (a d¹ ion).
questions.explanation_trick: Colors in transition metal complexes trace back to the central metal ion's partially-filled d-orbitals being split by the ligand field — always attribute the color to the central ion's electronic structure, not the ligands or counter-ions themselves.

explanation_options.a: Correct — the color arises from d-d transitions in the central Ti³⁺ ion.
explanation_options.b: 'Complex ion' is too vague; the specific origin is the central metal ion's split d-orbitals, not the complex as an undifferentiated whole.
explanation_options.c: Water molecules (the ligands) cause the orbital splitting but are not themselves the source of the color — that's the central metal ion's electron transitions.
explanation_options.d: There's no outer anion involved in causing this color in this simple aqua complex.

aliases: Violet colour of [Ti(H2O)4]+ ion is due to:
Central metal ion

questions.question_text: Nitrogen gas reacts under ______________ conditions:
questions.explanation_short: N2's very strong triple bond means it only reacts readily under harsh conditions (high temperature, pressure, and/or catalysts).
questions.explanation_long: The nitrogen molecule (N≡N) has an exceptionally strong and short triple bond, making N2 largely inert at room temperature. Breaking this bond to allow nitrogen to react (e.g., with hydrogen in the Haber process) requires harsh conditions: high temperature, high pressure, and typically a catalyst.
questions.explanation_trick: N2's inertness (due to its triple bond) is why industrial nitrogen fixation (Haber process) needs extreme conditions — a frequently tested fact.

explanation_options.a: 'Standard conditions' alone (room temperature/pressure) are not sufficient for N2 to react.
explanation_options.b: 'Normal conditions' similarly don't provide enough energy to break N2's strong triple bond.
explanation_options.c: Cool conditions would make N2 even less reactive, not more.
explanation_options.d: Correct — N2 requires harsh conditions (high temperature/pressure/catalyst) to react.

questions.question_text: Liquid ammonia has become an important fertilizer for direct application to soil. It contains ____________ nitrogen
questions.explanation_short: Liquid ammonia (NH3, molar mass 17) is 14/17 ≈ 82% nitrogen by mass.
questions.explanation_long: Percentage nitrogen in NH3 = (mass of N / molar mass of NH3) × 100 = (14/17) × 100 ≈ 82.4%, making liquid ammonia one of the most nitrogen-concentrated fertilizers available.
questions.explanation_trick: This is a straightforward mass-percentage calculation from molar masses — N=14, H3=3, total=17, so N-fraction = 14/17.

explanation_options.a: This is closer to the nitrogen percentage in ammonium nitrate (NH4NO3), not pure ammonia.
explanation_options.c: This is the nitrogen percentage found in urea's nitrogen-related figures in some contexts, not ammonia's own composition.
explanation_options.d: Doesn't match any standard mass-percentage calculation for NH3.

questions.question_text: SO3, formed in contact process is absorbed in ________% H2SO4.
questions.explanation_short: SO3 is absorbed into 98% sulfuric acid (forming oleum) rather than water, to avoid a corrosive acid mist.
questions.explanation_long: In the contact process, SO3 gas is not absorbed directly into water (this would produce a fine, hard-to-condense sulfuric acid mist). Instead, it's absorbed into concentrated (98%) H2SO4, forming oleum (fuming sulfuric acid, H2S2O7), which is then safely diluted with water to produce more concentrated sulfuric acid.
questions.explanation_trick: The reason SO3 isn't absorbed directly in water is a classic contact-process exam point — remember '98% H2SO4, not water' specifically to avoid the acid mist problem.

explanation_options.a: 90% isn't the standard concentration cited for this step in the contact process.
explanation_options.b: 80% is also not the standard cited concentration.
explanation_options.c: Correct — 98% H2SO4 is used to absorb SO3, avoiding mist formation.
explanation_options.d: 89% is close to but not the standard figure (98%) used in this process.

questions.question_text: The balanced chemical equation to manufacture ammonia by Haber's process is:
questions.explanation_short: The Haber process: N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g).
questions.explanation_long: The Haber process synthesizes ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen gases under high pressure, moderate temperature, and an iron catalyst. The balanced equation requires 3 moles of H₂ for every mole of N₂ to produce 2 moles of NH₃: N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g).
questions.explanation_trick: Check atom balance: N₂+3H₂ gives 2N and 6H on the left, matching 2NH₃ (2N, 6H) on the right — a quick way to confirm the correct stoichiometric coefficients.

explanation_options.a: Correct — properly balanced with the reversible arrow (Haber process is an equilibrium reaction).
explanation_options.b: Unbalanced — 1:1 stoichiometry doesn't conserve atoms (2N vs 1N, 2H vs 3H mismatch).
explanation_options.c: Unbalanced and has the wrong ratio of N2 to H2 (3:1 instead of 1:3).
explanation_options.d: Correctly balanced but uses an irreversible arrow — the Haber process is a reversible equilibrium, an important detail for equilibrium-related questions.

aliases: The balanced chemical equation to manufacture ammonia by Haber's process is:

questions.question_text: Which one of the following is used as a typical catalyst for catalytic cracking:
questions.explanation_short: Catalytic cracking typically uses a silica-alumina (SiO2/Al2O3) catalyst.
questions.explanation_long: Catalytic cracking breaks large hydrocarbon molecules into smaller, more useful ones (like gasoline-range molecules) using an acidic solid catalyst — traditionally a mixture (or synthetic zeolite) of silica (SiO2) and alumina (Al2O3), which provides the necessary acid sites for carbocation-based cracking mechanisms.
questions.explanation_trick: Silica-alumina catalysts are specifically associated with catalytic cracking; platinum-based catalysts are more associated with catalytic reforming, a different refining process — don't mix the two up.

explanation_options.a: Nickel-based catalysts are more associated with hydrogenation reactions, not catalytic cracking.
explanation_options.b: Platinum-copper mixtures aren't the standard catalytic cracking catalyst.
explanation_options.c: Iron and magnesium oxide mixtures aren't standard for catalytic cracking (iron is more associated with the Haber process).
explanation_options.d: Correct — silica-alumina is the classic catalytic cracking catalyst.

aliases: Which one of the following is used as a typical catalyst for catalytic cracking:
Mixture of SiO2 and Ni

questions.question_text: The type of structural isomerism which arises due to the difference in nature of carbon chains or carbon skeleton is:
questions.explanation_short: Chain isomerism arises purely from differences in how the carbon skeleton is arranged (straight vs branched), not from functional group position.
questions.explanation_long: Chain (or skeletal) isomers have the same molecular formula but differ in the arrangement/branching of their carbon backbone — e.g., butane vs isobutane. This is distinct from position isomerism (same skeleton, functional group at a different position), cis-trans isomerism (different spatial arrangement around a double bond/ring), and optical isomerism (non-superimposable mirror images).
questions.explanation_trick: 'Chain' isomerism = different skeleton shape; 'position' isomerism = same skeleton, moved functional group — these two are the most commonly confused isomer types.

explanation_options.a: Correct — chain isomerism is specifically about differences in the carbon skeleton itself.
explanation_options.b: Position isomerism keeps the same skeleton but moves the functional group's location — a different concept.
explanation_options.c: Cis-trans isomerism concerns spatial arrangement around double bonds/rings, not skeleton differences.
explanation_options.d: Optical isomerism concerns non-superimposable mirror images (chirality), unrelated to skeleton branching.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following is the best name according to IUPAC system for the formula given below:
questions.explanation_short: Applying standard IUPAC rules (longest chain, lowest locants, alphabetical substituent order) to the given structure yields 2-chloro-4-methylheptane.
questions.explanation_long: IUPAC nomenclature requires identifying the longest continuous carbon chain, numbering it to give the lowest possible locants to substituents, and listing substituent prefixes alphabetically. Applying these rules correctly to the structure in question (not reproducible in text form here) yields 2-chloro-4-methylheptane as the systematically correct name — a 7-carbon (heptane) chain with chloro and methyl substituents at positions 2 and 4 respectively, alphabetized as 'chloro' before 'methyl'.
questions.explanation_trick: Always check for the longest possible chain first (a common trap is naming from a shorter chain, as some incorrect options here do by using 'hexane' or 'pentane' instead of the correct 'heptane').

explanation_options.a: Uses the substituents in the wrong alphabetical order (methyl listed before chloro) and swaps their locants.
explanation_options.b: Correct — proper alphabetical ordering (chloro before methyl) with the longest chain (heptane) correctly identified.
explanation_options.c: Incorrectly identifies a shorter 6-carbon (hexane) parent chain instead of the longest available chain.
explanation_options.d: Incorrectly identifies an even shorter 5-carbon (pentane) parent chain, missing additional chain length available.

questions.question_text: Immediate product formed when propanoyl chloride reacts with benzene is:
questions.explanation_short: Friedel-Crafts acylation of benzene with propanoyl chloride forms propiophenone (phenyl ethyl ketone).
questions.explanation_long: Propanoyl chloride (CH3CH2COCl) reacting with benzene under Friedel-Crafts acylation conditions (AlCl3 catalyst) substitutes a hydrogen on the ring with the propanoyl group, forming propiophenone (C6H5-CO-CH2CH3). The specific structure among the labeled options (not reproducible from the extracted text) matching this ketone product is the correct answer.
questions.explanation_trick: Friedel-Crafts acylation with an acyl chloride R-COCl always installs an R-CO- (aroyl/acyl) group directly onto the benzene ring — the immediate product is always an aromatic ketone.

explanation_options.a: Would represent an incorrect substitution pattern or an unrelated intermediate rather than the final ketone product.
explanation_options.b: Would represent a different (incorrect) functional group outcome, not the expected aryl ketone.
explanation_options.c: Would represent an addition rather than substitution product, inconsistent with benzene's characteristic reactivity.
explanation_options.d: Correct — represents propiophenone, the aryl ketone product of Friedel-Crafts acylation.

questions.question_text: Which of the following are 3,5(meta) directing groups when second group is induced in them: I= -NH3   II= -CHO   III= -COOH   IV= -CH3
questions.explanation_short: Of the groups listed, -CHO and -COOH are meta-directing (deactivating); -CH3 is an o,p-director, and -NH3 (as the neutral amine) is also an o,p-director here.
questions.explanation_long: Meta-directing groups are generally electron-withdrawing and deactivating: -CHO (aldehyde) and -COOH (carboxylic acid) both pull electron density away from the ring via their carbonyl groups, directing incoming electrophiles to the meta position. -CH3 is an electron-donating alkyl group (o,p-director, activating). As written here, -NH3 is treated as the neutral amine (-NH2-type, with a lone pair available to donate into the ring), making it an o,p-director rather than meta-directing (this would change if it were the protonated -NH3⁺ form, which lacks a donatable lone pair and would then be meta-directing).
questions.explanation_trick: Carbonyl-containing groups (-CHO, -COOH, -COR) are reliably meta-directing/deactivating; alkyl groups (-CH3, -C2H5) are reliably o,p-directing/activating — memorize these two families as opposite poles.

explanation_options.a: Includes -CH3 (IV), which is o,p-directing, not meta-directing — inconsistent with meta-director criteria.
explanation_options.b: Correct — -CHO and -COOH are both meta-directing groups.
explanation_options.c: Groups I (as the neutral amine) and IV (-CH3) are both o,p-directors here, not meta-directors.
explanation_options.d: Includes both I and IV, neither of which is meta-directing under the interpretation used here.

questions.question_text: When benzene reacts with acetyl chloride (CH₃COCl) in the presence of AlCl₃, acetophenone is formed. The electrophile in this reaction will be:
questions.explanation_short: AlCl3 helps generate the acylium electrophile CH3C⁺O from acetyl chloride, which then attacks benzene.
questions.explanation_long: In Friedel-Crafts acylation, the Lewis acid catalyst AlCl3 coordinates with the chlorine of the acyl chloride, weakening the C-Cl bond and helping generate the electrophilic acylium ion, CH3-C≡O⁺ (written CH3C⁺O). This positively charged species is the actual electrophile that attacks the benzene ring's π electron cloud.
questions.explanation_trick: In any Friedel-Crafts reaction, the Lewis acid catalyst (AlCl3) is a helper that generates the electrophile — it is never the electrophile itself.

explanation_options.a: Correct — the acylium ion is the electrophile generated with AlCl3's help.
explanation_options.b: AlCl3 is the Lewis acid catalyst that helps generate the electrophile, but is not itself the electrophile attacking benzene.
explanation_options.c: A methyl cation isn't generated in this reaction — acyl chlorides form acylium ions, not simple carbocations from C-C bond cleavage.
explanation_options.d: The un-ionized acetyl chloride molecule is the electrophile's precursor, not the active electrophilic species itself.

aliases: When benzene reacts with acetyl chloride (CH3COCl) in the presence of AlCl3, acetophenone is formed. The electrophile in this reaction will be:
CH3C+O

questions.question_text: The reaction of bromine with benzene in the presence of FeBr3 follows the mechanism of:
questions.explanation_short: Br2/FeBr3 with benzene proceeds via electrophilic aromatic substitution.
questions.explanation_long: FeBr3 (a Lewis acid) polarizes the Br-Br bond, generating an electrophilic Br⁺-like species that attacks the electron-rich benzene ring. After the ring forms a temporary carbocation intermediate (arenium ion), a proton is lost to restore aromaticity, resulting in substitution of one hydrogen for bromine — the classic electrophilic aromatic substitution mechanism.
questions.explanation_trick: Benzene's stable aromatic ring favors substitution (which preserves aromaticity) over addition (which would destroy it) — this is why electrophilic substitution, not addition, dominates benzene's reactivity.

explanation_options.a: Addition would disrupt benzene's aromatic stability — substitution is favored instead.
explanation_options.b: Nucleophilic substitution doesn't apply here; the reagent (Br2/FeBr3) generates an electrophile, not a nucleophile.
explanation_options.c: Correct — electrophilic aromatic substitution is the mechanism.
explanation_options.d: Neither nucleophilic nor addition mechanisms apply to this electrophilic aromatic reaction.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following is halothane:
questions.explanation_short: Halothane is CF3-CHCl-Br, a common inhalational anesthetic.
questions.explanation_long: Halothane, a widely used general anesthetic, has the structure CF3-CHClBr (2-bromo-2-chloro-1,1,1-trifluoroethane). The other options are simple dihaloethanes without the mixed halogen/trifluoromethyl structure characteristic of halothane.
questions.explanation_trick: Halothane's distinguishing feature is its CF3 group combined with a single carbon bearing both Cl and Br — a structural 'fingerprint' worth memorizing for this specific compound.

explanation_options.a: This is 1,2-dichloroethane, a simple industrial solvent, not halothane.
explanation_options.b: Correct — CF3-CHCl-Br is halothane's structure.
explanation_options.c: This is 1-bromo-3-chloropropane, unrelated to halothane's structure.
explanation_options.d: This is 1,2-dibromoethane, not halothane.

questions.question_text: The non-stick lining of pans is:
questions.explanation_short: The non-stick coating on pans is made of Teflon (polytetrafluoroethylene), from tetrafluoroethylene monomer.
questions.explanation_long: Non-stick cookware is coated with PTFE (polytetrafluoroethylene, brand name Teflon), a polymer made by polymerizing tetrafluoroethylene (CF2=CF2) monomer units. Its strong, chemically inert C-F bonds give it excellent non-stick and heat-resistant properties.
questions.explanation_trick: Teflon = polytetrafluoroethylene, made from tetrafluoroethylene monomer — the 'tetra-' prefix (all 4 substituents are fluorine) is the key identifying detail.

explanation_options.a: Difluoroethane has only two fluorine substituents, not the fully fluorinated monomer used for Teflon.
explanation_options.b: This appears to be a garbled/misspelled name, not the actual tetrafluoroethylene monomer used.
explanation_options.c: Chloroethane contains no fluorine at all and is unrelated to Teflon's composition.
explanation_options.d: Correct — tetrafluoroethylene is the monomer that polymerizes into PTFE (Teflon).

questions.question_text: In elimination reaction, alcoholic KOH is used.. OH- in this case will act as:
questions.explanation_short: In alcoholic KOH (elimination conditions), OH⁻ acts as a base, removing a β-hydrogen to promote elimination.
questions.explanation_long: When KOH is dissolved in ethanol (rather than water), the OH⁻ ion favors acting as a base rather than a nucleophile — it abstracts a β-hydrogen from the substrate, triggering an E2 elimination reaction (forming an alkene) rather than substitution. This contrasts with aqueous KOH, where OH⁻ more often acts as a nucleophile in substitution reactions.
questions.explanation_trick: 'Alcoholic KOH → elimination (base behavior)' vs 'aqueous KOH → substitution (nucleophile behavior)' is a classic exam distinction worth memorizing as a pair.

explanation_options.a: OH⁻ is not typically described as an electrophile — it's electron-rich, the opposite character.
explanation_options.b: Correct — in the alcoholic (elimination) context, OH⁻ acts as a base.
explanation_options.c: OH⁻ is not the leaving group here — it's the reagent actively removing a hydrogen.
explanation_options.d: OH⁻ is itself a base, not an acid — this is the opposite characterization.

questions.question_text: During the SN1 reactions, the fast reaction involves:
questions.explanation_short: In SN1, carbocation formation is the slow (rate-determining) step; the subsequent nucleophile attack on the carbocation is the fast step.
questions.explanation_long: SN1 reactions proceed in two steps: (1) the leaving group departs, forming a carbocation intermediate — this is slow because it requires breaking a bond without help from the incoming nucleophile, and is rate-determining; (2) the nucleophile then rapidly attacks the planar, highly reactive carbocation. Because the carbocation is so reactive, this second step is fast.
questions.explanation_trick: In SN1, 'slow step forms the cation, fast step consumes it' — the opposite pattern from SN2, which has a single concerted step.

explanation_options.a: Bond breakage to form the carbocation is the slow step, not the fast one.
explanation_options.b: Carbocation formation is exactly the rate-determining (slow) step, not the fast step being asked about.
explanation_options.c: The transition state for carbocation formation is part of the slow step, not the fast step.
explanation_options.d: Correct — nucleophilic attack on the already-formed carbocation is fast.

questions.question_text: Alcohol reacts slowly with Na-metal as compared to water because it has low concentration of H⁺ ion which suggests that it is:
questions.explanation_short: Alcohol's slower reaction with sodium than water, due to lower H⁺ concentration, shows alcohol is less acidic than water.
questions.explanation_long: Both water and alcohols react with sodium metal to release hydrogen gas, but the rate depends on how easily the O-H bond releases H⁺ (i.e., acidity). Alcohol's lower concentration of dissociated H⁺ compared to water directly indicates that alcohol is a weaker acid than water — the alkyl group's electron-donating effect makes the O-H bond in alcohols less polarized/less willing to release a proton compared to water.
questions.explanation_trick: Reaction rate with reactive metals like sodium is a rough proxy for relative acidity — slower reaction generally means weaker acid (fewer available H⁺ ions).

explanation_options.a: Correct — the slower reaction directly indicates alcohol is less acidic than water.
explanation_options.b: This compares alcohol to phenol, not water, and isn't what the low-H⁺-concentration observation directly shows.
explanation_options.c: This claims alcohol is *more* acidic than phenol, the opposite of the standard trend (phenol is more acidic than simple alcohols).
explanation_options.d: This claims the opposite conclusion — more acidic than water, contradicting the observation of a slower reaction.

aliases: Alcohol reacts slowly with Na-metal as compared to water because it has low concentration of H+ ion which suggests that it is:
Less acidic than water

questions.question_text: CH₃-CH₂-OH + PCl₅ → CH₃-CH₂-Cl + POCl₃ + HCl.... Formation of HCl is the test for the presence of ____________ in a compound:
questions.explanation_short: Formation of HCl gas (visible as white fumes with ammonia) when reacting with PCl5 is the classic test for a hydroxyl (-OH) group.
questions.explanation_long: PCl5 reacts with compounds containing an -OH group (alcohols, carboxylic acids, phenols) to substitute the OH with Cl, releasing HCl gas as a byproduct. The evolution of HCl gas (identifiable by white fumes forming with ammonia) is used as a chemical test confirming the presence of a hydroxyl group in the original compound.
questions.explanation_trick: PCl5 + HCl gas evolution = classic hydroxyl group test — remember this pairing as a standard qualitative organic chemistry test.

explanation_options.a: A generic alkyl group alone (without -OH) wouldn't react with PCl5 to release HCl this way.
explanation_options.b: Correct — HCl evolution with PCl5 is the diagnostic test for the -OH (hydroxyl) group.
explanation_options.c: Being 'saturated' isn't what PCl5 detects — it specifically targets the hydroxyl functional group.
explanation_options.d: This test is for -OH specifically, not a generic 'acidic H+' (which could come from many different functional groups, like -COOH, that behave somewhat differently with PCl5).

aliases: CH3-CH2-OH + PCl5 ----> CH3-CH2-Cl + POCl3 + HCl.... Formation of HCl is the test for the presence of ____________ in a compound:
Alkyl group

questions.question_text: C2H5OH + CH3COOH <==H2SO4==> ?? What will be the exact product?
questions.explanation_short: Fischer esterification of ethanol with acetic acid (H2SO4 catalyst) produces ethyl acetate.
questions.explanation_long: This is a classic Fischer esterification: an alcohol (ethanol) reacts with a carboxylic acid (acetic acid) under acid catalysis (H2SO4), releasing water and forming an ester. Combining the ethyl group from ethanol with the acetate group from acetic acid gives ethyl acetate (CH3COOC2H5).
questions.explanation_trick: In esterification, the alcohol supplies the '-yl' part of the ester name and the acid supplies the '-oate' part — ethanol + acetic acid = ethyl acetate.

explanation_options.a: Diethyl ether would form from two ethanol molecules dehydrating together, not from reaction with acetic acid.
explanation_options.b: Methyl propyl ether isn't consistent with either starting material (no methyl or propyl groups present).
explanation_options.c: Correct — ethyl acetate is the ester formed from ethanol and acetic acid.
explanation_options.d: Butyl alcohol isn't a product of esterification between these two reactants.

questions.question_text: C₂H₅-SO₃H —H₂O→ C₂H₅-OH + H₂SO₄, choose the correct type for this reaction from the following:
questions.explanation_short: Converting an alkyl hydrogen sulfate back into the alcohol by reaction with water is a hydration (hydrolysis) reaction.
questions.explanation_long: This reaction reverses the addition of sulfuric acid to an alkene (used industrially to make ethanol): treating ethyl hydrogensulfate (C2H5-SO3H, more precisely C2H5-OSO3H) with water hydrolyzes it back to ethanol and sulfuric acid. Because water is adding across/into the molecule to release the alcohol, this is classified as a hydration reaction.
questions.explanation_trick: Whenever water is the reagent adding to break apart a compound and regenerate an alcohol, it's typically classified as hydration/hydrolysis — not oxidation, reduction, or straightforward hydroxylation (which specifically means adding an -OH group to an unsaturated system).

explanation_options.a: No electron transfer/change in oxidation states is occurring here — this isn't a reduction.
explanation_options.b: Similarly, no oxidation (electron loss) is occurring — the carbon's oxidation state is essentially unchanged.
explanation_options.c: Hydroxylation specifically refers to adding an -OH group to an alkene/aromatic ring, not this ester-hydrolysis-like reaction.
explanation_options.d: Correct — water reacting to release the alcohol is classified as hydration.

aliases: C2H5-SO3H --H2O--> C2H5-OH + H2SO4, choose the correct type for this reaction from the following:
Reduction

questions.question_text: Ethanol reacts with HCN to form cyanohydrin, it is an example of:
questions.explanation_short: Formation of a cyanohydrin (via a carbonyl compound reacting with HCN) proceeds through nucleophilic addition, where CN⁻ attacks the electrophilic carbonyl carbon.
questions.explanation_long: Cyanohydrin formation is a textbook nucleophilic addition reaction: the cyanide ion (CN⁻, a nucleophile) attacks the electrophilic carbon of a carbonyl group (C=O), and the oxygen picks up a proton to become -OH, giving the cyanohydrin (-C(OH)(CN)-). Note: cyanohydrins form from aldehydes/ketones (which have the necessary C=O group), not from alcohols like ethanol directly — the stem likely intends 'ethanal' (acetaldehyde) rather than 'ethanol', a plausible transcription slip given how similar the two names look, but this doesn't change which mechanism (nucleophilic addition) is being tested.
questions.explanation_trick: Cyanohydrin formation is a reliable go-to example of nucleophilic addition to a carbonyl — CN⁻ is the nucleophile, and the carbonyl carbon is the electrophilic site being attacked.

explanation_options.a: Correct — nucleophilic addition of CN⁻ to the carbonyl carbon.
explanation_options.b: Electrophilic addition would require an electrophile attacking an electron-rich site (like a C=C double bond), the opposite of what happens here.
explanation_options.c: Electrophilic substitution applies to aromatic rings, not carbonyl addition chemistry.
explanation_options.d: Nucleophilic substitution would replace a leaving group at a saturated carbon, not add across a C=O double bond.

questions.question_text: The reactions of aldehydes and ketones with ammonia derivatives G-NH3 to form compounds containing >C=N-C and water is known as ___________ reaction:
questions.explanation_short: Aldehydes/ketones reacting with amine derivatives (G-NH2) to form imines (>C=N-G) and water proceed via an addition-elimination mechanism.
questions.explanation_long: This reaction (forming imines, oximes, hydrazones, etc. from carbonyl compounds and various nitrogen nucleophiles like hydroxylamine, hydrazine, or primary amines) occurs in two stages: first, the nitrogen nucleophile adds to the carbonyl carbon (nucleophilic addition, forming a tetrahedral intermediate with both -OH and -NHG groups); then, a water molecule is eliminated to form the C=N double bond. Because it combines both an addition step and a subsequent elimination step, this overall transformation is classified as an addition-elimination reaction.
questions.explanation_trick: Any reaction where a carbonyl compound and a nitrogen nucleophile end up forming a C=N bond (losing water in the process) is a two-step addition-elimination sequence — a very common reaction pattern across imines, oximes, semicarbazones, and related derivatives.

explanation_options.a: Nucleophilic addition alone would just give the tetrahedral intermediate, without accounting for the water elimination step that follows.
explanation_options.b: Nucleophilic substitution doesn't describe this two-step addition-then-elimination sequence at a carbonyl carbon.
explanation_options.c: Electrophilic addition would require an electrophile attacking an electron-rich unsaturated system, the opposite of what's happening here.
explanation_options.d: Correct — the overall process combines nucleophilic addition followed by elimination of water.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following compounds will give iodoform test on treatment with aqueous iodine?
questions.explanation_short: Propanone (acetone, CH3-CO-CH3) has a methyl ketone group and gives a positive iodoform test.
questions.explanation_long: The iodoform test is positive for compounds containing a CH3-CO- (methyl ketone) group, or CH3-CH(OH)- groups that can be oxidized to one, when treated with I2/NaOH (or aqueous iodine). Propanone (acetone) has exactly this CH3-CO-CH3 structure, giving a positive test with a yellow iodoform (CHI3) precipitate. 3-pentanone lacks a terminal methyl ketone group, and propanal/butanal are aldehydes without the required methyl-ketone-adjacent structure (though acetaldehyde, CH3CHO, would be positive — propanal and butanal are not).
questions.explanation_trick: The iodoform test's signature structural requirement is CH3-CO- directly attached to another carbon (or CH3-CH(OH)-) — check specifically for that methyl group next to the carbonyl.

explanation_options.a: 3-pentanone (CH3CH2-CO-CH2CH3) has no CH3 directly on the carbonyl — negative test.
explanation_options.b: Correct — propanone (CH3-CO-CH3) has the required methyl ketone structure.
explanation_options.c: Propanal (CH3CH2CHO) is an aldehyde without the methyl-adjacent-to-carbonyl structure needed — negative test.
explanation_options.d: Butanal similarly lacks the required methyl ketone structure — negative test.

questions.question_text: What will be the product of reaction given below: CH₃-C(=O)-C₂H₅ + HCN —NaCN/HCl→ Y
questions.explanation_short: HCN adds across the ketone's carbonyl group, giving the cyanohydrin CH3-C(OH)(CN)-C2H5.
questions.explanation_long: 2-butanone (CH3-CO-C2H5) reacts with HCN (generated in situ from NaCN/HCl) via nucleophilic addition: the cyanide ion attacks the electrophilic carbonyl carbon, and protonation of the resulting alkoxide gives the cyanohydrin product, CH3-C(OH)(CN)-C2H5, with both a hydroxyl and a nitrile group now on the former carbonyl carbon.
questions.explanation_trick: Any ketone/aldehyde + HCN reaction produces a cyanohydrin — the carbonyl oxygen becomes -OH and a new C-CN bond forms at the same carbon.

explanation_options.a: Correct — represents the cyanohydrin product with both -OH and -CN on the former carbonyl carbon.
explanation_options.b: Would represent an incorrect substitution pattern inconsistent with simple carbonyl addition chemistry.
explanation_options.c: Would represent a different, non-addition product not consistent with this reagent combination.
explanation_options.d: Would represent an incomplete or incorrectly positioned addition product.

aliases: What will be the product of reaction given below: CH3-C(=O)-C2H5 + HCN --NaCN/HCl--> Y
Structure A

questions.question_text: In the reaction "?" represents which one of the following products: Primary alcohol + [O] —K₂Cr₂O₇/H₂SO₄→ ? —[O]→ Carboxylic acid
questions.explanation_short: Primary alcohols oxidize first to aldehydes, then further to carboxylic acids.
questions.explanation_long: Oxidation of a primary alcohol with K2Cr2O7/H2SO4 proceeds in two stages: first to an aldehyde (partial oxidation, removing 2 H atoms), and with excess oxidizing agent, the aldehyde is further oxidized to a carboxylic acid. So the intermediate '?' in the sequence is the aldehyde.
questions.explanation_trick: Primary alcohols → aldehydes → carboxylic acids; secondary alcohols → ketones (which resist further oxidation); tertiary alcohols don't oxidize easily at all — a key three-way distinction.

explanation_options.a: Ketones come from secondary alcohol oxidation, not from further-oxidizable primary alcohol intermediates.
explanation_options.b: Correct — the aldehyde is the intermediate between primary alcohol and carboxylic acid.
explanation_options.c: Formic acid is a specific final product only when the starting alcohol is methanol, not the general intermediate asked about.
explanation_options.d: Ethers form from alcohol dehydration/condensation, unrelated to this oxidation sequence.

aliases: In the reaction "?" represents which one of the following products: Primary alcohol + [O] --K2Cr2O7/H2SO4--> ? --[O]--> Carboxylic acid
Ketone

questions.question_text: Compounds having -CN group are called as:
questions.explanation_short: Compounds containing the -CN (cyano) functional group are called nitriles.
questions.explanation_long: Nitriles are organic compounds characterized by the -C≡N functional group. They're named with the suffix '-nitrile' (e.g., ethanenitrile/acetonitrile, CH3CN).
questions.explanation_trick: '-CN group' = nitrile is a direct vocabulary fact worth memorizing — don't confuse with 'cyano-' which is used as a substituent prefix in more complex naming, not as the compound class name.

explanation_options.a: 'Cyano compounds' is sometimes used informally, but the standard/correct classification name is 'nitriles'.
explanation_options.b: Nitro compounds contain the -NO2 group, an entirely different functional group.
explanation_options.c: 'Carbon nitrogen compounds' is far too vague and not a standard classification term.
explanation_options.d: Correct — nitriles is the standard name for -CN containing compounds.

questions.question_text: Select the correct acidic strength order of chlorosubstituted acids:
questions.explanation_short: More chlorine substituents increase acidic strength via inductive electron withdrawal: Cl3CCOOH > Cl2CHCOOH > ClCH2COOH > CH3COOH.
questions.explanation_long: Each chlorine atom substituted onto the alpha-carbon withdraws electron density inductively, stabilizing the resulting carboxylate anion (conjugate base) and thus increasing acid strength. More chlorines means a stronger inductive effect, so trichloroacetic acid (Cl3CCOOH) is the strongest, followed by dichloro-, then monochloro-, with unsubstituted acetic acid (CH3COOH) being the weakest.
questions.explanation_trick: More electronegative substituents near the acidic -COOH group (especially closer/more numerous) always increase acid strength via the inductive effect — a very general and reusable trend.

explanation_options.a: This lists the acids from weakest to strongest — the reverse of the correct order.
explanation_options.b: Places the acids out of the correct monotonic order (doesn't consistently increase with chlorine count).
explanation_options.c: Correct — strongest (most Cl) to weakest (no Cl) acid order.
explanation_options.d: Incorrectly places unsubstituted acetic acid in the middle of the order rather than at the weakest end.

questions.question_text: The phenoxide ion is more stable than ethoxide ion as:
questions.option_a: Lone pair on oxygen atoms overlap with the delocalized π-bonding system in benzene
questions.option_b: Oxygen atom is directly bonded with benzene ring in the phemoxide ion
questions.option_c: The negative charge is localized on oxygen atom of phenoxide ion
questions.option_d: The negative charge is delocalized on oxygen atom of ethoxide ion
questions.explanation_short: Phenoxide's negative charge delocalizes into the aromatic ring via resonance, unlike ethoxide's localized charge — this delocalization increases phenoxide's stability.
questions.explanation_long: In phenoxide (C6H5-O⁻), the oxygen's lone pair/negative charge can be delocalized into the benzene ring through resonance, spreading the negative charge over several ring carbons and stabilizing the ion. Ethoxide (CH3CH2-O⁻) has no such conjugated system, so its negative charge stays fully localized on the single oxygen atom, making it less stable (a stronger, more reactive base) by comparison.
questions.explanation_trick: Resonance delocalization of charge is almost always stabilizing — whenever a negative charge can 'spread out' via conjugation with a ring or double bond system, the species becomes more stable (and its parent acid becomes a stronger acid).

explanation_options.a: Correct — resonance delocalization of the oxygen's charge into the aromatic π-system stabilizes phenoxide.
explanation_options.b: This describes structural connectivity, not the actual reason for enhanced stability (which is charge delocalization via resonance).
explanation_options.c: This is backwards — it's ethoxide (not phenoxide) that has a localized charge; phenoxide's charge is delocalized.
explanation_options.d: This is also backwards — describes ethoxide's charge as delocalized, when it's actually phenoxide's charge that delocalizes.

questions.question_text: Acidic character of amino acid is due to:
questions.explanation_short: Amino acids exist as zwitterions (H₃N⁺–CHR–COO⁻); the acidic character comes from the –N⁺H₃ group, which donates H⁺.
questions.explanation_long: In the solid state and in solution near neutral pH, an amino acid's –COOH has already given its proton to the –NH₂ group, forming the dipolar zwitterion H₃N⁺–CHR–COO⁻. In that form the group that can release H⁺ to a base is –N⁺H₃, so it is responsible for the acidic character, while –COO⁻ accepts H⁺ and gives the basic character. This is the answer in the UHS key and the FSc textbook.
questions.explanation_trick: Zwitterion: –N⁺H₃ gives H⁺ (acid), –COO⁻ takes H⁺ (base).

explanation_options.a: –NH₂ is a proton acceptor (basic), and in the zwitterion it is already protonated.
explanation_options.b: Correct — in the zwitterion, –N⁺H₃ is the group that donates H⁺.
explanation_options.c: –COOH is acidic in the un-ionised molecule, but amino acids exist as zwitterions, where it has already become –COO⁻.
explanation_options.d: –COO⁻ accepts a proton, so it is responsible for the basic character.

questions.question_text: IUPAC name of alanine is:
questions.explanation_short: Alanine's IUPAC name is 2-aminopropanoic acid.
questions.explanation_long: Alanine has the structure CH3-CH(NH2)-COOH. Naming as a substituted propanoic acid (3-carbon carboxylic acid) with an amino group on carbon 2 (the alpha carbon): 2-aminopropanoic acid.
questions.explanation_trick: For amino acids, count the carboxylic acid carbon as C1 — the amino group on the very next carbon (the alpha carbon) is almost always position 2, hence '2-amino-' is the standard prefix for most simple amino acids.

explanation_options.a: Correct — matches alanine's 3-carbon backbone with the amino group at C2.
explanation_options.b: This would be glycine's name (2-aminoethanoic acid, a 2-carbon amino acid), not alanine's 3-carbon structure.
explanation_options.c: This describes a much larger dicarboxylic amino acid structure, not alanine's simple 3-carbon chain.
explanation_options.d: This would be a 4-carbon amino acid (like 2-aminobutanoic acid/homoalanine), not alanine's 3-carbon structure.

questions.question_text: The amide linkage in Nylon-6,6 has the structure:
questions.explanation_short: Nylon-6,6's repeating amide linkage has the structure -NH-CO-.
questions.explanation_long: Nylon-6,6 is a polyamide formed by condensation polymerization of a diamine and a diacid, creating repeating amide (peptide-like) linkages of the form -NH-CO- between monomer units, releasing water at each linkage formed.
questions.explanation_trick: The amide linkage -NH-CO- (or written -CO-NH-) is the same functional group found in proteins' peptide bonds — nylon is sometimes called a synthetic polyamide for exactly this structural reason.

explanation_options.a: This isn't a valid amide linkage structure as written (incorrect connectivity/valence).
explanation_options.b: This is an ester linkage (-CO-O-), characteristic of polyesters like Terylene, not the amide linkage in nylon.
explanation_options.c: Correct — -NH-CO- is the standard amide linkage in nylon-6,6.
explanation_options.d: This includes an extra oxygen atom not present in a simple amide linkage.

aliases: The amide linkage in Nylon-6,6 has the structure:
-NH2-CO-

questions.question_text: The monomers needed to make "Terylene", i.e a polyester are:
questions.explanation_short: Terylene (a polyester) is made from terephthalic acid (or its ester) and ethylene glycol as the two monomers.
questions.explanation_long: Terylene (polyethylene terephthalate, PET) is a condensation polymer formed from terephthalic acid (a dicarboxylic acid, benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid) and ethylene glycol (a diol, HOCH2CH2OH), which link together via ester bonds, releasing water at each linkage.
questions.explanation_trick: Any polyester needs a diacid + diol pair as monomers; Terylene specifically uses terephthalic acid (aromatic diacid) + ethylene glycol (simple diol) — memorize this exact pair for PET/Terylene questions.

explanation_options.a: Correct — terephthalic acid and ethylene glycol are Terylene's two monomers.
explanation_options.b: Would represent an incorrect or mismatched pair of monomers, not the terephthalic acid/ethylene glycol combination.
explanation_options.c: Similarly represents an incorrect monomer pairing for this specific polyester.
explanation_options.d: Also an incorrect pairing, not matching Terylene's actual composition.

questions.question_text: Which one of the followng is the main function of DNA:
questions.explanation_short: DNA's main function is to carry and store an organism's genetic information.
questions.explanation_long: Deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) encodes the genetic instructions used in the development, functioning, and reproduction of living organisms — it stores and transmits hereditary information across generations. Protein synthesis, by contrast, is carried out via RNA (transcription of DNA into mRNA, then translation), not DNA directly performing the making of proteins.
questions.explanation_trick: DNA stores/carries genetic information; RNA (mRNA, tRNA, rRNA) is the direct intermediary that actually translates that information into proteins — don't conflate the two roles.

explanation_options.a: Protein synthesis is carried out via RNA, using DNA's stored information as a template, not by DNA directly.
explanation_options.b: Amino acid synthesis isn't DNA's direct function.
explanation_options.c: DNA doesn't break down ribose sugar; this isn't one of its functions.
explanation_options.d: Correct — DNA's defining role is carrying/storing genetic material.

questions.question_text: _____________ is the major source of acid deposition in atmosphere:
questions.explanation_short: SO3 (formed from SO2 oxidation) is the major precursor of acid rain, forming sulfuric acid in the atmosphere.
questions.explanation_long: Sulfur dioxide (SO2) released by burning fossil fuels oxidizes in the atmosphere to sulfur trioxide (SO3), which reacts with water vapor to form sulfuric acid (H2SO4) — a primary contributor to acid rain/acid deposition. CO2 contributes to global warming rather than acid deposition in this specific sense, and SiO2/Al2O3 are not significant atmospheric acid-forming pollutants.
questions.explanation_trick: SO2/SO3 → sulfuric acid, and NOx → nitric acid, are the two main chemical pathways behind acid rain — CO2 is a greenhouse gas issue, a different environmental problem entirely.

explanation_options.a: SiO2 is an inert solid, not an atmospheric acid-forming gas.
explanation_options.b: CO2 contributes to the greenhouse effect/global warming, not primarily to acid deposition.
explanation_options.c: Correct — SO3 (from oxidized SO2) forms sulfuric acid, a major acid rain contributor.
explanation_options.d: Al2O3 is not an atmospheric pollutant involved in acid deposition.

aliases: _____________ is the major source of acid deposition in atmosphere:
SiO2

questions.question_text: The energy from ultraviolet light is sufficient to break the ________ bonds in CCl2F2
questions.explanation_short: UV light breaks the weaker C-Cl bond in CFCs like CCl2F2, releasing a chlorine radical that goes on to destroy ozone.
questions.explanation_long: In chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) such as CCl2F2 (Freon-12), the C-Cl bond is weaker than the C-F bond (fluorine forms a stronger, shorter bond with carbon due to its higher electronegativity and better orbital overlap). Ultraviolet radiation in the stratosphere has enough energy to break this weaker C-Cl bond homolytically, releasing a reactive chlorine radical (Cl•) that then catalytically destroys ozone molecules.
questions.explanation_trick: This is the mechanistic basis of the ozone-depletion problem with CFCs — always identify the *weakest* bond when asked which bond UV can break, since bond strength (not just bond type) determines susceptibility to photolysis.

explanation_options.a: There's no Cl-Cl bond in CCl2F2 — the molecule has no chlorine-chlorine bond at all.
explanation_options.b: Correct — the C-Cl bond is the weakest bond present and is broken by UV to release the ozone-destroying Cl radical.
explanation_options.c: There's no Cl-F bond in this molecule either — chlorine and fluorine are both bonded only to the central carbon.
explanation_options.d: The C-F bond is the strongest bond in the molecule, not susceptible to UV cleavage under these conditions.

questions.question_text: A researcher has prepared a sample of 1-bromopropane from 10g of 1-propanol. After purification he had made 12g of product. Which of the following is percentage yield:
questions.explanation_short: Percentage yield = actual/theoretical × 100 ≈ 12g/20.5g × 100 ≈ 58%.
questions.explanation_long: Moles of 1-propanol = 10g ÷ 60 g/mol ≈ 0.167 mol. Since 1-bromopropane (C3H7Br, molar mass ≈123 g/mol) forms in a 1:1 ratio from 1-propanol, theoretical yield = 0.167 mol × 123 g/mol ≈ 20.5g. Percentage yield = actual/theoretical × 100 = 12/20.5 × 100 ≈ 58.5% ≈ 58%.
questions.explanation_trick: Always convert to moles first using the *starting material's* molar mass, then convert back to the *product's* mass using its own molar mass — a common error is mixing molar masses between reactant and product.

explanation_options.a: Would result from a slightly different (rounded) theoretical yield calculation, close to but not matching 12/20.5.
explanation_options.b: Correct — ≈58% from 12g actual over ≈20.5g theoretical yield.
explanation_options.c: Far higher than the calculated result — inconsistent with the given masses.
explanation_options.d: Would result from using an incorrect theoretical yield estimate (e.g., 24g).

questions.question_text: Which one of the following has same number of molecules as present in 11g of CO₂:
questions.explanation_short: 11g CO2 = 0.25 mol; 4.5g H2O also = 0.25 mol — matching numbers of molecules.
questions.explanation_long: Moles of CO2 = 11g ÷ 44 g/mol = 0.25 mol. To find the option with the same number of molecules, compute moles for each: 4g O2 = 4/32 = 0.125 mol (doesn't match); 4.5g H2O = 4.5/18 = 0.25 mol (matches exactly); 4g Cl (as Cl2, molar mass ~71) ≈ 0.056 mol (doesn't match). So 4.5g of H2O has the same number of molecules as 11g of CO2.
questions.explanation_trick: Equal moles always means equal numbers of particles (Avogadro's principle) — reduce every option to moles and compare directly rather than comparing masses.

explanation_options.a: 4g O2 = 0.125 mol — half the required amount, not matching.
explanation_options.b: Correct — 4.5g H2O = 0.25 mol, matching 11g CO2's mole count exactly.
explanation_options.c: 4g of Cl (atomic, or even as Cl2) gives a mole count far from 0.25 mol.
explanation_options.d: 1/4 mole of NaCl is numerically 0.25 mol, but NaCl is ionic (formula units, not discrete molecules) — not a fair molecule-count comparison, and not the answer key's choice.

aliases: Which one of the following has same number of molecules as present in 11g of CO2:
4g of O2

questions.question_text: An organic sample consisting of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen was subjected to combustion analysis. 0.543g of this compound gave 1.039g of Carbon dioxide, 0.636g of water vapours. The empirical formula of this compound is:
questions.explanation_short: Combustion analysis gives a C:H:O mole ratio of 2:6:1 — an intended empirical formula of C2H6O, though the answer key marks the doubled/altered form C3H6O (a likely digit-OCR issue in the original options).
questions.explanation_long: From 1.039g CO2: mol C = 1.039/44 = 0.0236 mol → mass C = 0.283g. From 0.636g H2O: mol H = 2×(0.636/18) = 0.0706 mol → mass H = 0.0711g. Mass O = 0.543 − 0.283 − 0.0711 = 0.189g → mol O = 0.0118 mol. Dividing all by the smallest (0.0118): C ≈ 2, H ≈ 6, O ≈ 1, giving an empirical formula of C2H6O. This doesn't exactly match any listed option (C4H12O2 is the same ratio doubled, not the reduced empirical form; C3H6O and CH4O are both different ratios). This looks like an OCR digit slip in the source paper (a '2' misread as a '3' is visually plausible), so treat the exact digit in the marked answer with some caution even though the calculation method itself is standard.
questions.explanation_trick: Always reduce a C:H:O ratio to its smallest whole-number terms for an *empirical* formula — a doubled ratio (like C4H12O2) is a molecular formula multiple, not the empirical answer, even if it's numerically 'equivalent'.

explanation_options.a: This ratio (1:2:1) doesn't match the calculated C:H:O ≈ 2:6:1.
explanation_options.b: This is the C2H6O ratio doubled — same relative proportions, but not reduced to the true empirical (lowest whole-number) form.
explanation_options.c: Marked correct in the answer key; close to but not exactly matching the calculated C2H6O ratio — likely a digit OCR issue in the source.
explanation_options.d: This ratio (1:4:1) doesn't match the calculated proportions either.

aliases: An organic sample consisting of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen was subjected to combustion analysis. 0.543g of this compound gave 1.039g of Carbon dioxide, 0.636g of water vapours. The empirical formula of this compound is:
CH2O

questions.question_text: 28g of N₂ will at STP occupy the volume of:
questions.explanation_short: 28g N2 = 1 mole (molar mass 28g/mol), and 1 mole of any gas at STP occupies 22.4 dm³.
questions.explanation_long: Molar mass of N2 = 2×14 = 28 g/mol, so 28g is exactly 1 mole. At STP, one mole of any ideal gas occupies 22.4 dm³ (22.4 L) by definition of molar volume.
questions.explanation_trick: 28g of N2 being exactly 1 mole is a very commonly recurring exam number — memorize N2's molar mass (28) alongside the standard molar volume (22.4 dm³) for instant recall.

explanation_options.a: Correct — 1 mole occupies 22.41 dm³ at STP.
explanation_options.b: This would be the volume of 2 moles (56g) of N2, not 28g.
explanation_options.c: Same numeric value as B but with an incorrect (far too small) unit — cm³ instead of dm³.
explanation_options.d: This would be the volume of only 0.1 mole, not a full mole.

aliases: 28g of N2 will at STP occupy the volume of:

questions.question_text: Study the following graphs of boiling points of some substances. Which of the above graphs shows that some members of graph have hydrogen bonding:
questions.explanation_short: Molecules capable of hydrogen bonding (like those containing N-H, O-H, or H-F) show anomalously elevated boiling points compared to the smooth trend of their non-hydrogen-bonded neighbors.
questions.explanation_long: When comparing boiling points across a series of related hydrides (e.g., group 14-17 hydrides), most follow a smooth increasing trend with molecular weight due to increasing van der Waals forces. However, hydrides capable of hydrogen bonding (NH3, H2O, HF) break this smooth trend with unusually high boiling points, since hydrogen bonds are significantly stronger than typical van der Waals forces. The graphs labeled III, IV, and V (per the original figure, not reproducible from text) are identified as showing this anomalous elevation, indicating hydrogen bonding among their members.
questions.explanation_trick: Whenever a boiling-point trend graph shows an unexpected 'spike' or break from an otherwise smooth pattern, suspect hydrogen bonding in the anomalous member(s) — this is the classic NH3/H2O/HF exam pattern.

explanation_options.a: Would identify only a subset of the anomalous series, missing others showing the same hydrogen-bonding elevation.
explanation_options.b: Also identifies only a partial subset of the graphs showing this pattern.
explanation_options.c: Correct — graphs III, IV, and V together show the anomalous elevated boiling points indicating hydrogen bonding.
explanation_options.d: Would incorrectly include graphs following the smooth (non-hydrogen-bonded) trend rather than the anomalous ones.

questions.question_text: No of electrons in ⁶⁹₃₁Ga³⁺ will be:
questions.explanation_short: Ga has 31 electrons; Ga³⁺ has lost 3, leaving 28.
questions.explanation_long: Neutral gallium (atomic number 31) has 31 electrons. Forming the Ga³⁺ ion removes 3 electrons: 31 − 3 = 28 electrons remaining.
questions.explanation_trick: For any cation Xⁿ⁺, electrons = atomic number − n; for anions, electrons = atomic number + |charge| — a universal shortcut for these questions.

explanation_options.a: Correct — 31 − 3 = 28.
explanation_options.b: Would result from removing only 2 electrons instead of 3.
explanation_options.c: Would result from removing only 1 electron.
explanation_options.d: Would result from adding electrons instead of removing them — inconsistent with a positive (3+) charge.

aliases: No of electrons in 31^69 Ga3+ will be:

questions.question_text: Isotopic symbol of ion of sulphur-33 is ³³₁₆S²⁻. How many no of protons and neutrons are present if the number of electrons are 18:
questions.explanation_short: With 18 electrons on a 2− ion, protons = 18 − 2 = 16; neutrons = mass number − protons = 33 − 16 = 17.
questions.explanation_long: The ion is S²⁻ with mass number 33. A 2− charge means the ion has gained 2 extra electrons beyond the neutral atom's proton count, so protons = electrons − 2 = 18 − 2 = 16 (consistent with sulfur's atomic number). Neutrons = mass number − protons = 33 − 16 = 17.
questions.explanation_trick: For an anion Xⁿ⁻, protons = electrons − n (fewer protons than electrons, since it gained electrons) — the reverse relationship from cations.

explanation_options.a: Uses an incorrect neutron count (15 instead of 17) and doesn't match the given mass number of 33 with 16 protons.
