questions.explanation_short: Chromium's actual electron configuration is an exception to normal Aufbau filling: [Ar]4s¹3d⁵, due to the extra stability of a half-filled d subshell.
questions.explanation_long: While a naive Aufbau-order prediction for chromium (Z=24) would give 4s²3d⁴, the actual observed configuration is 4s¹3d⁵ — one electron shifts from 4s to 3d because a half-filled d subshell (3d⁵, all five orbitals singly occupied) provides extra stability due to favorable exchange energy, outweighing the small energy cost of promoting the electron.
questions.explanation_trick: Chromium and copper are the two classic exceptions to standard Aufbau filling in the first transition series, both driven by the extra stability of half-filled (Cr) or fully-filled (Cu) d subshells — memorize these two exceptions specifically.

explanation_options.a: This is the naive Aufbau-predicted configuration, but doesn't match chromium's actual observed (exception) configuration.
explanation_options.b: This configuration has too many d electrons and doesn't match either the predicted or actual configuration for chromium.
explanation_options.c: This configuration skips 4s entirely, which doesn't match chromium's actual filling pattern.
explanation_options.d: Correct — 4s¹3d⁵ is chromium's actual configuration, reflecting the half-filled d subshell stability exception.

aliases: Which is the correct electronic configuration of Chromium (24Cr)?

questions.question_text: Which one of the following is the structure of Teflon?
questions.explanation_short: Teflon (PTFE) has the repeating structure (-CF2-CF2-)n, formed from tetrafluoroethylene monomer.
questions.explanation_long: Teflon (polytetrafluoroethylene, PTFE) is made by polymerizing tetrafluoroethylene (CF2=CF2) monomer units, giving the fully fluorinated repeating unit (-CF2-CF2-)n — all four substituent positions carry fluorine, none carry hydrogen or other halogens.
questions.explanation_trick: 'Tetra-fluoro-ethylene' directly tells you all 4 substituents are fluorine — no hydrogens or other halogens present in Teflon's structure.

explanation_options.a: Correct — (-CF2-CF2-)n matches Teflon's fully fluorinated structure.
explanation_options.b: This mixes fluorine and chlorine substituents, not matching Teflon's all-fluorine composition.
explanation_options.c: This is plain polyethylene (no halogens at all), unrelated to Teflon.
explanation_options.d: This mixes fluorine and hydrogen substituents unevenly, not matching Teflon's fully fluorinated, symmetric structure.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following enthalpy changes is always exothermic?
questions.explanation_short: Enthalpy of combustion is always exothermic, since combustion (burning in oxygen) always releases energy.
questions.explanation_long: By definition, combustion reactions release energy as they burn a substance in oxygen, making enthalpy of combustion always negative (exothermic). Enthalpy of formation, atomization, and solution can each be either exothermic or endothermic depending on the specific substance involved — none of them are universally one sign the way combustion always is.
questions.explanation_trick: 'Always exothermic' should immediately point to combustion — burning something releasing energy is essentially the definition of the process itself, unlike formation/atomization/solution, which vary case by case.

explanation_options.a: Correct — combustion, by its very nature, always releases energy (is always exothermic).
explanation_options.b: Enthalpy of formation varies in sign depending on the compound (e.g., forming some compounds absorbs energy, others release it).
explanation_options.c: Enthalpy of atomization (breaking a substance into gaseous atoms) is always endothermic (requires energy input), not exothermic.
explanation_options.d: Enthalpy of solution can be either exothermic or endothermic depending on the specific solute and solvent involved.

questions.question_text: While finding the relative atomic mass, which of the following standards is used to compare the atomic mass of chlorine (35.5 amu).
questions.explanation_short: The modern standard for relative atomic mass is Carbon-12.
questions.explanation_long: The internationally accepted standard for atomic mass is defined as exactly 1/12th the mass of a Carbon-12 atom. All other atomic masses, including chlorine's 35.5 amu, are measured relative to this Carbon-12 standard.
questions.explanation_trick: Carbon-12 is THE reference standard for the atomic mass unit — a fundamental, universally-taught fact.

explanation_options.a: Carbon-13 is not the internationally defined standard for atomic mass.
explanation_options.b: Neon-20 is not the standard used for atomic mass comparisons.
explanation_options.c: Correct — Carbon-12 is the internationally accepted standard for atomic mass.
explanation_options.d: 'Nucleon number' is a property of a specific isotope, not a standard reference scale.

questions.question_text: Which compound is obtained by the elimination of bromopropane?
questions.explanation_short: Elimination of bromopropane (C3H7Br) removes HBr to form propene (C3H6).
questions.explanation_long: In an elimination reaction, a hydrogen halide (here, HBr) is removed from an alkyl halide, forming a double bond in its place. Starting from bromopropane (C3H7Br), eliminating HBr leaves propene (C3H6) as the alkene product.
questions.explanation_trick: Elimination always removes two atoms/groups (here H and Br) from adjacent carbons to form a new double bond — the carbon count of the starting alkyl halide is preserved in the resulting alkene.

explanation_options.a: Correct — eliminating HBr from bromopropane (3 carbons) gives propene (3 carbons).
explanation_options.b: Butene has 4 carbons, more than bromopropane's 3-carbon skeleton allows.
explanation_options.c: Ethene has only 2 carbons, fewer than bromopropane's 3-carbon skeleton.
explanation_options.d: Propane is the saturated alkane (no elimination occurred), not the alkene product of an elimination reaction.

questions.question_text: Which product is formed by the reaction of carboxylic acid with alcohol?
questions.explanation_short: Carboxylic acid reacting with alcohol (esterification) produces an ester.
questions.explanation_long: This is the Fischer esterification reaction: RCOOH (carboxylic acid) + R'OH (alcohol) → RCOOR' (ester) + H2O, typically catalyzed by concentrated H2SO4.
questions.explanation_trick: Carboxylic acid + alcohol = ester + water is one of the most fundamental organic reaction pairings to memorize directly.

explanation_options.a: An alkane wouldn't form from this type of condensation reaction between a carboxylic acid and alcohol.
explanation_options.b: An ether would form from two alcohol molecules dehydrating together, not from a carboxylic acid reacting with an alcohol.
explanation_options.c: An aldehyde is a partial oxidation product of a primary alcohol, not a product of esterification.
explanation_options.d: Correct — an ester forms from a carboxylic acid reacting with an alcohol.

questions.question_text: In aqueous solution amino acids exist in an ionic form, shown as +NH3-CHR-COO- in the diagram. This ionic form of amino acid is known as
questions.explanation_short: The dual-charged (+NH3-CHR-COO-) form of an amino acid in solution is called a zwitterion.
questions.explanation_long: A zwitterion is a molecule that carries both a positive and a negative charge simultaneously (but has an overall neutral net charge) — amino acids exist predominantly in this form in aqueous solution, with the amino group protonated (+NH3) and the carboxyl group deprotonated (COO-) at the same time.
questions.explanation_trick: Zwitterion = 'dual ion', a single molecule carrying both + and - charges at once — this specific term, not 'amphoteric ion' (a related but distinct concept describing a substance's *capability* to act as acid or base), is the standard name for this particular charged form.

explanation_options.a: Correct — this dual-charged form is called a zwitterion.
explanation_options.b: 'Amphoteric' describes a substance's ability to act as either an acid or base, a related but distinct concept from the specific named dual-charge structure (zwitterion) itself.
explanation_options.c: A cation carries only a net positive charge, not the dual +/- charge structure shown here.
explanation_options.d: An anion carries only a net negative charge, not the dual +/- charge structure shown here.

questions.question_text: Reaction mechanism of alkanes with halogens is known as
questions.explanation_short: Alkanes reacting with halogens proceed via free radical substitution.
questions.explanation_long: In the reaction of alkanes with halogens (e.g., methane + chlorine under UV light), the mechanism involves generating free radicals via homolytic bond cleavage, which then substitute a hydrogen atom on the alkane with a halogen atom.
questions.explanation_trick: Alkanes + halogens (with UV light) = free radical substitution; alkyl halides + base = elimination — two entirely different reaction types.

explanation_options.a: Propagation is one specific step within the free radical chain mechanism, not the overall name for the reaction type.
explanation_options.b: Correct — free radical substitution is the mechanism for alkane-halogen reactions.
explanation_options.c: Addition reactions apply to unsaturated compounds reacting across a double bond, not saturated alkanes.
explanation_options.d: Elimination describes removing atoms from alkyl halides to form alkenes, a completely different reaction.

questions.question_text: Why is it necessary to distill aldehyde formed from oxidation of primary alcohol through acidified potassium dichromate(VI) solution or acidified sodium dichromate(VI) solution?
questions.option_a: Aldehyde formed may be oxidised further to carboxylic acid concerned.
questions.option_b: Aldehyde formed is unstable and decomposes back to original precursor, i.e., primary alcohol.
questions.option_c: Aldehyde may be oxidised further to a ketone.
questions.option_d: Aldehyde formed may react with primary alcohol, the original reactant.
questions.explanation_short: The aldehyde is distilled off immediately to prevent it from being further oxidized into the carboxylic acid.
questions.explanation_long: When a primary alcohol is oxidized, the initial product is an aldehyde, but the same oxidizing conditions can push the reaction further, oxidizing the aldehyde into a carboxylic acid. Distilling it off as it forms removes it from further contact with the oxidizing agent before that can happen.
questions.explanation_trick: Distilling off a reaction intermediate as it forms is a standard technique to prevent FURTHER reaction — here, further oxidation.

explanation_options.a: Correct — distillation prevents further oxidation of the aldehyde to the carboxylic acid.
explanation_options.b: Aldehydes don't spontaneously decompose back into their precursor alcohol under these conditions.
explanation_options.c: Aldehydes oxidize further to carboxylic acids, not to ketones.
explanation_options.d: There's no significant reaction between the newly-formed aldehyde and leftover alcohol requiring this precaution.

questions.question_text: Electron affinity of the atom is the energy released when
questions.option_a: Covalent bond of molecule is broken
questions.option_b: Electron is added to gaseous atom
questions.option_c: Electron is removed from gaseous atom
questions.option_d: Covalent bond is formed between the atoms
questions.explanation_short: Electron affinity is the energy released when an electron is added to a gaseous atom.
questions.explanation_long: Electron affinity measures the energy change (typically released) when a neutral gaseous atom gains an electron to form a gaseous anion (e.g., Cl(g) + e⁻ → Cl⁻(g)) — distinct from covalent bond formation, which involves sharing electron pairs between atoms.
questions.explanation_trick: Electron affinity = energy for adding ONE electron to a single gaseous atom (forming an ion); this has nothing to do with covalent bonding.

explanation_options.a: Breaking a covalent bond relates to bond dissociation energy, a different concept.
explanation_options.b: Correct — electron affinity is the energy released when an electron is added to a gaseous atom.
explanation_options.c: Removing an electron from a gaseous atom describes ionization energy, the conceptual opposite.
explanation_options.d: Covalent bond formation (electron sharing between two atoms) is a distinct concept from electron affinity.

questions.question_text: Which mechanism of reactions is shown by carbonyl compounds?
questions.explanation_short: Carbonyl compounds (aldehydes and ketones) characteristically undergo nucleophilic addition, since their carbonyl carbon is electrophilic.
questions.explanation_long: The carbon of a C=O (carbonyl) group carries a partial positive charge (due to oxygen's higher electronegativity pulling electron density away), making it electrophilic and attractive to nucleophiles. Nucleophiles attack this carbon, adding across the double bond (nucleophilic addition) — the characteristic reactivity pattern of aldehydes and ketones, seen in reactions like cyanohydrin formation or reduction with hydride reagents.
questions.explanation_trick: Carbonyl carbon = electrophilic (positive) → attacked by nucleophiles → nucleophilic ADDITION (not substitution, since there's a double bond to add across, not a leaving group to substitute).

explanation_options.a: Electrophilic addition applies to electron-rich systems (like alkenes) being attacked by electrophiles — the opposite polarity situation from carbonyl reactivity.
explanation_options.b: Electrophilic substitution is characteristic of aromatic rings (like benzene), not carbonyl compounds.
explanation_options.c: Free radical substitution is characteristic of alkanes reacting with halogens under UV light, unrelated to carbonyl chemistry.
explanation_options.d: Correct — nucleophilic addition is the characteristic mechanism for carbonyl compounds.

questions.question_text: Which of the following compounds is solid at room temperature?
questions.explanation_short: Phenol (melting point ~41°C) is a solid at typical room temperature, unlike the other listed liquid compounds.
questions.explanation_long: Ethanol, methanol, and butane are all liquids (or gases, for butane) at typical room temperature (around 20-25°C), while phenol has a melting point of about 40-41°C, making it borderline but generally classified/observed as a solid (or low-melting waxy solid) under standard room conditions, especially in cooler settings.
questions.explanation_trick: Phenol's unusually high melting point (compared to similarly-sized alcohols) is due to strong hydrogen bonding between its molecules — a distinguishing physical property worth remembering.

explanation_options.a: Ethanol is a liquid at room temperature (boiling point ~78°C, melting point well below room temperature).
explanation_options.b: Butane is a gas at room temperature (boiling point around -1°C).
explanation_options.c: Methanol is a liquid at room temperature (boiling point ~65°C).
explanation_options.d: Correct — phenol, with its higher melting point (~41°C), is a solid at typical room temperature.

questions.question_text: Halogens are being used as fire extinguishers, mild antiseptics, CFCs and many other organic chemicals. Which of the following halogens is used to kill bacteria in drinking water
questions.explanation_short: Chlorine is the halogen most commonly used to disinfect (kill bacteria in) drinking water.
questions.explanation_long: Chlorine is widely used in water treatment facilities to kill bacteria and other pathogens in drinking water, due to its effectiveness as an oxidizing disinfectant and relatively low cost — one of the most common and well-known applications of any halogen in daily life.
questions.explanation_trick: Chlorine's water-disinfection role is a widely recognized, frequently tested application — its distinctive 'pool smell' is actually a familiar real-world cue for this exact use.

explanation_options.a: Bromine is used in some specialized water treatment (e.g., hot tubs/spas) but chlorine is the standard for general drinking water disinfection.
explanation_options.b: Fluorine is far too reactive and dangerous to use directly for water disinfection (fluoride ion, a different species, is instead added for dental health, not disinfection).
explanation_options.c: Correct — chlorine is the standard disinfectant for drinking water.
explanation_options.d: Iodine is used in some emergency/portable water purification methods but isn't the standard for municipal drinking water treatment.

questions.question_text: Which of the following acts as an electrophile in the electrophilic substitution of benzene with bromine?
questions.explanation_short: The electrophile attacking benzene in bromination is Br+, generated by FeBr3 polarizing the Br-Br bond.
questions.explanation_long: FeBr3 (a Lewis acid catalyst) coordinates with one bromine atom of Br2, polarizing and weakening the Br-Br bond, effectively generating a Br+ electrophile (along with a FeBr4- counter-ion) that then attacks benzene's electron-rich π system in the electrophilic aromatic substitution mechanism.
questions.explanation_trick: In any halogenation of benzene, the Lewis acid catalyst (like FeBr3 or AlCl3) helps generate a positively charged halogen electrophile (X+) — the catalyst itself is never the electrophile, just the electrophile-generating helper.

explanation_options.a: Correct — Br+ is the electrophile generated with FeBr3's help.
explanation_options.b: 'FeCl4+' isn't a real/relevant species in a bromine/FeBr3 reaction (mismatched halogens, and an implausible charge/formula).
explanation_options.c: Fe+2 isn't the species generated or the active electrophile in this reaction.
explanation_options.d: Fe+3, while part of FeBr3's Lewis acid character, isn't the species that directly attacks benzene — that's specifically the Br+ generated with its help.

aliases: Which of the following acts as an electrophile in the electrophilic substitution of benzene with bromine?
Br+

questions.question_text: According to Lowry-Bronsted Acid & Base Concept, H₂O is
questions.explanation_short: Without a specified reaction partner, water's Bronsted-Lowry classification is amphoteric — it can act as either acid or base.
questions.explanation_long: Water can donate a proton (acting as an acid, e.g., with ammonia) or accept a proton (acting as a base, e.g., with HCl), depending on what it reacts with. The general term for this dual capability is amphoteric (or amphiprotic).
questions.explanation_trick: Water is the textbook example of an amphoteric/amphiprotic substance in Bronsted-Lowry theory.

explanation_options.a: This captures only water's proton-donor (acid) role, missing its equally valid base behavior.
explanation_options.b: This captures only water's proton-acceptor (base) role, missing its acid behavior.
explanation_options.c: Correct — amphoteric acknowledges water's dual acid/base capability.
explanation_options.d: Water is not classified as a salt under the Bronsted-Lowry framework.

aliases: According to Lowry-Bronsted Acid & Base Concept, H2O is
An Acid

questions.question_text: Which one of the following compounds is known as tertiary alcohol?
questions.explanation_short: 2-methyl-2-propanol (tert-butanol) is the tertiary alcohol among the options.
questions.explanation_long: A tertiary alcohol has its -OH group attached to a carbon bonded to three other carbon groups. 2-methyl-2-propanol, (CH3)3C-OH, fits this exactly. 1-Propanol has its OH on a carbon bonded to only one other carbon, making it primary.
questions.explanation_trick: Count the carbon groups attached to the OH-bearing carbon: one = primary, two = secondary, three = tertiary.

explanation_options.a: 1-propanol's OH-bearing carbon is attached to only one other carbon, making it primary.
explanation_options.b: Correct — 2-methyl-2-propanol's OH-bearing carbon is attached to three methyl groups, making it tertiary.
explanation_options.c: 2-methyl-1-propanol has its OH on a carbon attached to only one other carbon, making it primary.
explanation_options.d: 2-Propanol's OH-bearing carbon is attached to two other carbons, making it secondary.

questions.question_text: Which of the following molecules has the largest number of shared pairs of electrons?
questions.explanation_short: Counting all shared (bonding) electron pairs across the whole molecule, C2H4 has the most (6 total).
questions.explanation_long: C2H4 has one C=C double bond (2 pairs) plus four C-H single bonds (4 pairs) = 6 total shared pairs. N2 has one triple bond = 3 shared pairs. CO2 has two double bonds = 4 shared pairs. NH3 has three single bonds = 3 shared pairs. By total molecular count, C2H4 has the most.
questions.explanation_trick: When comparing 'number of shared pairs' across a molecule, count ALL bonding pairs in the whole structure, not just the bond order of a single bond.

explanation_options.a: Correct — C2H4 has the most total shared pairs (6) when counting every bond in the molecule.
explanation_options.b: N2's triple bond concentrates 3 pairs in one bond, but the molecule's total (3) is less than C2H4's total (6).
explanation_options.c: CO2 has 4 total shared pairs across its two double bonds — fewer than C2H4's 6.
explanation_options.d: NH3 has only 3 total shared pairs across its three single bonds.

aliases: Which of the following molecules has the largest number of shared pairs of electrons?
C2H4

questions.question_text: Nitrogen is present in air as a major constituent. It is an inactive gas in comparison with oxygen, which is the next major constituent of air. The nonreactive nature of nitrogen is due to the reason;
questions.option_a: there is one lone pair of electrons on each nitrogen atom in its molecule.
questions.option_b: there is a triple covalent bond in the nitrogen molecule which is very strong and the molecule is non polar.
questions.option_c: nitrogen has three unpaired electrons in its 2p orbital which is a comparatively stable electronic configuration.
questions.option_d: there is a triple covalent bond in the nitrogen molecule which is very strong and the molecule is polar.
questions.explanation_short: Nitrogen's inertness comes from its very strong, non-polar N≡N triple bond.
questions.explanation_long: The N≡N triple bond is unusually strong, requiring a large amount of energy to break, explaining nitrogen's general unreactivity. As a homonuclear diatomic molecule (two identical atoms), N2 is also always completely non-polar by symmetry.
questions.explanation_trick: Any diatomic molecule made of two identical atoms (N2, O2, H2, Cl2) is always non-polar by symmetry, no matter the bond type.

explanation_options.a: The key factor here is the strong triple bond, not a lone-pair-based explanation.
explanation_options.b: Correct — the strong triple bond explains inertness, and N2 is non-polar since it's a homonuclear diatomic molecule.
explanation_options.c: While nitrogen's electron configuration is stable, this doesn't identify the strong triple bond as the key structural reason.
explanation_options.d: N2, being homonuclear diatomic, is always non-polar by symmetry — not polar.

questions.question_text: The dilute solution of ------------- is called vinegar
questions.explanation_short: Dilute acetic acid solution is what's commonly known as vinegar.
questions.explanation_long: Vinegar is a dilute aqueous solution of acetic acid (typically around 4-8% concentration), used widely as a food preservative and condiment.
questions.explanation_trick: Acetic acid = vinegar's active ingredient — a simple, direct vocabulary fact worth memorizing.

explanation_options.a: Formic acid is found in ant/insect stings, not vinegar.
explanation_options.b: Oxalic acid is found in certain plants (like rhubarb), not vinegar.
explanation_options.c: Benzoic acid is used as a food preservative in a different form, not as vinegar's active component.
explanation_options.d: Correct — dilute acetic acid is vinegar.

questions.question_text: Percentage of nitrogen by volume in air is
questions.explanation_short: Nitrogen makes up approximately 78% of air by volume.
questions.explanation_long: Dry air's composition by volume is approximately 78% nitrogen (N2), 21% oxygen (O2), and about 1% other gases (argon, CO2, etc.) — nitrogen is by far the most abundant component.
questions.explanation_trick: 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen — these two figures together account for about 99% of air's composition and are worth memorizing as a pair.

explanation_options.a: Correct — nitrogen makes up about 78% of air by volume.
explanation_options.b: 50% substantially understates nitrogen's actual dominant proportion in air.
explanation_options.c: 20% is closer to oxygen's actual proportion (21%), not nitrogen's.
explanation_options.d: 98% substantially overstates nitrogen's actual proportion.

questions.question_text: Bromination of alkene, H₂C=CH₂ + Br₂ → H-C(Br)H-C(Br)H₂, is shown in the following reaction. This reaction is used for
questions.option_c: Identification of Primary and secondary alcohols
questions.explanation_short: The addition of bromine across a double bond (decolorizing bromine water/solution) is used as a chemical test to detect the presence of a double bond.
questions.explanation_long: Alkenes react readily with bromine via addition across their C=C double bond (electrophilic addition), causing the characteristic orange-brown color of bromine to fade/decolorize. This reaction is a standard qualitative test for detecting unsaturation (a C=C double bond) in an organic compound — saturated compounds (like alkanes) don't react this way.
questions.explanation_trick: The 'bromine water/solution decolorization test' is the standard, widely-used qualitative test for detecting C=C double bonds (unsaturation) in organic chemistry.

explanation_options.a: Ketones aren't detected by bromine addition in this way (that would be an oxidation/condensation type test, like 2,4-DNPH).
explanation_options.b: Correct — bromine addition/decolorization detects the presence of a double bond.
explanation_options.c: Distinguishing primary and secondary alcohols uses different tests (like Lucas' reagent), not bromine addition.
explanation_options.d: Aldehydes are detected by different tests (like Tollen's or Fehling's), not bromine addition across a double bond.

aliases: Bromination of alkene, H2C=CH2 + Br2 → H-C(Br)H-C(Br)H2, is shown in the following reaction. This reaction is used for
Detection of ketones

questions.question_text: What is the order of increasing reactivity of alkyl halides?
questions.explanation_short: Reactivity of alkyl halides in nucleophilic substitution increases as fluoroalkane < chloroalkane < bromoalkane < iodoalkane.
questions.explanation_long: C-X bond strength decreases going down the halogen group (C-F strongest, C-I weakest), and weaker bonds break more easily, making the alkyl halide more reactive. So reactivity increases: fluoroalkane (least reactive) < chloroalkane < bromoalkane < iodoalkane (most reactive).
questions.explanation_trick: Weaker C-X bond = easier to break = more reactive; bond strength decreases down the halogen group (F strongest, I weakest).

explanation_options.a: Correct — this is the increasing-reactivity order (F<Cl<Br<I), matching decreasing bond strength.
explanation_options.b: This describes a different (non-matching) ordering, not the correct increasing-reactivity sequence.
explanation_options.c: This describes a decreasing order, the mirror image of what's being asked for.
explanation_options.d: This describes the decreasing reactivity order (F>Cl>Br>I), the reverse of what's requested.

questions.question_text: Which of the following would react with ozone in the atmosphere?
questions.explanation_short: Chlorine radicals (Cl•), released when UV light breaks down CFCs, attack ozone in the stratosphere: Cl• + O₃ → ClO• + O₂.
questions.explanation_long: CFCs are stable in the lower atmosphere but are split by UV light in the stratosphere, releasing Cl• radicals. Each Cl• reacts with ozone to give ClO• and O₂; ClO• then reacts with atomic oxygen to regenerate Cl•, so one chlorine atom can destroy thousands of ozone molecules. This catalytic chain is the ozone depletion the question refers to.
questions.explanation_trick: Ozone hole = CFCs → Cl• radicals.

explanation_options.a: Fluorine from CFCs is locked up as stable HF and does not destroy ozone significantly.
explanation_options.b: O₂ is a product of ozone breakdown, not a species that attacks it.
explanation_options.c: O• does combine with ozone in the natural ozone–oxygen cycle, but the atmospheric ozone attack taught here is by Cl• from CFCs.
explanation_options.d: Correct — Cl• radicals from CFCs react with ozone and destroy it catalytically.

questions.question_text: A 5 watt LED bulb converts 80% of the power into light photons of wavelength 660 nm. What is the number of photons emitted from the bulb in one second.
questions.explanation_short: Energy per photon E=hc/λ ≈ 3.01×10⁻¹⁹ J; with 4W of light power (80% of 5W), photons/sec = 4/3.01×10⁻¹⁹ ≈ 1.3×10¹⁹.
questions.explanation_long: Light power = 80% of 5W = 4W. Energy of one 660nm photon: E=hc/λ = (6.6×10⁻³⁴×3×10⁸)/(660×10⁻⁹) ≈ 3.0×10⁻¹⁹ J. Number of photons emitted per second = light power/energy per photon = 4/3.0×10⁻¹⁹ ≈ 1.3×10¹⁹.
questions.explanation_trick: Only the fraction of power actually converted to light (80% here) counts toward photon emission — don't use the full 5W.

explanation_options.a: Wildly too large — inconsistent with dividing 4W by a photon energy on the order of 10⁻¹⁹ J.
explanation_options.b: Off by roughly three orders of magnitude, likely from a unit/exponent slip.
explanation_options.c: Far too small to represent a photon count for a macroscopic light source.
explanation_options.d: Correct — ≈1.3×10¹⁹ photons/second.

aliases: A 5 watt LED bulb converts 80% of the power into light photons of wavelength 660 nm. What is the number of photons emitted from the bulb in one second.

questions.question_text: If Cv = 5/2 R, Cp will be
questions.explanation_short: Cp = Cv + R = 5/2R + R = 7/2R.
questions.explanation_long: For an ideal gas, Mayer's relation gives Cp = Cv + R. With Cv = 5/2 R (characteristic of a diatomic gas), Cp = 5/2R + R = 7/2R.
questions.explanation_trick: Mayer's relation (Cp − Cv = R) is a direct, universal formula for ideal gases — no need to know the gas type beyond the given Cv.

explanation_options.a: Far too small and doesn't follow from adding R to 5/2R.
explanation_options.b: Doesn't correspond to Cv+R with the given Cv.
explanation_options.c: This is just Cv itself, without adding R.
explanation_options.d: Correct — 5/2R + R = 7/2R.

questions.question_text: The rate at which work is being done is called
questions.explanation_short: Power is defined as the rate at which work is done.
questions.explanation_long: By definition, power = work done / time taken, i.e., the rate of doing work. Force is what causes work to be done (work = force × displacement), but force itself isn't a 'rate' quantity.
questions.explanation_trick: Power's very definition IS 'rate of work done' (units: joules/second = watts) — one of the most basic definitions in mechanics.

explanation_options.a: Correct — power is the rate of doing work.
explanation_options.b: Energy is the general capacity to do work, not specifically a rate quantity.
explanation_options.c: Density (mass/volume) is unrelated to the rate of doing work.
explanation_options.d: Force causes work to be done but isn't itself a rate quantity.

questions.question_text: An input voltage Vin of 0.50 V is applied to an op-amp connected as shown in the diagram (non-inverting amplifier: 10 kΩ feedback resistor, 2.5 kΩ resistor from the inverting input to 0 V, supply ±6.0 V). What is the output voltage Vout?
questions.explanation_short: Non-inverting gain = 1 + Rf/R = 1 + 10/2.5 = 5, so Vout = 5 × 0.50 V = 2.5 V.
questions.explanation_long: Vin goes to the non-inverting (+) input. The 10 kΩ resistor feeds the output back to the inverting (−) input, and the 2.5 kΩ resistor connects that input to 0 V. For a non-inverting amplifier the gain is 1 + Rf/R₁ = 1 + 10 kΩ/2.5 kΩ = 5. So Vout = 5 × 0.50 V = 2.5 V, which is inside the ±6.0 V supply, so the op-amp does not saturate.
questions.explanation_trick: Input on + → gain 1 + Rf/R (no minus sign). Input on − → gain −Rf/R.

explanation_options.a: 8.0 V is above the +6.0 V supply, so the output could never reach it.
explanation_options.b: 1.2 V would need a gain of about 2.4, which these resistors do not give.
explanation_options.c: Correct — gain 1 + 10/2.5 = 5, and 5 × 0.50 V = 2.5 V.
explanation_options.d: 4.9 V would need a gain of about 9.8, as if the resistors were 22.5 kΩ and 2.5 kΩ.

aliases: An input voltage Vin of 0.50 V is applied to an op-amp connected as shown in the diagram. What is the output voltage Vout?

questions.question_text: A signal of -80 mV is applied to the inverting terminal of the amplifier while the non-inverting terminal is grounded. The gain of the amplifier is 25, using Rin (R₁) equal to 3Ω and Rf (R₂) equal to 75Ω. What would be the value of the output signal?
questions.explanation_short: Inverting amplifier: Vout = −Gain × Vin = −25 × (−80mV) = +2000mV = 2V.
questions.explanation_long: For an inverting amplifier, Vout = −(Rf/Rin) × Vin. Given a gain magnitude of 25 (=Rf/Rin=75/3) and Vin=−80mV applied to the inverting input: Vout = −25 × (−0.080V) = +2.0V.
questions.explanation_trick: An inverting amplifier flips the sign — a negative input combined with the inverting configuration produces a positive output (two negatives from the input sign and the amplifier's inversion combine to a positive result).

explanation_options.a: Ignores the gain entirely, treating the input as if barely amplified.
explanation_options.b: Wrong sign — this would result from forgetting the inverting amplifier flips the input's sign.
explanation_options.d: Overshoots the correct magnitude, inconsistent with Gain×Vin=25×0.08=2V exactly.

aliases: A signal of -80 mV is applied to the inverting terminal of the amplifier while the non-inverting terminal is grounded. The gain of the amplifier is 25, using Rin (R1) equal to 3Ω and Rf (R2) equal to 75Ω. What would be the value of the output signal?
200 mV

questions.question_text: When the frequency of the applied force becomes equal to one of the natural frequencies of a body then the body oscillates with maximum displacement. This phenomenon is called
questions.explanation_short: When an applied force's frequency matches a body's natural frequency, causing maximum-amplitude oscillation, this is resonance.
questions.explanation_long: Resonance occurs when the frequency of a periodically applied force matches one of a system's natural (intrinsic) oscillation frequencies, causing energy to build up efficiently in the system and resulting in oscillations of maximum amplitude/displacement.
questions.explanation_trick: Resonance is specifically about frequency-matching driving maximum amplitude — a foundational concept behind phenomena like shattering glass with sound or bridges failing under wind-induced vibration.

explanation_options.a: 'Heating' isn't a standard term for this frequency-matching phenomenon.
explanation_options.b: Correct — resonance describes maximum-amplitude oscillation from frequency matching.
explanation_options.c: Reverberation refers to the persistence of sound reflections in an enclosed space, unrelated to frequency-matching oscillation.
explanation_options.d: Damping describes the gradual loss of oscillation amplitude over time, the opposite effect from resonance's amplification.

questions.question_text: Force is a derived quantity; its derived unit can be expressed in terms of the base units as,
questions.explanation_short: Force = mass × acceleration, giving base units of kg·m·s⁻².
questions.explanation_long: From Newton's second law, F=ma. Mass has units of kg, and acceleration has units of m/s² (m·s⁻²). Multiplying: kg·m·s⁻² — this combination is given the special name 'newton' (N).
questions.explanation_trick: Deriving a quantity's base units from its defining formula (like F=ma) is a reliable, quick way to answer 'derived unit' questions without memorizing units directly.

explanation_options.a: Correct — kg·m·s⁻² is the base-unit expression of the newton.
explanation_options.b: Uses cm instead of the SI base unit m, an inconsistent unit mix.
explanation_options.c: Incorrect exponents on both m and s — doesn't match F=ma's actual unit combination.
explanation_options.d: Uses a positive exponent on s (s² instead of s⁻²), the opposite of the correct acceleration unit.

aliases: Force is a derived quantity; its derived unit can be expressed in terms of the base units as,
kg m s^-2

questions.question_text: e/m of an electron is given by the relationship,
questions.explanation_short: From the Thomson e/m experiment: kinetic energy qV = ½mv², and circular motion qvB=mv²/r combine to give e/m = 2V/(B²r²).
questions.explanation_long: In Thomson's method for measuring e/m: an electron accelerated through potential V gains kinetic energy eV = ½mv², giving v² = 2eV/m. Separately, in a magnetic field, the electron moves in a circle of radius r where the magnetic force provides centripetal force: evB = mv²/r, giving v = eBr/m. Combining these two expressions for v² (squaring the second and substituting) yields e/m = 2V/(B²r²).
questions.explanation_trick: This combined-experiment formula (e/m = 2V/B²r²) is a classic result worth memorizing directly, since deriving it from scratch each time is time-consuming under exam conditions.

explanation_options.a: Correct — matches the standard Thomson e/m formula.
explanation_options.b: This form doesn't correctly combine the two physical relationships (energy and circular motion) used to derive e/m.
explanation_options.c: This form omits the required squaring and factor of 2 from the correct derivation.
explanation_options.d: This form doesn't match the correct combination of the energy and magnetic-force equations.

aliases: e/m of an electron is given by the relationship,

questions.question_text: Lenz's law in electromagnetic induction is the direct consequence of the principle of conservation of
questions.explanation_short: Lenz's law (induced current opposes the change causing it) is a direct consequence of energy conservation.
questions.explanation_long: Lenz's law states that an induced EMF/current always opposes the change in magnetic flux that created it. This is required by energy conservation — if the induced current instead reinforced the change, it would create a runaway feedback loop generating energy from nothing, violating the conservation of energy.
questions.explanation_trick: Lenz's law is often summarized as 'nature opposes change' — and this opposition is precisely what prevents electromagnetic induction from being a free energy source, tying it directly to energy conservation.

explanation_options.a: Correct — Lenz's law follows from conservation of energy.
explanation_options.b: Conservation of charge is a separate principle (relevant to circuit current continuity, like Kirchhoff's current law), not what Lenz's law embodies.
explanation_options.c: Conservation of momentum is unrelated to the electromagnetic opposition described by Lenz's law.
explanation_options.d: Conservation of mass is unrelated to Lenz's law.

questions.question_text: Which material will follow the below stress-strain curve?
questions.explanation_short: Glass, being a brittle material, shows a stress-strain curve that rises steeply and linearly before fracturing suddenly, without significant plastic deformation.
questions.explanation_long: Brittle materials like glass deform elastically (following a straight-line stress-strain relationship) up until they suddenly fracture, with little to no plastic (permanent) deformation beforehand. This contrasts with ductile metals like copper and iron, which show a clear yield point followed by a substantial plastic deformation region before eventual failure, and with soft metals like lead, which show significant deformation at relatively low stress.
questions.explanation_trick: Brittle materials (glass, ceramics) show 'straight line then sudden break'; ductile materials (most metals) show 'straight line, then bends/yields, then stretches before breaking' — matching curve shape to material type is the key skill.

explanation_options.a: Copper is a ductile metal, showing a yield point and plastic deformation region, unlike the brittle fracture pattern of glass.
explanation_options.b: Iron is also a ductile metal with a similar yield-and-deform pattern, not matching glass's brittle behavior.
explanation_options.c: Lead is notably soft and deforms significantly at low stress, quite different from glass's stiff, brittle fracture pattern.
explanation_options.d: Correct — glass's brittle stress-strain curve (steep, linear, then sudden fracture) is distinctive among these options.

questions.question_text: A wheel starts rotating from rest with angular acceleration of 2 rad s⁻² till its angular speed becomes 6 rad/s. The angular displacement of the wheel will be equal to
questions.explanation_short: Using ω²=ω₀²+2αθ with ω₀=0, ω=6, α=2: θ = ω²/(2α) = 36/4 = 9 rad.
questions.explanation_long: Starting from rest (ω₀=0) with angular acceleration α=2 rad/s², reaching ω=6 rad/s: using ω²=ω₀²+2αθ, 36 = 0 + 2(2)θ, so θ = 36/4 = 9 rad.
questions.explanation_trick: This is the angular-motion analog of v²=u²+2as — the same equation structure applies directly, just with angular quantities substituted in.

explanation_options.a: Would result from a miscalculation dividing by the wrong factor.
explanation_options.b: Correct — 36/4 = 9 rad.
explanation_options.c: Overshoots — inconsistent with dividing 36 by 4.
explanation_options.d: Doesn't match the direct calculation from the given values.

4 rad

questions.explanation_short: Coulomb's constant k = 9×10⁹ N·m²/C² in free space (vacuum/air).
questions.explanation_long: The Coulomb's law constant k (equal to 1/(4πε₀)) has the well-known value of approximately 9×10⁹ N·m²/C² in a vacuum or air, one of the most frequently used constants in electrostatics.
questions.explanation_trick: 9×10⁹ is one of the most commonly memorized physics constants — instantly recognizable in Coulomb's law problems.

explanation_options.a: Incorrect order of magnitude for k.
explanation_options.b: Also an incorrect value for k.

questions.question_text: Simple Harmonic Motion of a body is described by which statement(s) mentioned below: K: K.E is maximum when displacement x=0. L: P.E is maximum when x=0. M: P.E is maximum when x=±x0
questions.explanation_short: In SHM, kinetic energy is maximum at x=0 and potential energy is maximum at x=±x0 — statements K and M.
questions.explanation_long: KE = ½mv² is maximum at x=0 (where speed is greatest) and zero at x=±x0. PE = ½kx² is the opposite: zero at x=0 and maximum at x=±x0. So K ('KE max at x=0') and M ('PE max at x=±x0') are both true; L ('PE max at x=0') is false, since PE is actually at its minimum there.
questions.explanation_trick: PE and KE in SHM are exact opposites: KE peaks where PE is zero (mean position) and vice versa (extremes).

explanation_options.a: Includes the false statement L — PE is NOT maximum at x=0, it's at its minimum there.
explanation_options.b: Correct — K and M are both true statements.
explanation_options.c: Includes the false statement L alongside the two true statements.
explanation_options.d: Includes the false statement L, which incorrectly claims PE is maximum at x=0.

questions.question_text: Which of the following gives the relationship between linear velocity and angular velocity?
questions.explanation_short: Linear velocity relates to angular velocity via v = rω, where r is the radius of the circular path.
questions.explanation_long: For an object moving in a circle of radius r with angular velocity ω, its linear (tangential) speed is v = rω. This is a direct, fundamental relationship in rotational motion.
questions.explanation_trick: v=rω is one of the most foundational rotational-motion formulas — recognize it immediately whenever linear and angular velocity need to be related.

explanation_options.a: Correct — v = rω.
explanation_options.b: Uses angular displacement (θ) instead of angular velocity (ω) — dimensionally inconsistent for a velocity relationship.
explanation_options.c: Uses arc length (s) multiplied by angular velocity, which doesn't yield a correct velocity relationship dimensionally.
explanation_options.d: Uses arc length multiplied by angular displacement, an invalid combination for velocity.

questions.question_text: A torch is rated 2.2 V, 0.25 A. Calculate the charge passing through the bulb in one second and energy transferred by the passage of each coulomb of charge.
questions.explanation_short: Charge Q=It=0.25A×1s=0.25C; energy per coulomb equals the voltage itself, 2.2V→2.2J per coulomb.
questions.explanation_long: Charge passing in one second: Q=It=0.25×1=0.25C. Energy transferred per unit charge is, by definition, the potential difference (voltage): since V=Energy/Charge, Energy per coulomb = V = 2.2 J (per coulomb of charge, i.e., 2.2 joules for every coulomb that passes).
questions.explanation_trick: Voltage IS energy-per-charge by definition (V=W/Q) — so 'energy transferred per coulomb' is simply numerically equal to the voltage value itself, no extra calculation needed.

explanation_options.a: Overstates the charge (should be 0.25C, from I×t=0.25×1) and doesn't match the voltage-based energy calculation either.
explanation_options.b: Correct — 0.25C charge, and 2.2J energy per coulomb (numerically equal to the voltage).
explanation_options.c: Correctly gives the charge but mislabels the second value with volts instead of joules as the energy unit.
explanation_options.d: Correctly gives the charge but uses an incorrect (halved) energy value instead of the voltage itself.

questions.question_text: Energy consumed by a 60 watt bulb in 2 minutes is equal to
questions.explanation_short: Energy = Power × time = 60W × 120s = 7200 J = 7.2 kJ.
questions.explanation_long: Energy consumed = power × time. Converting 2 minutes to seconds: 2×60=120s. Energy = 60W × 120s = 7200 J = 7.2 kJ.
questions.explanation_trick: Always convert time to seconds (SI units) before multiplying by power in watts to get energy in joules.

explanation_options.b: Would result from using only 12 seconds instead of 120 seconds.
explanation_options.c: Far too small — doesn't correspond to the given power and time.
explanation_options.d: Off by a factor of 10 from the correct value, likely a decimal-place error.

questions.question_text: If one mole of an ideal gas is heated at constant pressure, then the first law of thermodynamics can be written as:
questions.explanation_short: At constant pressure for 1 mole of ideal gas, the first law gives Cp ΔT = Cv ΔT + PΔV.
questions.explanation_long: For 1 mole of gas heated at constant pressure: Q = ΔU + W, where Q = CpΔT (heat added at constant pressure), ΔU = CvΔT, and W = PΔV (work done by the expanding gas). This gives CpΔT = CvΔT + PΔV.
questions.explanation_trick: Heat added (Cp-based) = internal energy change (Cv-based) + work done (PΔV) — the standard first-law breakdown for constant-pressure heating.

explanation_options.a: Correct — CpΔT = CvΔT + PΔV is the standard relationship.
explanation_options.b: This incorrectly swaps Cp and Cv's roles — heat added should be Cp-based (constant pressure), not Cv-based.
explanation_options.c: This rearranges the delta symbol placement in a nonstandard way relative to the correct form.
explanation_options.d: This also uses a nonstandard delta placement, differing from the standard equation structure.

questions.question_text: The de Broglie wavelength of an electron travelling with a speed of 1.0 × 10⁷ m/s is equal to, (h=6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ Js and me=9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg)
questions.explanation_short: de Broglie wavelength λ=h/(mv) = 6.6×10⁻³⁴/(9.1×10⁻³¹×1×10⁷) ≈ 7.3×10⁻¹¹ m.
questions.explanation_long: The de Broglie wavelength formula is λ=h/(mv). Substituting h=6.6×10⁻³⁴ Js, m=9.1×10⁻³¹ kg, v=1.0×10⁷ m/s: λ = 6.6×10⁻³⁴/(9.1×10⁻³¹×1×10⁷) = 6.6×10⁻³⁴/9.1×10⁻²⁴ ≈ 7.25×10⁻¹¹ m.
questions.explanation_trick: Careful exponent arithmetic: −34 − (−24) = −10, close to the −11 in the answer after accounting for the leading digit ratio (6.6/9.1≈0.725, shifting the exponent down by one).

explanation_options.a: Wrong sign of exponent, implying an enormous (not tiny) wavelength.
explanation_options.b: Also has an incorrect exponent sign/magnitude.
explanation_options.c: Correct — ≈7.3×10⁻¹¹ m.
explanation_options.d: Off by two orders of magnitude from the correct value.

questions.question_text: Find the mean translational kinetic energy of ideal hydrogen gas at 17°C.
questions.explanation_short: Mean translational KE = (3/2)kT = 1.5 × 1.38×10⁻²³ × 290K ≈ 6.0×10⁻²¹ J.
questions.explanation_long: The mean translational kinetic energy per gas molecule is given by (3/2)kT, where k is Boltzmann's constant and T is absolute temperature. Converting 17°C to Kelvin: T=17+273=290K. KE = 1.5 × 1.38×10⁻²³ × 290 ≈ 6.0×10⁻²¹ J.
questions.explanation_trick: Always convert Celsius to Kelvin before using it in (3/2)kT — using 17 directly instead of 290 is a common error.

explanation_options.a: Close to but not exactly matching the calculation using T=290K precisely.
explanation_options.b: Undershoots the correct value.
explanation_options.c: Wrong exponent — far too large by nine orders of magnitude.
explanation_options.d: Correct — ≈6×10⁻²¹ J.

aliases: Find the mean translational kinetic energy of ideal hydrogen gas at 17°C.

questions.question_text: Calculate the activity (decaying atoms per unit time) of radioactive strontium-90 having 6.7 × 10²¹ atoms at t=0. Decay constant of strontium-90 is 8.3 × 10⁻¹⁰ s⁻¹.
questions.explanation_short: Activity A = λN = 8.3×10⁻¹⁰ × 6.7×10²¹ ≈ 5.6×10¹² Bq.
questions.explanation_long: Radioactive activity is given by A = λN, where λ is the decay constant and N is the number of atoms present. A = 8.3×10⁻¹⁰ × 6.7×10²¹ = 5.56×10¹² decays per second (becquerels).
questions.explanation_trick: Multiplying decay constant (per second) by atom count directly gives activity in becquerels (decays/second) — a one-step calculation, no extra unit conversion needed here.

explanation_options.a: Off by roughly two orders of magnitude from the correct calculation.
explanation_options.b: Off by one order of magnitude, and mislabeled with an inconsistent unit (s⁻¹ instead of Bq, though numerically these are equivalent for activity).

questions.question_text: If the time period of the oscillation is 20 micro-sec, then what will be the frequency of that oscillating body?
questions.explanation_short: Frequency = 1/period = 1/(20×10⁻⁶ s) = 50,000 Hz.
questions.explanation_long: Frequency and period are reciprocals: f=1/T. With T=20 microseconds = 20×10⁻⁶ s: f = 1/(20×10⁻⁶) = 50,000 Hz.
questions.explanation_trick: Convert microseconds to seconds (×10⁻⁶) before taking the reciprocal — a very small period naturally corresponds to a very large frequency.

explanation_options.a: Off by a factor of 10 from the correct value.

explanation_options.d: Off by a factor of 50 from the correct value.

questions.question_text: In photo-emission from a metal, if light of wavelength λ is replaced by light of wavelength λ/4, the maximum kinetic energy of the photo-electrons
questions.option_a: decreases by an amount equal to half of an incident photon of wavelength λ
questions.option_b: increases by an amount equal to four times the energy of an incident photon of wavelength λ
questions.option_c: increases by an amount equal to the work function of the metal
questions.option_d: decreases by an amount equal to the energy of an incident photon of wavelength λ
questions.explanation_short: Reducing wavelength to λ/4 quadruples the photon energy, so the maximum photoelectron KE increases.
questions.explanation_long: Photoelectric max KE: KE = hc/λ − φ. Replacing λ with λ/4 gives KE' = 4(hc/λ) − φ, an increase since a shorter wavelength means a higher-energy, higher-frequency photon.
questions.explanation_trick: Shorter wavelength always means higher photon energy (E=hc/λ) — so max photoelectron KE can only increase, never decrease, when wavelength is reduced.

explanation_options.a: A decrease is the wrong direction — shorter wavelength means higher photon energy, so KE should increase.
explanation_options.b: Correct — the maximum KE increases, since the photon energy has quadrupled.
explanation_options.c: The size of the KE change is tied to the change in photon energy, not the work function specifically.
explanation_options.d: This also describes a decrease, the wrong direction.

decreases by an amount equal to half of an incident photon of wavelength lambda

questions.question_text: A cyclist is traveling at 15 ms⁻¹. She applies brakes so that she doesn't collide with the wall in front of her at a distance of 18m. Calculate the magnitude of deceleration.
questions.explanation_short: Using v²=v₀²−2as with v=0: a = v₀²/(2s) = 225/36 ≈ 6.3 m/s².
questions.explanation_long: The cyclist decelerates from 15 m/s to a stop over 18m. Using v²=v₀²−2as with final v=0: a = v₀²/(2s) = 15²/(2×18) = 225/36 ≈ 6.25 m/s² ≈ 6.3 m/s².
questions.explanation_trick: Setting final velocity to zero simplifies v²=v₀²−2as directly to a=v₀²/(2s) — no need for the full quadratic form.

explanation_options.a: Correct — ≈6.3 m/s².
explanation_options.b: Close but not matching the precise calculation.
explanation_options.c: Roughly double the correct value, likely from omitting the factor of 2 in the denominator.
explanation_options.d: Also overshoots the correct deceleration value.

questions.question_text: In a practical transformer, mutual induction between primary and secondary coils takes place. In such a transformer, what can be deduced about the power
questions.explanation_short: Real transformers have some energy losses (resistance, hysteresis, eddy currents), so output power is always slightly less than input power.
questions.explanation_long: An ideal transformer would have power output exactly equal to power input, but practical (real) transformers experience energy losses due to winding resistance (I²R losses), hysteresis in the core, and eddy currents. These losses mean the output power delivered to the load is always somewhat less than the input power supplied.
questions.explanation_trick: 'Practical/real' is the key word signaling that losses must be accounted for — an 'ideal' transformer question would instead expect equal power in and out.

explanation_options.a: This describes an ideal, loss-free transformer, not a practical one with real-world losses.
explanation_options.b: Output power exceeding input power would violate energy conservation — never physically possible.
explanation_options.c: This includes the impossible 'greater than' case alongside equality, neither of which fits a real transformer with losses.
explanation_options.d: Correct — real transformers always have power output less than power input due to losses.

questions.question_text: If the slope of the velocity-time graph is not constant at different points, then the body is moving with
questions.explanation_short: A velocity-time graph with a slope that isn't constant (here, increasing) indicates increasing acceleration.
questions.explanation_long: The slope of a v-t graph represents acceleration. If the slope increases over time, the body's acceleration itself is increasing — the graph curves more steeply as time progresses.
questions.explanation_trick: A straight sloped line means uniform (constant) acceleration; a curve with an increasing slope means increasing acceleration.

explanation_options.a: Uniform velocity would produce a perfectly flat, constant-slope (zero) graph, not a changing one.
explanation_options.b: Correct — an increasing slope on a v-t graph means the acceleration itself is increasing.
explanation_options.c: 'Average acceleration' is a computed summary value, not a description of this changing motion pattern.
explanation_options.d: Constant acceleration would produce a straight (constant-slope) line, not a changing one.

questions.question_text: Electric potential due to a 2 μC charge at a distance of one meter is equal to
questions.explanation_short: Electric potential V=kq/r = (9×10⁹)(2×10⁻⁶)/1 = 1.8×10⁴ V.

questions.explanation_trick: Electric potential (V=kq/r) has one less power of r than electric field (E=kq/r²) — a common point of confusion when a question doesn't explicitly say 'field' vs 'potential'.

explanation_options.a: Off by roughly an order of magnitude from the correct calculation.
explanation_options.b: Off by two orders of magnitude, too large.

questions.question_text: Kirchhoff's first law is a manifestation of
questions.explanation_short: Kirchhoff's current law is a manifestation of conservation of electric charge.
questions.explanation_long: Kirchhoff's first law states that total current into a junction equals total current out — reflecting conservation of electric charge, since charge doesn't accumulate or vanish at a junction.
questions.explanation_trick: Kirchhoff's current law = charge conservation; Kirchhoff's voltage law = energy conservation — memorize this pairing.

explanation_options.a: Conservation of momentum is unrelated to current flow at a junction.
explanation_options.b: Conservation of mass has no direct connection to current flow at a junction.
explanation_options.c: Conservation of energy is the principle behind Kirchhoff's second (voltage) law, not the first (current) law.
explanation_options.d: Correct — charge conservation underlies Kirchhoff's current law.

questions.question_text: Light photons, each of energy 3.5 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, fall on the cathode of a photocell. The current through the cell is reduced to zero by taking the cathode to a potential +0.25 V relative to the anode. The work function of the cathode is:
questions.explanation_short: Work function = photon energy − max KE = 3.5×10⁻¹⁹ J − eV₀ ≈ 3.1×10⁻¹⁹ J.
questions.explanation_long: The stopping potential of 0.25V means KEmax = eV₀ = 1.6×10⁻¹⁹×0.25 = 4×10⁻²⁰ J. Work function φ = photon energy − KEmax = 3.5×10⁻¹⁹ − 0.4×10⁻¹⁹ = 3.1×10⁻¹⁹ J.
questions.explanation_trick: Work function is always LESS than the incident photon energy by exactly the photoelectron's KE.

explanation_options.a: Close to but not exactly matching the precise calculation.
explanation_options.b: This equals the full photon energy, as if the stopping potential were zero — ignoring the given 0.25V.
explanation_options.c: Close to but not exactly matching the precise calculated work function.

questions.explanation_long: Grating spacing d = 1/(lines per unit length) = 1mm/500 = 0.002mm = 2×10⁻⁶ m (using 1mm=10⁻³m).

questions.question_text: In the case of linear deformation, the ratio of tensile stress to tensile strain is called
questions.option_a: energy stored in a stretched wire
questions.explanation_short: The ratio of tensile stress to tensile strain, by definition, is Young's modulus.
questions.explanation_long: Young's modulus is defined as the ratio of tensile (longitudinal) stress to tensile strain within the elastic limit: E = stress/strain — a material property describing stiffness.
questions.explanation_trick: Stress/strain = Young's modulus (stiffness); ½×stress×strain×volume = stored elastic energy — two different quantities from the same data.

explanation_options.a: 'Energy stored' is a different quantity (involving a factor of ½ and volume) from the direct stress/strain ratio.
explanation_options.b: Young's double-slit experiment is an unrelated optics phenomenon.
explanation_options.c: Bulk modulus relates volumetric stress to volumetric strain, not tensile (linear) stress-to-strain.
explanation_options.d: Correct — this is the standard definition of Young's modulus.

questions.question_text: What is the name of the energy which is released when an atom is formed from its constituent particles?
questions.explanation_short: The energy released when a nucleus forms from its separate constituent nucleons is called binding energy.
questions.explanation_long: Binding energy is the energy that would need to be supplied to completely separate a nucleus into its individual protons and neutrons — equivalently, it's the energy released when those separate nucleons come together to form the bound nucleus (via E=Δmc², using the mass defect between the nucleus and its separate constituents).
questions.explanation_trick: 'Binding energy' specifically refers to the energy tied to holding nucleons together (formation from parts) — distinct from 'nuclear energy' (a broader term for energy from nuclear reactions generally) or 'radioactive energy' (informal, not a standard term).

explanation_options.a: 'Atomic energy' is a broad, informal term for nuclear-related energy generally, not the specific formation-from-constituents concept.
explanation_options.b: 'Radioactive energy' isn't a standard physics term for this specific concept.
explanation_options.c: 'Nuclear energy' is a broader umbrella term (covering fission, fusion, etc.), not the precise term for formation-from-constituents energy.
explanation_options.d: Correct — binding energy is released when a nucleus forms from its constituent particles.

questions.question_text: Calculate the half life of bismuth-214, which has a decay constant of 4.3 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹.
questions.explanation_short: Per the official answer key, the half-life works out to 1.6×10⁻⁴ s.
questions.explanation_long: Using t½=ln(2)/λ with the decay constant as stated gives a result inconsistent with all listed options under a literal reading — but reconstructing backward from the officially marked answer (1.6×10⁻⁴s) matches treating the decay constant's exponent as positive (+4.3×10³ s⁻¹) rather than negative, consistent with a likely printing inconsistency between the stem and the exam's own intended solution.

questions.question_text: What is the main feature required by the optical fiber for the propagation of light in an optical fiber?
questions.option_b: Light should be totally confined within the fiber.
questions.option_c: They are cheaper than copper wire
questions.explanation_short: The fundamental requirement for light propagation in an optical fiber is total internal reflection — light staying confined within the fiber.
questions.explanation_long: Optical fibers work by total internal reflection: light entering the fiber core reflects repeatedly off the core-cladding boundary, staying confined as it travels along the fiber's length. This is the essential physical principle enabling fiber-optic transmission.
questions.explanation_trick: Total internal reflection (light staying confined) is THE defining physical principle of fiber optics — distinct from secondary/practical choices like light source type or material cost.

explanation_options.a: Cleanliness of the glass is a manufacturing/maintenance consideration, not the fundamental requirement.
explanation_options.b: Correct — total internal reflection/confinement is the core physical principle.
explanation_options.c: Cost comparison to copper wire is an economic consideration, not a physical requirement.
explanation_options.d: The choice of LED (vs. another light source) is a practical/engineering detail, not the fundamental principle.

questions.question_text: Two long, parallel conductors which are free to move are arranged 1.0 cm apart. A steady current of 20 A flows in each of the conductors in the same direction. The conductors
questions.option_d: move at right angles to each other
questions.explanation_short: Parallel currents flowing in the SAME direction attract each other (move toward each other); opposite directions repel.
questions.explanation_long: Two current-carrying conductors exert magnetic forces on each other. When currents flow in the same direction, the conductors attract (move toward each other); when currents flow in opposite directions, they repel (move apart) — this is a standard result of the magnetic forces between parallel current-carrying wires.
questions.explanation_trick: 'Same direction attracts, opposite direction repels' for parallel currents — the reverse of the more intuitive 'like charges repel' rule for static charges, so keep them distinct.

explanation_options.a: Free-moving conductors would not remain stationary — a magnetic force does act between them given the stated currents.
explanation_options.b: Correct — same-direction currents attract, moving the conductors toward each other.
explanation_options.c: Moving apart would be the result if currents were in opposite directions, not the same direction as stated.
explanation_options.d: There's no physical mechanism causing perpendicular motion between simple parallel current-carrying conductors.

questions.question_text: A stone of mass 2.0 kg is dropped from a rest position 5.0m above the ground. What is its velocity at a height of 3.0m above the ground?
questions.explanation_short: Falling 2m (from 5m to 3m height) from rest gives v=√(2×9.8×2)≈6.3 m/s.

questions.explanation_trick: In free fall, the object's mass doesn't affect its velocity — the '2.0 kg' figure is irrelevant to this calculation.

explanation_options.a: Doesn't match the calculation for falling 2m to reach a height of 3m.
explanation_options.c: Close to but not exactly matching a free-fall calculation with the given numbers.

questions.question_text: In case of half wave rectification, the resistance of the diode during the negative half of A.C is
questions.explanation_short: During the negative half-cycle of AC in half-wave rectification, the diode is reverse-biased and presents very high resistance, blocking current flow.
questions.explanation_long: A diode conducts easily (low resistance) when forward-biased and blocks current (very high resistance) when reverse-biased. In half-wave rectification, the negative half of the AC cycle reverse-biases the diode, giving it very high resistance and effectively stopping current flow during that half-cycle — this is precisely what makes half-wave rectification work (only the positive half-cycle passes through).
questions.explanation_trick: Forward bias = low resistance (conducts); reverse bias = very high resistance (blocks) — this on/off behavior is exactly what a diode contributes to rectification.

explanation_options.a: Correct — the diode's resistance is very high (reverse-biased) during the negative half-cycle.
explanation_options.b: Very low resistance describes the diode's forward-biased (conducting) state, the opposite of the negative half-cycle condition.
explanation_options.c: 'A few ohms' describes a low-resistance forward-biased state, not the blocking reverse-biased state.
explanation_options.d: Resistance is a magnitude and isn't described as 'negative' — this isn't a standard/correct description of diode behavior.

questions.question_text: Newton's first law of motion is also known as
questions.explanation_short: Newton's first law is universally known as the law of inertia.
questions.explanation_long: Newton's first law states that an object remains at rest or in uniform motion unless acted upon by a net external force — the defining statement of inertia, universally called the 'law of inertia'.
questions.explanation_trick: 'Newton's first law = law of inertia' is one of the most universally taught, unambiguous facts in introductory mechanics.

explanation_options.a: Correct — Newton's first law is the law of inertia.
explanation_options.b: Newton's first law has no direct connection to electromagnetism.
explanation_options.c: The law of universal gravitation is a separate principle from Newton's first law.
explanation_options.d: Conservation of momentum is a distinct (if related) principle, not the specific 'law of inertia' identity.

questions.question_text: When a potential difference is applied across the ends of a uniform wire of length l and radius r, a current I flows in the wire. If the same potential difference is applied to the ends of another wire of the same material but of length 2l and radius 2r, the current in the wire is
questions.explanation_short: Doubling both length and radius makes resistance R'=R/2, so the current doubles (I'=2I).
questions.explanation_long: Resistance R=ρL/A, where A=πr². For the second wire: L'=2L, r'=2r, so A'=4A. New resistance R'=ρ(2L)/(4A)=R/2. Since I=V/R: I'=V/(R/2)=2I.
questions.explanation_trick: When both length and radius scale by the same factor k, resistance scales by k/k²=1/k — here k=2, so R halves and current doubles.

explanation_options.a: Doesn't match the calculation — the current should double, not quarter.
explanation_options.b: Correct — the current doubles, since resistance halves.
explanation_options.c: Would only be correct if resistance were unchanged, which isn't the case here.
explanation_options.d: Doesn't match the calculated relationship between the two wires' resistances.

questions.question_text: A shock wave is produced due to an earthquake which makes the buildings move in the direction of the shock wave. Which progressive wave would this be?
questions.explanation_short: An earthquake shock wave that moves buildings in the same direction the wave travels is a longitudinal wave (compression-type, like a P-wave).
questions.explanation_long: In a longitudinal wave, particle displacement occurs parallel to (in the same direction as) the wave's direction of travel — exactly matching the description of buildings being pushed in the direction of the shock wave, similar to how seismic P-waves (primary/pressure waves) propagate. Transverse waves, by contrast, displace particles perpendicular to the wave's travel direction.
questions.explanation_trick: 'Displacement parallel to wave travel' = longitudinal (like sound waves or seismic P-waves); 'displacement perpendicular to wave travel' = transverse (like light waves or seismic S-waves).

explanation_options.a: Correct — displacement in the direction of wave travel defines a longitudinal wave.
explanation_options.b: Transverse waves displace particles perpendicular to the wave's travel direction, not parallel as described.
explanation_options.c: 'Material wave' isn't a standard classification term distinguishing wave types by displacement direction.
explanation_options.d: 'Particle wave' isn't a standard classification term for this distinction either.

questions.question_text: A neutron having mass equal to a proton (mₚ=1.6 × 10⁻²⁷ kg) is moving in a magnetic field of intensity 1.20 × 10⁻³ T with a speed of 2.0 × 10⁷ ms⁻¹. What is the Maximum force experienced by the neutron.
questions.explanation_short: A neutron carries no electric charge, so it experiences zero magnetic force regardless of its speed or the field strength.
questions.explanation_long: The magnetic force on a moving charge is F=qvBsinθ. Since a neutron has zero net electric charge (q=0), this force is always exactly zero, no matter how fast it moves or how strong the magnetic field is — the given mass and speed values in the stem are a deliberate distractor, since they're irrelevant once you recognize the neutron's charge is zero.
questions.explanation_trick: Always check the charge of the particle first in magnetic force problems — a neutral particle (like a neutron) experiences zero magnetic force by definition, no matter what other numbers are given.

explanation_options.a: Would result from incorrectly treating the neutron as if it carried a charge equal to the proton's.
explanation_options.b: Correct — zero force, since the neutron is electrically neutral.
explanation_options.c: Also incorrectly assumes a nonzero charge.
explanation_options.d: Same error as A and C, just with a different (still incorrect) nonzero numerical result.

questions.question_text: In S.H.M the kinetic energy of the body is maximum when
questions.option_a: The body is at mean position
questions.option_b: The body is at extreme position from the mean.
questions.option_c: The body is exactly half way down between mean and extreme position
questions.option_d: The body is somewhere between mean and extreme position.
questions.explanation_short: Kinetic energy in SHM is maximum at the mean (equilibrium) position, where speed is greatest.
questions.explanation_long: In simple harmonic motion, the restoring force is zero at the mean (equilibrium) position, meaning the object experiences maximum acceleration change/speed there since it has been accelerating toward this point the whole approach — kinetic energy (½mv²) is therefore at its maximum at the mean position, while potential energy is simultaneously at its minimum (zero) there.
questions.explanation_trick: Mean position = max speed = max KE = min PE; extreme positions = zero speed = zero KE = max PE — memorize this direct correspondence.

explanation_options.a: Correct — KE is maximum at the mean position.
explanation_options.b: At the extreme position, velocity (and thus KE) is momentarily zero — this is where PE is maximum instead.
explanation_options.c: KE decreases smoothly from the mean position outward — it isn't maximum at any halfway point specifically.
explanation_options.d: KE is maximum specifically at the mean position, not at some unspecified point between mean and extreme.

questions.question_text: Force experienced per unit positive test charge at a point in an electric field is the definition of:
questions.explanation_short: Force per unit positive test charge at a point defines electric field strength.
questions.explanation_long: Electric field strength (E) is defined as the force experienced by a small positive test charge placed at a point, divided by the magnitude of that test charge: E=F/q. This distinguishes it from electric potential (energy per unit charge, a scalar) and electric potential energy (the actual energy a charge has due to its position).
questions.explanation_trick: 'Force per charge' = electric field (a vector); 'energy per charge' = electric potential (a scalar) — keep these two closely related but distinct definitions separate.

explanation_options.a: Electric potential energy is the actual energy a charge possesses at a point, not a force-per-charge ratio.
explanation_options.b: Correct — force per unit positive test charge defines electric field strength.
explanation_options.c: Electric potential is defined as potential energy per unit charge (energy-based), not force-based.
explanation_options.d: 'Electric field' alone (without 'strength') is sometimes used loosely for the same concept, but the precise textbook definition given here specifically describes field strength.

questions.question_text: A metal rod of length 10.0 cm is moving at a speed of 0.5 ms⁻¹ in a direction perpendicular to a 0.20 T magnetic field. Find the emf produced in the rod.
questions.explanation_long: Motional EMF is given by EMF=BLv. Using B=0.20T, L=10.0cm=0.10m, v=0.5 m/s: EMF = 0.20×0.10×0.5 = 0.01V = 1.0×10⁻² V.
questions.explanation_trick: Always convert length to meters (10.0cm = 0.10m) before multiplying in EMF=BLv — a decimal-place slip is a common source of a factor-of-10 error.

explanation_options.a: Off by roughly a factor of 5 from the correct calculation.
explanation_options.b: Same numeric magnitude written differently, but not the standard form of the answer.
explanation_options.d: Off by a factor of 10 — this would only match if the rod's length were 1.0cm rather than 10.0cm.

aliases: A metal rod of length 10.0 cm is moving at a speed of 0.5 ms^-1 in a direction perpendicular to a 0.20 T magnetic field. Find the emf produced in the rod.

questions.question_text: That is just an example of what I complain__________.
questions.explanation_short: 'Complain of' something is the standard idiomatic preposition pairing.
questions.explanation_long: The fixed phrase is 'complain of' a problem or ailment (e.g., 'complain of a headache', or 'complain of an issue') — 'complain off/to/with' are not standard English constructions.
questions.explanation_trick: 'Complain of' is a fixed collocation worth memorizing directly, especially since it's a common source of preposition-choice questions.

explanation_options.a: Correct — 'complain of' is the standard idiom.
explanation_options.b: 'Complain off' is not a standard English construction.
explanation_options.c: 'Complain to' is used specifically to indicate who you're complaining TO (a person), not what you're complaining ABOUT.
explanation_options.d: 'Complain with' is not a standard English construction.

questions.question_text: The region __________ which they were passing was known as the Land of Thirst and Death
questions.explanation_short: 'The region through which they were passing' uses the correct preposition — one passes 'through' a region.
questions.explanation_long: 'Through' correctly describes movement traversing the interior of a region or area — 'by', 'in', and 'from' don't capture this specific sense of passing through the middle of a place.
questions.explanation_trick: 'Through' pairs with movement across/inside an extended area — a common preposition choice when describing travel through terrain, regions, or tunnels.

explanation_options.a: Correct — 'through which they were passing' properly describes traversing the region.
explanation_options.b: 'By' would suggest passing alongside the region, not through its interior.
explanation_options.c: 'In' would describe being located within the region, not the ongoing motion of passing through it.
explanation_options.d: 'From' would indicate a starting point, not the traversal described here.

questions.question_text: I know how to __________ a throat for inspection.
questions.explanation_short: To "expose" something is to uncover it so it can be seen — a doctor exposes a throat for inspection.
questions.explanation_long: The sentence needs a verb meaning to make the throat visible for examination. "Expose" fits exactly. "Force" suggests violence, "prepare" does not mean making it visible, and "open a throat" would mean cutting it.
questions.explanation_trick: Expose = uncover for viewing.

explanation_options.a: 'Force a throat' is unidiomatic and suggests violence.
explanation_options.b: 'Prepare a throat' does not mean making it visible for inspection.
explanation_options.c: Correct — you expose a throat for inspection.
explanation_options.d: 'Open a throat' would mean cutting it open.

questions.question_text: It is better for me to __________ than to shed the blood of an innocent boy.
questions.explanation_short: After 'better... to', the bare infinitive form 'die' correctly parallels the earlier infinitive 'to die' — 'die' matches the required infinitive form, not a past or perfect form.
questions.explanation_long: The sentence structure 'It is better... to die than to shed the blood...' requires the base/infinitive form of the verb ('die') to correctly parallel the second infinitive phrase ('to shed'). Past tense ('died') or perfect forms ('had died', 'have died') don't fit this infinitive construction.
questions.explanation_trick: After 'to' in an infinitive phrase, always use the base form of the verb — never a past tense or perfect form.

explanation_options.a: 'Died' is a past tense form, not the infinitive form needed after 'to'.
