explanation_options.b: Low pressure works against the favorable shift needed for maximum ammonia yield.
explanation_options.c: High temperature actually shifts this exothermic equilibrium backward, reducing yield.
explanation_options.d: Continually ADDING ammonia (a product) would shift equilibrium backward, reducing yield, not increasing it.

aliases: Identify the CORRECT option required for the maximum yield of ammonia by Haber's process:
High pressure low temperature continual

questions.question_text: Consider the following reaction in equilibrium and tell addition of which chemical will turn the cloudy solution into clear solution? BiCl₃ + H₂O ⇌ BiOCl + 2HCl
questions.explanation_short: Adding HCl (a product) shifts the equilibrium back, redissolving the cloudy BiOCl precipitate.
questions.explanation_long: By Le Chatelier's principle, adding more of a product (HCl here) to BiCl3+H2O⇌BiOCl+2HCl pushes the equilibrium in reverse, converting solid BiOCl back into dissolved BiCl3 — clearing the cloudy solution. This is the classic common-ion-effect demonstration.
questions.explanation_trick: Adding a product shifts equilibrium backward — use that to dissolve the precipitate.

explanation_options.a: Adding BiCl3 (a reactant) would shift equilibrium forward, making the solution cloudier, not clearer.
explanation_options.b: Adding H2O (a reactant) would likewise shift forward, increasing cloudiness.
explanation_options.c: BiOCl is the very precipitate causing the cloudiness — adding more of it can't clear the solution.
explanation_options.d: Correct — adding HCl (a product) reverses the reaction, redissolving the precipitate.

aliases: Consider the following reaction in equilibrium and tell addition of which chemical will turn the cloudy solution into clear solution? BiCl3 + H2O <=> BiOCl + 2HCl
BiCl3

questions.question_text: Identify the correct formula to calculate rate of reaction:

questions.option_d: Time taken for the change x Change in concentration of substance
questions.explanation_short: Rate of reaction = change in concentration of a substance divided by time taken.
questions.explanation_long: Reaction rate is defined as how fast a reactant's (or product's) concentration changes over time: Rate = Δ[concentration] / Δtime.
questions.explanation_trick: Rate = concentration change ÷ time — keep numerator and denominator in the right places.

explanation_options.a: Correct — rate equals concentration change divided by time.
explanation_options.b: This flips the ratio (time divided by concentration change), which is the inverse of rate.
explanation_options.c: This also has the ratio inverted relative to the correct definition.
explanation_options.d: This introduces an incorrect extra multiplication/percentage factor not part of the rate definition.

questions.question_text: Consider the hypothetical equation aA + bB → cC + dD: Which of the following represents correct rate equation?

questions.explanation_long: The rate law expresses reaction rate as proportional to reactant concentrations raised to powers matching their (experimentally determined) reaction orders — generically written using the stoichiometric coefficients a and b as exponents here.
questions.explanation_trick: Rate law exponents match the coefficients as labeled in this generic/hypothetical equation (a and b), not necessarily simple powers of 1 or 2.

explanation_options.a: This omits the exponents a and b entirely, an incomplete general rate law.

questions.question_text: If a reaction rate does not change with concentration then it is
questions.explanation_short: A reaction whose rate doesn't change with concentration is zero order.
questions.explanation_long: For a zero-order reaction, Rate = k[Reactant]^0 = k — the rate is constant, independent of reactant concentration.
questions.explanation_trick: Order = 0 means concentration has no effect on rate — a constant rate regardless of how much reactant is present.

explanation_options.a: Third order reactions have rate strongly dependent on concentration (to the 3rd power).
explanation_options.b: Second order reactions have rate proportional to concentration squared.
explanation_options.c: First order reactions have rate directly proportional to concentration.
explanation_options.d: Correct — zero order means rate is independent of concentration.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is CORRECT Arrhenius equation?
questions.explanation_short: The Arrhenius equation is K = Ae^(-Ea/RT).
questions.explanation_long: The Arrhenius equation relates the rate constant K to the activation energy Ea, temperature T, the gas constant R, and the pre-exponential factor A: K = Ae^(-Ea/RT).
questions.explanation_trick: Memorize 'R' (gas constant) in the exponent — the other letters (Q, S, U) are decoys.

explanation_options.a: 'Q' isn't the gas constant used in the Arrhenius equation.
explanation_options.b: Correct — R (the gas constant) belongs in the exponent of the Arrhenius equation.
explanation_options.c: 'S' isn't the gas constant symbol used here.
explanation_options.d: 'U' isn't the gas constant symbol used here.

questions.question_text: In endothermic reaction, the heat content of the
questions.option_b: Reactants is more than that of products
questions.option_c: Products is more than that of reactants
questions.explanation_short: In an endothermic reaction, products end up with more heat content (enthalpy) than the reactants.
questions.explanation_long: Endothermic reactions absorb heat from the surroundings, so the energy is stored in the products — meaning products have higher enthalpy (heat content) than the reactants that started with less.
questions.explanation_trick: Endothermic = absorbs heat = products end up higher in energy than reactants (opposite of exothermic).

explanation_options.a: Equal heat content would mean no net energy change, not a true endothermic reaction.
explanation_options.b: This describes an exothermic reaction (reactants higher in energy), the opposite case.
explanation_options.c: Correct — in an endothermic reaction, products hold more heat content than reactants.
explanation_options.d: Heat content of reactants and products does change in a reaction — that's the whole basis of enthalpy change.

questions.question_text: All of the following steps are used to calculate the lattice energy in Born-Haber cycle EXCEPT
questions.explanation_short: 'Deionizing the metal' is not a real Born-Haber cycle step — metals get ionized, not deionized.
questions.explanation_long: The Born-Haber cycle for lattice energy includes atomization of the metal, successive ionization of the metal (forming cations), and ionization (electron gain) of the non-metal — but never a 'deionization' step, which isn't part of the thermochemical cycle at all.
questions.explanation_trick: Born-Haber steps always ADD or REMOVE electrons in one clear direction (ionize metal → lose e-, non-metal gains e-) — 'deionize' doesn't fit this pattern.

explanation_options.a: Atomizing the metal genuinely IS a real Born-Haber cycle step.
explanation_options.b: Ionizing the metal (removing electrons to form the cation) genuinely IS a real step.
explanation_options.c: Correct — 'deionizing the metal' is not an actual Born-Haber cycle step.
explanation_options.d: Ionizing the non-metal (its electron affinity step) genuinely IS a real step.

questions.question_text: The enthalpy change when 1 Mole of water is formed by the reaction of acid with an alkali under standard conditions is known as:
questions.explanation_short: Enthalpy of neutralization is the heat change when an acid and base react to form exactly 1 mole of water.
questions.explanation_long: This is the standard definition: the enthalpy of neutralization is the heat released (or absorbed) when one mole of water forms from the reaction of an acid with a base under standard conditions.
questions.explanation_trick: 'Acid + alkali → 1 mole water' is the specific signature phrasing of enthalpy of NEUTRALIZATION, distinct from formation/combustion/reaction.

explanation_options.a: Enthalpy of formation is defined for compounds forming from their elements, not acid-base neutralization.
explanation_options.b: Enthalpy of reaction is a general term, not specific to the acid-base-to-water definition given.
explanation_options.c: Enthalpy of combustion involves burning a substance in oxygen, unrelated to acid-base neutralization.
explanation_options.d: Correct — this is the specific definition of enthalpy of neutralization.

questions.question_text: Oxidation number of 'Mn' in KMnO₄ is
questions.explanation_short: Mn's oxidation number in KMnO4 is +7.
questions.explanation_long: K is always +1, and the 4 oxygens contribute -8 total; since the compound is neutral, Mn must balance to +7 (+1 + x + (-8) = 0 → x = +7).
questions.explanation_trick: K=+1, O=-2×4=-8, solve for Mn to make the sum zero: Mn = +7.

explanation_options.a: An oxidation number of 0 wouldn't balance the compound's overall neutral charge.
explanation_options.b: +1 is far too low to balance against the -8 total from oxygen.
explanation_options.c: -7 has the wrong sign — Mn must be strongly positive here, not negative.
explanation_options.d: Correct — +7 balances +1 (K) and -8 (4 oxygens) to zero overall charge.

questions.question_text: Which step is irrelevant with respect to balancing of redox equations by oxidation number method?
questions.option_a: Split the reaction into two half reactions
questions.option_b: Assign oxidation number to all the atoms involved in the equation
questions.option_c: Identify the element undergoing a change in oxidation number
questions.option_d: Equalize the number of electrons lost and gained
questions.explanation_short: Splitting a reaction into two half-reactions belongs to the ion-electron method, not the oxidation-number method.
questions.explanation_long: The oxidation-number method for balancing redox equations works by tracking oxidation number changes directly, without separating into half-reactions — that half-reaction split is instead the defining step of the alternative ion-electron (half-reaction) method.
questions.explanation_trick: 'Half-reactions' = ion-electron method; the oxidation-number method never splits the equation that way.

explanation_options.a: Correct — splitting into half-reactions is irrelevant to (not part of) the oxidation-number method.
explanation_options.b: Assigning oxidation numbers to all atoms IS a genuine step of this method.
explanation_options.c: Identifying which element changes oxidation number IS a genuine step.
explanation_options.d: Equalizing electrons lost and gained (via oxidation number change) IS a genuine step of this method.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is NOT a correct feature of electrolytic cells?
questions.option_c: Alternating current source is connected to electrodes
questions.explanation_short: Electrolytic cells run on direct current (DC), not alternating current (AC) — that's the incorrect feature listed.
questions.explanation_long: Electrolytic cells require a DC power source to drive a non-spontaneous redox reaction in a fixed direction; an AC source would constantly reverse the current direction and couldn't sustain consistent electrolysis.
questions.explanation_trick: Electrolytic cells need DC (fixed-direction current) to keep oxidation/reduction happening at the same electrodes consistently.

explanation_options.a: Reduction genuinely DOES occur at the cathode in an electrolytic cell.
explanation_options.b: Oxidation genuinely DOES occur at the anode.
explanation_options.c: Correct — this is the FALSE statement; electrolytic cells need a DC (not AC) source.
explanation_options.d: Electrochemical reactions genuinely DO take place at the electrodes.

questions.question_text: Which of the following has a coordinate bond?
questions.explanation_short: NH3BF3 contains a coordinate (dative) bond, formed by ammonia's lone pair donating into boron's empty orbital.
questions.explanation_long: In the NH3-BF3 adduct, nitrogen's lone pair is donated entirely from ammonia into an empty orbital on boron (which is electron-deficient in BF3), forming a coordinate covalent bond — unlike the ionic (NaCl, CaO) or simple covalent (H2O) bonds in the other options.
questions.explanation_trick: Coordinate bonds form when one atom (with a lone pair) donates both electrons to another atom with an empty orbital — classic Lewis acid-base adduct.

explanation_options.a: NaCl is an ionic compound, not a coordinate-bonded one.
explanation_options.b: CaO is likewise ionic.
explanation_options.c: Correct — NH3BF3 forms via a coordinate (dative) bond from N to B.
explanation_options.d: H2O has ordinary covalent O-H bonds, not a coordinate bond in its basic structure.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is NOT a feature of Valence Shell Electron Pair Repulsion theory?
questions.option_a: It determines the shape of molecule
questions.option_b: Pairs of electrons repel each other
questions.option_c: It helps in understanding interaction of medicinal drug molecules
questions.option_d: Only lone pairs participate in determining geometry of molecules
questions.explanation_short: VSEPR considers BOTH bonding and lone electron pairs — it's not true that only lone pairs matter.
questions.explanation_long: Valence Shell Electron Pair Repulsion theory predicts molecular geometry based on the repulsion between ALL electron pairs around a central atom, both bonding pairs and lone pairs — so claiming only lone pairs determine geometry misrepresents the theory.
questions.explanation_trick: VSEPR = repulsion of ALL electron pairs (bonding + lone), not lone pairs exclusively.

explanation_options.a: VSEPR genuinely DOES determine molecular shape — that's its core purpose.
explanation_options.b: Electron pair repulsion IS the theory's basic mechanism.
explanation_options.c: VSEPR-predicted shapes genuinely DO help explain molecular interactions in various contexts.
explanation_options.d: Correct — this is the FALSE statement; both bonding and lone pairs (not lone pairs alone) determine geometry.

questions.question_text: Which of the following has smallest atomic radius
questions.explanation_short: Sulfur (S) has the smallest atomic radius among Mg, S, P, and Na.
questions.explanation_long: Across a period, atomic radius decreases left to right as nuclear charge increases while electrons fill the same shell. Among these third-period elements, sulfur has the highest atomic number and thus the smallest radius.
questions.explanation_trick: Same-period trend: radius shrinks as you move right — pick the element furthest right/highest atomic number.

explanation_options.a: Mg is further left (lower atomic number) than S, so it has a larger radius.
explanation_options.b: Correct — sulfur, furthest right among these, has the smallest atomic radius.
explanation_options.c: P is one position left of S, giving it a slightly larger radius.
explanation_options.d: Na is furthest left (lowest atomic number), giving it the largest radius among these four.

questions.question_text: The difference of lithium from the other alkali metals is mainly because of:
questions.option_a: Large radius and low charge density
questions.option_b: Small radius and low charge density
questions.option_c: Large radius and high charge density
questions.option_d: Small radius and high charge density
questions.explanation_short: Lithium's anomalous behavior versus other alkali metals stems from its small radius and high charge density.
questions.explanation_long: Lithium is the smallest alkali metal, so its charge is concentrated into a small volume (high charge density), giving it stronger polarizing power and more covalent-like character than the larger, lower charge-density alkali metals below it.
questions.explanation_trick: Small size + high charge concentrated on it = 'high charge density' = the classic explanation for lithium's odd-one-out behavior.

explanation_options.a: Large radius and low charge density describes the heavier alkali metals, not lithium.
explanation_options.b: Small radius is right, but 'low charge density' contradicts lithium's actual high charge density.
explanation_options.c: Large radius is wrong for lithium, which is the smallest alkali metal.
explanation_options.d: Correct — lithium's small radius combined with high charge density explains its distinct behavior.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is not Basic in nature

questions.question_text: The solubility of sulphates of alkaline metals generally

explanation_options.d: Solubility does change noticeably down the group, it doesn't stay constant.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is NOT an Alloy
questions.explanation_short: Graphite is a pure carbon allotrope, not a metal alloy, unlike steel, brass, and bronze.
questions.explanation_long: Steel (iron+carbon), brass (copper+zinc), and bronze (copper+tin) are all true metal alloys. Graphite, however, is a non-metallic allotrope of pure carbon, with no alloying involved.
questions.explanation_trick: Alloys are always metal mixtures — graphite (a carbon allotrope) never qualifies.

questions.question_text: Electronic configuration of chromium (Proton number 24) is:
questions.explanation_short: Chromium's electron configuration is the exception [Ar]3d5 4s1, not the expected [Ar]3d4 4s2.
questions.explanation_long: Chromium adopts [Ar]3d⁵4s¹ instead of the 'expected' [Ar]3d⁴4s² because a half-filled d subshell (3d⁵) provides extra stability, favoring one electron shifting from 4s into 3d.
questions.explanation_trick: Cr and Cu are the two classic 'exception' elements — memorize Cr as 3d⁵4s¹ (half-filled d stability).

explanation_options.a: [Ar]3d⁴4s² is the naively expected (but incorrect) configuration — chromium doesn't actually follow this.
explanation_options.b: [Ar]3d⁵4s² would have one too many electrons (7 total after Ar's 18, giving 25, not 24).

questions.question_text: Which of the following is NOT a property of transition elements?

questions.question_text: 1-Butene and two Butene are showing which type of isomerism?
questions.explanation_short: 1-butene and 2-butene differ only in where the double bond sits — that's position isomerism.
questions.explanation_long: Both compounds share the same molecular formula (C4H8) and carbon skeleton, differing only in the double bond's position along the chain (between C1-C2 versus C2-C3) — the defining feature of position (positional) isomerism.
questions.explanation_trick: Same skeleton, same functional group, different location on the chain = position isomerism.

explanation_options.b: Correct — differing double-bond position along an otherwise identical chain is position isomerism.
explanation_options.c: Metamerism involves different alkyl groups on either side of a functional group (like ethers/amines), not double-bond position.
explanation_options.d: Chain isomerism involves a different carbon skeleton (branching), not just a shifted double bond.

questions.question_text: Which type of isomerism is displayed by compounds having same structural formula but different position of atoms on both sides of carbon bond?

questions.explanation_long: When atoms/groups are arranged differently on either side of a rigid double bond despite identical structural (connectivity) formulas, that's geometric isomerism — e.g. cis and trans forms of an alkene.
questions.explanation_trick: Same connections, different 3D arrangement across a rigid bond = geometric (cis/trans) isomerism.

explanation_options.a: Chain isomerism differs in the carbon skeleton itself, not spatial arrangement across a bond.
explanation_options.b: Metamerism involves different alkyl groups on either side of a functional group, a different concept.
explanation_options.c: Correct — geometric isomerism describes differing spatial arrangement across a double bond with identical connectivity.
explanation_options.d: Tautomerism involves interconverting structural isomers (e.g. keto-enol), not fixed spatial arrangement.

questions.question_text: Homocyclic organic compounds are sub divided into two types namely:

questions.question_text: Which of the following is an example of substituent group which release electrons to benzene ring:
questions.explanation_short: -NH2 is an electron-releasing (donating) group on a benzene ring, unlike -CN, -NR3+, and -NO2.

questions.question_text: Identify correct ascending order of reactivity of alkyl halides:

questions.question_text: The blue color of Fehling solution is changed to red when warmed with an aldehyde due to formation of which of the following?

questions.explanation_long: Aldehydes reduce the Cu2+ ions in Fehling's solution (blue) to Cu+, which precipitates as brick-red copper(I) oxide (Cu2O) — a classic positive test distinguishing aldehydes from ketones.
questions.explanation_trick: Fehling's positive result = brick-red Cu2O precipitate, the aldehyde-detection signature.

explanation_options.a: NO2 isn't the product formed in Fehling's test.
explanation_options.b: Correct — Cu2O (red precipitate) forms when Fehling's solution reacts with an aldehyde.
explanation_options.c: AgO isn't the product of Fehling's test (silver mirror test uses Tollens' reagent instead, forming metallic Ag).
explanation_options.d: SO2 is unrelated to Fehling's test chemistry.

aliases: The blue color of Fehling solution is changed to red when warmed with an aldehyde due to formation of which of the following?
NO2

questions.question_text: Reaction of HCN with formaldehyde is a:
questions.explanation_short: HCN adds across formaldehyde's C=O bond via nucleophilic addition, forming a cyanohydrin.
questions.explanation_long: The cyanide ion (nucleophile) attacks the electrophilic carbonyl carbon of formaldehyde, and after protonation this gives a cyanohydrin — a classic nucleophilic addition reaction at a carbonyl group.
questions.explanation_trick: Carbonyl compounds (aldehydes/ketones) undergo nucleophilic ADDITION, not substitution, because the C=O double bond opens up to accept the nucleophile.

explanation_options.a: Correct — HCN's nucleophilic addition to formaldehyde's carbonyl gives a cyanohydrin.
explanation_options.b: There's no leaving group to be substituted in this carbonyl-addition reaction.
explanation_options.c: The carbonyl carbon is electrophilic, and CN- is a nucleophile, not an electrophile, ruling out an electrophilic mechanism.
explanation_options.d: This isn't an aromatic-ring-type electrophilic substitution — it's an aliphatic carbonyl addition.

questions.question_text: Which of the following alcohol can give lodoform reaction?
questions.explanation_short: Ethanol gives a positive iodoform test, because it has the required CH3-CH(OH)- (methyl carbinol) group.
questions.explanation_long: The iodoform reaction requires a CH3-CO- group or a CH3-CH(OH)- group that can be oxidized to it. Among these options, ethanol (CH3CH2OH) has exactly this methyl-carbinol arrangement, unlike methanol, 1-butanol, or 1-propanol.
questions.explanation_trick: Iodoform-positive alcohols specifically have a methyl group directly next to the carbinol carbon (CH3-CHOH-) — ethanol and isopropanol are the classic examples.

explanation_options.a: Methanol (CH3OH) has no carbon chain beyond the OH carbon, so it lacks the required CH3-CHOH- pattern.
explanation_options.b: 1-Butanol's OH-bearing carbon isn't attached to a methyl group directly, so it fails the iodoform test.
explanation_options.c: 1-Propanol also lacks a methyl group directly on the carbinol carbon, so it fails the test.
explanation_options.d: Correct — ethanol's CH3-CH2OH structure has the methyl-carbinol pattern needed for a positive iodoform test.

questions.question_text: Common name of 2-hydroxy propanoic acid is:
questions.explanation_short: 2-hydroxypropanoic acid's common name is lactic acid.
questions.explanation_long: Lactic acid (CH3-CH(OH)-COOH) is the common name for 2-hydroxypropanoic acid, famous as the compound produced by anaerobic (lactic acid) fermentation in muscles and by certain bacteria.
questions.explanation_trick: Lactic acid = 2-hydroxypropanoic acid, a direct name-to-structure pairing worth memorizing.

explanation_options.a: Tartaric acid is a dihydroxy dicarboxylic acid (from grapes), a different structure entirely.
explanation_options.b: Correct — lactic acid is the common name for 2-hydroxypropanoic acid.
explanation_options.c: Phthalic acid is an aromatic dicarboxylic acid, unrelated to this structure.
explanation_options.d: Formic acid (HCOOH) is the simplest carboxylic acid, with no hydroxyl substituent.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is correct regarding phenol
questions.option_a: Phenol and water are equally acidic
questions.option_b: Phenol is less acidic than carboxylic acid
questions.option_c: Phenol is less acidic than water
questions.option_d: Phenol is less acidic than ethanol
questions.explanation_short: Phenol is less acidic than carboxylic acids, though more acidic than plain alcohols like ethanol.
questions.explanation_long: Acidity order: carboxylic acids > carbonic acid > phenol > water > alcohols (like ethanol). Phenol's acidity comes from resonance stabilization of its phenoxide ion, but this stabilization is weaker than the resonance stabilization in a carboxylate ion, making phenol the weaker acid of the two.
questions.explanation_trick: Memorize the acidity ladder: carboxylic acid > phenol > water > alcohol — phenol sits in the middle, not at either extreme.

explanation_options.a: Phenol is actually noticeably more acidic than water, not equally acidic.
explanation_options.b: Correct — phenol is less acidic than carboxylic acids.
explanation_options.c: Phenol is actually MORE acidic than water, not less.
explanation_options.d: Phenol is actually MORE acidic than ethanol, not less.

questions.question_text: When carboxylic acid are heated with alcohol in the presence of sulphuric acid one of the following is formed
questions.explanation_short: Carboxylic acid + alcohol with H2SO4 catalyst gives an ester (Fischer esterification).
questions.explanation_long: This is the classic Fischer esterification reaction: an acid catalyst (like concentrated H2SO4) drives a carboxylic acid and an alcohol to condense into an ester, releasing water.
questions.explanation_trick: Acid + alcohol + acid catalyst = ester (Fischer esterification) — a very frequently tested named reaction.

explanation_options.a: Amides form from acids reacting with ammonia/amines, not alcohols.
explanation_options.b: Acyl chlorides form using reagents like SOCl2 or PCl5, not simple acid-catalyzed reaction with alcohol.
explanation_options.c: Correct — Fischer esterification gives an ester from an acid and alcohol under acid catalysis.
explanation_options.d: Acid anhydrides form from two carboxylic acid molecules (losing water), not from reaction with an alcohol.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following is not an amino acid
questions.explanation_short: Folic acid is a vitamin (B9), not an amino acid — unlike glutamic acid, glycine, and lysine.
questions.explanation_long: Glutamic acid, glycine, and lysine are all genuine proteinogenic amino acids, while folic acid is a B-vitamin involved in nucleotide synthesis and cell division, structurally unrelated to the amino acid category.
questions.explanation_trick: 'Folic acid' sounds chemistry-adjacent but it's a vitamin — don't let the '-ic acid' naming pattern mislead you.

explanation_options.a: Correct — folic acid is a vitamin, not an amino acid.
explanation_options.b: Glutamic acid genuinely IS a standard amino acid.
explanation_options.c: Glycine genuinely IS a standard amino acid.
explanation_options.d: Lysine genuinely IS a standard (essential) amino acid.

questions.question_text: In an elastic collision the total kinetic energy
questions.option_d: Before and after collision remains same
questions.explanation_short: In an elastic collision, total kinetic energy is conserved — it's the same before and after.
questions.explanation_long: By definition, an elastic collision conserves both momentum AND kinetic energy; no KE is lost to heat, sound, or deformation, unlike an inelastic collision.
questions.explanation_trick: 'Elastic' is your cue word for 'KE conserved' — don't confuse it with inelastic collisions, where KE is lost.

explanation_options.a: KE dissipating describes an inelastic collision, not an elastic one.
explanation_options.b: KE cannot spontaneously increase in a simple collision — that would violate energy conservation.
explanation_options.c: KE reducing describes an inelastic collision.
explanation_options.d: Correct — total KE remains the same before and after an elastic collision.

questions.question_text: The instantaneous velocity along the curved path is;
questions.explanation_short: Instantaneous velocity on a curved path always points along the tangent to the curve at that point.
questions.explanation_long: At any instant, an object's velocity direction is tangential to its path — this holds for straight or curved motion alike, since velocity describes the direction of momentary displacement.
questions.explanation_trick: Velocity is always tangent to the path; acceleration (centripetal) points toward the centre (along the radius) in circular motion — don't mix the two up.

explanation_options.a: Correct — instantaneous velocity is always along the tangent to the path.
explanation_options.b: Perpendicular to the slope isn't how velocity direction is defined.
explanation_options.c: Parallel to the radius describes a radial direction, which is the direction of centripetal acceleration, not velocity.
explanation_options.d: Anti-parallel to the radius is also a radial (acceleration-related) direction, not the velocity direction.

questions.question_text: The range of projectile will be maximum if the factor sin2θ becomes
questions.explanation_short: Projectile range is maximum when sin(2θ) = 1, i.e. at a launch angle of 45°.
questions.explanation_long: Range R = (v²sin2θ)/g is maximized when sin2θ reaches its peak value of 1, which happens at 2θ=90°, i.e. θ=45°.
questions.explanation_trick: sin(2θ)=1 → 2θ=90° → θ=45°, the classic 'maximum range' launch angle.

explanation_options.a: sin2θ=0 would give zero range (θ=0° or 90°), the minimum, not maximum.
explanation_options.b: Correct — sin2θ=1 gives the maximum possible range.
explanation_options.c: sin2θ=-1 isn't achievable for a physical launch angle between 0-90°.
explanation_options.d: sin2θ can never exceed 1 — this value is impossible for the sine function.

aliases: The range of projectile will be maximum if the factor sin2q becomes
Zero

questions.question_text: The two dimensional motion under constant acceleration due to gravity is called:
questions.explanation_short: Two-dimensional motion under constant gravitational acceleration is called projectile motion.
questions.explanation_long: Projectile motion combines constant horizontal velocity with constant vertical acceleration (due to gravity), tracing a parabolic path — the standard definition tested here.
questions.explanation_trick: '2D motion + constant g' = projectile motion, distinct from circular motion (constant speed, changing direction) or vibratory motion (oscillation).

explanation_options.a: Circular motion involves constant-radius motion, not free motion under gravity.
explanation_options.b: Rotational motion describes spinning about an axis, unrelated to gravity-driven 2D motion.
explanation_options.c: Correct — this is the definition of projectile motion.
explanation_options.d: Vibratory motion is oscillatory back-and-forth motion, not a gravity-driven trajectory.

questions.question_text: In velocity time graph the area under graph is equal to the:
questions.explanation_short: The area under a velocity-time graph equals the distance covered by the object.
questions.explanation_long: Since velocity × time gives distance, integrating (finding the area under) a v-t graph over an interval yields the total distance travelled during that interval.
questions.explanation_trick: v-t graph: slope = acceleration, area under curve = distance/displacement.

explanation_options.a: Speed itself is what's plotted on the graph (the y-axis value), not the area.
explanation_options.b: Velocity is likewise the plotted quantity, not the area under the curve.
explanation_options.c: Correct — the area under a v-t graph gives distance covered.
explanation_options.d: Acceleration is the graph's slope, not the area under it.

questions.question_text: According to Newton's Law of Motion the mass of the object is a quantitative measure of its:
questions.explanation_short: Mass quantifies an object's inertia — its resistance to a change in motion.
questions.explanation_long: Newton's laws define mass as the measure of an object's inertia: the more massive an object, the more it resists acceleration for a given applied force (F=ma).
questions.explanation_trick: Mass = inertia, a core Newtonian definition distinct from weight (a force).

explanation_options.a: Weight is the gravitational force on a mass (F=mg), a related but distinct concept.
explanation_options.b: Correct — mass quantifies inertia.
explanation_options.c: Speed is a kinematic quantity, unrelated to what mass measures.
explanation_options.d: Acceleration results from force acting on mass; it isn't what mass itself measures.

questions.explanation_long: A kilowatt-hour is energy: power (1000 W) multiplied by time (1 hour = 3600 s), giving 3,600,000 J, which is 3.6 megajoules.
questions.explanation_trick: Multiply 1000 (kilo) by 3600 (seconds in an hour) to get 3.6 million joules = 3.6 MJ.

explanation_options.a: 3.6 J is far too small — off by a factor of a million.
explanation_options.b: 3.6 kJ is still far too small — off by a factor of a thousand.
explanation_options.c: Correct — 1 kWh equals 3.6 MJ.
explanation_options.d: 3.6 GJ is a thousand times too large.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a non-conservative force?
questions.explanation_short: Friction is the classic non-conservative force, dissipating energy as heat.
questions.explanation_long: A non-conservative force does work that depends on the path taken and converts mechanical energy into other forms (like heat) — friction is the textbook example, unlike gravity, electric, and (ideal) spring forces, which are conservative.
questions.explanation_trick: Conservative forces (gravity, electric, spring) have associated potential energy; friction does not — energy 'lost' to friction becomes heat, not recoverable PE.

explanation_options.a: Correct — friction is the standard non-conservative force.
explanation_options.b: Electric force (like gravity) is conservative, with an associated potential energy.
explanation_options.c: Ideal elastic spring force is conservative too, with elastic potential energy.
explanation_options.d: Gravitational force is a classic conservative force.

questions.question_text: Work done is equal to:
questions.explanation_short: Work done equals force (effort) multiplied by distance moved.
questions.explanation_long: The basic definition of mechanical work is W = F × d — the force applied times the distance over which it acts (in the direction of the force).
questions.explanation_trick: Work = Force × distance (multiplication), not addition, subtraction, or division.

explanation_options.a: Correct — work equals effort (force) multiplied by distance.
explanation_options.b: Addition doesn't match the physical definition of work.
explanation_options.c: Subtraction doesn't match the definition either.
explanation_options.d: Division would give a completely different (and dimensionally wrong) quantity.

questions.question_text: When a force of 1N displaces its point of application by 1m in the direction of force, the work done is
questions.explanation_short: A 1N force moving its point of application 1m in its own direction does exactly 1 Joule of work.
questions.explanation_long: By the definition W=F×d, a force of 1 Newton acting over a displacement of 1 metre (in the same direction) produces exactly 1 Joule of work — in fact, this is literally how the Joule is defined.
questions.explanation_trick: 1N × 1m = 1J is the textbook definition of the Joule itself.

explanation_options.a: Correct — 1N × 1m = 1J, by definition.
explanation_options.b: 10 J would require either a 10N force or 10m distance, not the 1N/1m given here.
explanation_options.c: 0 J would only result if the force and displacement were perpendicular (no component along each other), which isn't the case here.
explanation_options.d: This option is malformed/incomplete, not a valid numeric answer.

questions.question_text: An electric motor is used to lift the weight of 2.0N through a vertical distance of 100 cm in 4 sec. What is the power output of the motor?
questions.explanation_short: Power = Work/time = (2.0N × 1.0m) / 4s = 0.5 W.
questions.explanation_long: Work done lifting the weight = Force × height = 2.0N × 1.0m = 2.0 J. Power = Work/time = 2.0J / 4s = 0.5 W.
questions.explanation_trick: Convert 100 cm to 1 m first, then apply Power = (Force × distance)/time directly.

explanation_options.a: 0.25 W would result from dividing by 8s instead of the given 4s.
explanation_options.c: 0.75 W doesn't match the straightforward calculation.
explanation_options.d: 1 W would only result from a 2s time or 4N force, not what's given.

questions.question_text: The centripetal acceleration of an object moving along a circle of radius 'r' with an angular speed 'ω' is given by the formula:
questions.explanation_short: Centripetal acceleration is given by a = rω².
questions.explanation_long: For circular motion with angular speed ω and radius r, the centripetal acceleration formula is a = rω² (equivalently a = v²/r, since v=rω).
questions.explanation_trick: Memorize a=rω² — the angular-speed-squared version of centripetal acceleration.

explanation_options.a: Correct — a = rω² is the standard centripetal acceleration formula.
explanation_options.b: a=rω lacks the necessary squaring of ω (this would actually give velocity, v=rω, not acceleration).
explanation_options.c: a=r²ω has the wrong power distribution between r and ω.
explanation_options.d: A=r²ω² also has the wrong power distribution — r shouldn't be squared here.

aliases: The centripetal acceleration of an object moving along a circle of radius 'r' with an angular speed 'w' is given by the formula:
a = rw^2

questions.question_text: An air craft makes a turn in a horizontal circle of radius 100m. It is travelling with a velocity of 250m/sec. The angular velocity of the air craft will be:
questions.explanation_short: Angular velocity ω = v/r = 250/100 = 2.5 rad/s.
questions.explanation_long: For circular motion, angular velocity relates to linear velocity via ω = v/r. Plugging in v=250 m/s and r=100m gives ω = 2.5 rad/s.
questions.explanation_trick: Just divide linear velocity by radius: ω = v/r.

explanation_options.a: 1.5 rad/sec doesn't match dividing 250 by 100.
explanation_options.b: Correct — 250m/s ÷ 100m = 2.5 rad/s.
explanation_options.c: 3 rad/sec is too high for this division.
explanation_options.d: 3.5 rad/sec is also too high.

questions.question_text: A particle of mass 'm' is moving on a circular path of radius 'r' with velocity 'v', then centripetal force acting on it is F. if the velocity of particle increases by 2 times and radius of circular path increases by 4 times then new centripetal force F' will be;
questions.explanation_short: With v doubled and r quadrupled, the centripetal force stays exactly the same: F' = F.
questions.explanation_long: F = mv²/r. Doubling v means v² becomes 4v², and quadrupling r divides by 4 — these effects exactly cancel: F' = m(2v)²/(4r) = 4mv²/4r = mv²/r = F.
questions.explanation_trick: When v² scales up by 4 and r scales up by 4 simultaneously, they cancel out exactly — F stays unchanged.

explanation_options.a: F'=2F would result from only doubling v² alone without also quadrupling r's effect.
explanation_options.b: F'=½F doesn't match the calculation — the two scalings exactly cancel, not leave a net halving.
explanation_options.c: F'=4F doesn't account for the radius increase reducing the force back down.
explanation_options.d: Correct — the 4× increase in v² and the 4× increase in r cancel exactly, leaving F unchanged.

questions.question_text: A roller coaster is moving with 30 m s⁻¹ on a circular track of radius 30m. the net mass of coaster + passengers is 'm' the centripetal force acting on it is;
questions.explanation_short: Centripetal force = mv²/r = m(30²)/30 = 30m.
questions.explanation_long: Plugging v=30 m/s and r=30m into F=mv²/r gives F = m(900)/30 = 30m — the v² and r conveniently simplify to just 30 times the mass.
questions.explanation_trick: F=mv²/r — with v=30 and r=30, this simplifies neatly to 30m (since 30²/30=30).

explanation_options.a: 900m would result from omitting the division by r entirely.
explanation_options.b: 'm' alone would require v²/r to equal 1, which isn't the case here.
explanation_options.c: 450m doesn't match the correct division (900/30=30, not 450/30=15... check: 900/2=450, an arithmetic slip, not the right calculation).
explanation_options.d: Correct — mv²/r = m(900)/30 = 30m.

aliases: A roller coaster is moving with 30 ms-1 on a circular track of radius 30m. the net mass of coaster + passengers is 'm' the centripetal force acting on it is;

questions.question_text: Amplitude in the given wave figure is given as:
questions.explanation_short: Reading directly off the wave graph, the amplitude (peak displacement from the mean line) is 1m.
questions.explanation_long: Amplitude is the maximum displacement from the equilibrium (mean) position, shown on the graph's vertical axis — here the wave peaks at the 1m mark.
questions.explanation_trick: Amplitude = peak height from the centre line, read straight off the y-axis of the wave diagram.

explanation_options.a: 2m would be double the actual peak height shown on the graph.
explanation_options.b: 1/2m undershoots the graph's marked peak value.
explanation_options.c: 1/4m undershoots the peak value even further.
explanation_options.d: Correct — the graph's peak height from the mean line is 1m.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following is INCORRECT about the nodes when the string is plucked;
questions.option_b: Do not move along the string
questions.option_c: Produced at the fixed ends of strings
questions.option_d: Distance between consecutive nodes is 1 wavelength
questions.explanation_short: It's INCORRECT to say the distance between consecutive nodes is one full wavelength — it's actually half a wavelength.
questions.explanation_long: In a stationary (standing) wave, adjacent nodes are separated by half a wavelength (λ/2), not a full wavelength — this is the false statement the question wants identified. Nodes themselves genuinely have zero amplitude, stay fixed, and form at the string's fixed ends.
questions.explanation_trick: Standing wave spacing: node-to-node (or antinode-to-antinode) = λ/2; node-to-adjacent-antinode = λ/4.

explanation_options.a: This IS true — nodes genuinely have zero vibration amplitude.
explanation_options.b: This IS true — nodes are fixed points that don't move along the string.
explanation_options.c: This IS true — nodes form at the fixed ends of a plucked string.
explanation_options.d: Correct — this is the FALSE statement; consecutive nodes are actually λ/2 apart, not a full wavelength.

questions.question_text: In transverse waves the portion above the mean level is called:
questions.explanation_short: The portion of a transverse wave above the mean (equilibrium) level is called the crest.
questions.explanation_long: In a transverse wave, the highest point above the equilibrium line is the crest, while the lowest point below it is the trough.
questions.explanation_trick: Crest = above the line (hump up); trough = below the line (dip down).

explanation_options.a: 'Wave front' refers to a surface of constant phase, not the crest/trough distinction.
explanation_options.b: Correct — the portion above the mean level is the crest.
explanation_options.c: Wave trough is the portion BELOW the mean level, the opposite of what's asked.
explanation_options.d: Wavelength is a distance measurement (one full cycle), not a vertical-position term.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following does not cause stationary waves?
questions.option_d: Two waves travelling in opposite directions
questions.explanation_short: Two waves with unequal amplitudes generally fail to produce a clean, fully-formed stationary wave pattern.
questions.explanation_long: Ideal stationary waves require two waves of equal frequency, equal speed, and equal amplitude travelling in opposite directions, superimposing to create fixed nodes and antinodes. Unequal amplitudes prevent the nodes from having truly zero net displacement, breaking the classic stationary-wave pattern.
questions.explanation_trick: Stationary waves need matched waves in every respect (frequency, speed, amplitude) except direction — unequal amplitude is the one condition that spoils it.

explanation_options.a: Equal frequency IS a required condition for forming stationary waves, not a cause of failure.
explanation_options.b: Same speed IS also a required condition.
explanation_options.c: Correct — unequal amplitude is what prevents proper stationary wave formation.
explanation_options.d: Opposite travel direction IS a required condition for stationary waves to form.

questions.question_text: Select the appropriate Doppler equation when source is approaching the stationary observer where fo is the observed frequency, fs is frequency of source, v is the speed of sound, vs is the speed of source relative to observer
questions.explanation_short: When the source approaches a stationary observer, fo = v/(v-vs) × fs.
questions.explanation_long: As the source moves toward the observer, sound waves bunch up ahead of it, effectively shortening wavelength and raising observed frequency — captured by dividing by (v−vs), which is smaller than v, making fo greater than fs.
questions.explanation_trick: Source approaching → denominator (v−vs), a smaller number → higher observed frequency; source receding uses (v+vs) instead, lowering it.

explanation_options.a: Correct — this is the Doppler formula for an approaching source with a stationary observer.
explanation_options.b: fo=v/(v+vs)fs describes a RECEDING source, not an approaching one.
explanation_options.c: This form doesn't match the standard approaching-source Doppler equation.
explanation_options.d: This more complex form applies to different combined-motion scenarios, not simply an approaching source and stationary observer.

questions.question_text: The distance between two successive particles which are exactly in the same state of vibration is called
questions.explanation_short: The distance between two particles in exactly the same vibration state (phase) is called the wavelength.
questions.explanation_long: Wavelength is defined as the distance over which a wave's shape repeats — equivalently, the distance between two consecutive particles that are in phase (same displacement and velocity direction) at a given instant.
questions.explanation_trick: 'Same state of vibration' = 'same phase' = the defining condition for wavelength.

explanation_options.a: Frequency measures oscillations per second (a time-based rate), not a spatial distance.
explanation_options.b: Amplitude measures maximum displacement, not a distance between particles.
explanation_options.c: Correct — this distance-between-same-phase-particles definition is wavelength.
explanation_options.d: Time period is the time for one oscillation, not a spatial distance.

questions.question_text: During the isothermal process, the temperature
questions.option_a: remains constant during the initial phase of the process
questions.explanation_short: In an isothermal process, temperature stays constant throughout (that's the defining condition).
questions.explanation_long: 'Isothermal' literally means 'same temperature' — by definition, the temperature of the system remains unchanged for the entire duration of the process, even as pressure and volume vary.
questions.explanation_trick: 'Iso-thermal' = constant temperature, by the very name of the process.

explanation_options.a: Temperature staying constant only 'initially' contradicts the whole-process definition of isothermal.
explanation_options.b: Correct — temperature remains constant throughout an isothermal process, by definition.
explanation_options.c: Temperature altering throughout would make the process non-isothermal.
explanation_options.d: Temperature increasing throughout would describe some other thermodynamic process, not isothermal.

questions.question_text: What is the value of heat energy (Q) in an adiabatic process?
questions.explanation_short: In an adiabatic process, no heat is exchanged with the surroundings, so Q = 0.
questions.explanation_long: 'Adiabatic' means no heat transfer occurs into or out of the system during the process (the system is thermally insulated) — so Q, the heat exchanged, is exactly zero by definition.
questions.explanation_trick: Adiabatic = Q=0 (no heat flow); isothermal = ΔT=0 (no temperature change) — keep these two paired definitions separate.

explanation_options.a: Q=+1 implies heat absorbed, contradicting the adiabatic (no heat exchange) condition.
explanation_options.b: Q=-1 implies heat released, also contradicting adiabatic conditions.
explanation_options.c: Correct — Q=0 defines an adiabatic process.
explanation_options.d: Q=+2 again implies nonzero heat exchange, contradicting adiabatic conditions.

questions.question_text: The Coulomb's law states
questions.option_a: Force between two point charges is inversely proportional to the product of the charges and directly proportional to the square of the distance between them
questions.option_b: Force between two point charges is directly proportional to the product of the charges and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them
questions.option_c: Force between two point charges is directly proportional to the sum of the charges and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them
questions.option_d: Force between two point charges is directly proportional to the product of the charges and the square of the distance between them
questions.explanation_short: Coulomb's law: force between two point charges is directly proportional to the product of the charges and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them.
questions.explanation_long: F = kq1q2/r² — the force scales up with the product of the two charge magnitudes and scales down with the square of the separation distance, the two combined proportionalities that define Coulomb's law.
questions.explanation_trick: Coulomb's law needs BOTH proportionalities together: directly with q1×q2, and inversely with r² — a statement missing either half is wrong.

explanation_options.a: This option is incomplete, describing only an inverse relationship without properly pairing it with the direct charge-product proportionality.
explanation_options.b: Correct — combines direct proportionality to the charge product with inverse-square proportionality to distance.
explanation_options.c: This option is incomplete, describing only a direct relationship without the inverse-square distance part.
explanation_options.d: This describes proportionality to the SUM of charges, not their product — an incorrect statement of the law.
