questions.question_text: A virus spreads rapidly in the town, infecting: First day: 8, Second day: 16, Third day: 32. How many people will be infected on the next day?
questions.explanation_short: 64 people will be infected on the next (fourth) day, following the doubling pattern.
questions.explanation_long: The infection pattern doubles each day: Day 1: 8, Day 2: 16, Day 3: 32. Following this doubling pattern, Day 4: 32 × 2 = 64.
questions.explanation_trick: Recognize the pattern as doubling (×2 each day), not simple addition — a common mistake would be adding a fixed increment instead of continuing the multiplicative pattern.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — 44 doesn't fit a doubling (×2) pattern from 32.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — 56 doesn't fit the doubling pattern either.
explanation_options.c: Correct — 32 × 2 = 64, continuing the doubling pattern.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — 74 doesn't fit the doubling pattern from 32.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a result of poor design that could cause an accident in the workplace?
questions.explanation_short: An unplanned workspace layout is a result of poor design that could cause workplace accidents.
questions.explanation_long: 'Poor design' specifically refers to flaws in how something was planned or engineered (like a badly laid-out workspace), as opposed to operational/maintenance issues (equipment failure), physical hazards from wear (slippery surfaces), or environmental factors (insufficient lighting), which stem from other root causes.
questions.explanation_trick: Distinguish DESIGN flaws (planning/layout issues, built in from the start) from OPERATIONAL/maintenance hazards (things that develop or are situational, like spills or bulb failures) — the question specifically asks about a design-originated cause.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — equipment failure is typically a maintenance/mechanical issue, not a design flaw.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — slippery surfaces are usually a situational/maintenance hazard, not primarily a design issue.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — insufficient lighting is more of a maintenance/facilities issue than a workspace 'design' flaw per se.
explanation_options.d: Correct — an unplanned workspace layout is directly a result of poor design.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is the main cause of accidents involving equipment?
questions.explanation_short: Insufficient maintenance is the main cause of equipment-related accidents.
questions.explanation_long: Equipment accidents most commonly result from a lack of proper upkeep — insufficient maintenance leads to worn parts, malfunctions, and failures, distinguishing it from human-factor causes like overconfidence, fatigue, or poor training, which relate more to operator behavior than the equipment's own condition.
questions.explanation_trick: The question specifically asks about causes tied to the EQUIPMENT itself, not the operator — 'insufficient maintenance' addresses equipment condition directly, while overconfidence/fatigue/training are human-factor causes.

explanation_options.a: Wrong — overconfidence is a human/behavioral factor, not directly about equipment condition.
explanation_options.b: Correct — insufficient maintenance directly causes equipment malfunctions/accidents.
explanation_options.c: Wrong — fatigue is a human factor, not an equipment-condition cause.
explanation_options.d: Wrong — poor training is a human/operator factor, not an equipment-condition cause.

questions.question_text: Asad bought 50 packets of biscuits for Rs. 500, while Anum bought 25 packets of chips for Rs. 1000. Which statement correctly compares the prices?
questions.option_a: Price of 4 packets of biscuits is equal to the price of 1 packet of chips
questions.option_b: Price of 1 packet of biscuits is equal to the price of 4 packets of chips
questions.option_c: Price of 2 packets of biscuits is equal to the price of 1 packet of chips
questions.option_d: Price of 1 packet of biscuits is equal to the price of 2 packets of chips
questions.explanation_short: Price of 4 packets of biscuits equals the price of 1 packet of chips.
questions.explanation_long: Biscuits: 50 packets for Rs.500 → Rs.10 per packet. Chips: 25 packets for Rs.1000 → Rs.40 per packet. Since Rs.40 ÷ Rs.10 = 4, one packet of chips costs the same as 4 packets of biscuits.
questions.explanation_trick: Always reduce to a per-unit (per-packet) price first before comparing — mixing up which item is more expensive per unit is the easy way to pick the wrong ratio direction.

explanation_options.a: Correct — 4 × Rs.10 (biscuits) = Rs.40 = price of 1 packet of chips.
explanation_options.b: Wrong — this reverses the ratio; 1 biscuit packet (Rs.10) is NOT equal to 4 chip packets (4×Rs.40=Rs.160).
explanation_options.c: Wrong — 2 biscuit packets (Rs.20) don't equal 1 chip packet (Rs.40).
explanation_options.d: Wrong — 1 biscuit packet (Rs.10) doesn't equal 2 chip packets (Rs.80).
